### The Lorentz group {#sec-sr-lorentz-group}

The second step of the construction defines the group in four dimensions. Its definition is the condition that the
Minkowski form be preserved, exactly as the orthogonal group is defined by the Euclidean one (@prp-minkowski-values gives
the values of the form).

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-sr-lorentz-group}
#### Lorentz group

The **Lorentz group** is $O(1, 3) = \{\Lambda \in GL(4, \mathbb{R}) : \Lambda^T\eta\Lambda = \eta\}$, in components $\eta_{\alpha\beta}\Lambda^\alpha{}_\mu\Lambda^\beta{}_\nu = \eta_{\mu\nu}$. Its elements are
**proper** if $\det\Lambda = 1$ and **orthochronous** if $\Lambda^0{}_0 > 0$; the proper orthochronous ones form $SO^+(1, 3)$. **Parity** and **time
reversal** are $P = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1)$ and $T = \operatorname{diag}(-1, 1, 1, 1)$, and the **rotations** are the matrices $\operatorname{diag}(1, R)$ with
$R \in SO(3)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
![The four components of the Lorentz group. Two thousand products of random boosts, rotations and the reflections $P$, $T$
are plotted by $\det\Lambda$ (horizontal, jittered) and $\Lambda^0{}_0$ (vertical, clipped at $\pm5$): they fall into four clusters, and
none enters the shaded band $|\Lambda^0{}_0| < 1$. Generated by `figures/sr-components.sage`.](figures/sr-components.svg){#fig-sr-components width=60%}

Rotations of space leave time alone and preserve $|\vec x|^2$. The first example confirms that they are Lorentz
transformations, so that $SO(3)$ is a subgroup of $SO^+(1, 3)$.

::: {#exm-sr-lg-rotations}
#### Rotations

For $\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(1, R)$, $\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(1, -R^TR) = \eta$ exactly when $R^TR = 1$. For $R \in SO(3)$, $\det\Lambda = 1$ and $\Lambda^0{}_0 = 1$, so the
rotations lie in $SO^+(1, 3)$; for $R = -1$ one gets $P$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Boosts in any direction are the other basic elements. The second example records the matrix of @exr-sr-general-boost in
its active form.

::: {#exm-sr-lg-boosts}
#### Boosts in any direction

For $|\vec v| < 1$ the active boost
$$
B(\vec v) = \begin{pmatrix}\gamma & \gamma\vec v^T \\ \gamma\vec v & 1 + (\gamma - 1)\hat v\hat v^T\end{pmatrix}
$$ {#eq-sr-boost-matrix}
satisfies $B^T\eta B = \eta$ (@exr-sr-general-boost, where the passive version $B(-\vec v)$ was checked), has $\det B = 1$ and $B^0{}_0 = \gamma \geq 1$, and sends the
rest vector $e_0$ to the four-velocity $\gamma(1, \vec v)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The discrete transformations complete the list of basic elements. The third example notes that $PT = -1$ is central and
reverses every four-vector.

::: {#exm-sr-lg-discrete}
#### Parity, time reversal and their product

$P$, $T$ and $PT = -1$ preserve $\eta$ because they are diagonal with entries $\pm1$. $P$ reverses spatial vectors and keeps $t$, $T$ reverses $t$, and
$PT$ sends every four-vector to its negative, commuting with all of $O(1, 3)$. Of the three only $PT$ is proper, and none is
orthochronous except $P$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise repeats the group axioms in four dimensions and finds the inverse without inverting a matrix. The formula for the inverse avoids any matrix inversion and is used constantly.

::: {#exr-sr-lg-inverse}
#### The inverse of a Lorentz matrix

Show that $O(1, 3)$ is a subgroup of $GL(4, \mathbb{R})$, that $\Lambda^{-1} = \eta\Lambda^T\eta$, and that $\Lambda^T \in O(1, 3)$ whenever $\Lambda$ is.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
As in @exr-sr-o11-group: $(\Lambda_1\Lambda_2)^T\eta\Lambda_1\Lambda_2 = \Lambda_2^T\eta\Lambda_2 = \eta$, $\eta^2 = 1$ gives $(\eta\Lambda^T\eta)\Lambda = 1$, and then $\Lambda\eta\Lambda^T = \eta$. In components,
$(\Lambda^{-1})^\mu{}_\nu = \eta^{\mu\alpha}\Lambda^\beta{}_\alpha\eta_{\beta\nu} = \Lambda_\nu{}^\mu$, the identity of @exm-sr-lowered-lambda.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The columns of a Lorentz matrix are the images of the frame vectors. The second exercise shows that they form a new
inertial frame, possibly with reversed time or orientation.

::: {#exr-sr-lg-columns}
#### Columns form an orthonormal frame

Show that $\Lambda \in O(1, 3)$ if and only if its columns $\Lambda e_\mu$ satisfy $(\Lambda e_\mu)\cdot(\Lambda e_\nu) = \eta_{\mu\nu}$, and the same for its rows with $\eta$
inserted. Check it for $B(\vec v)R$ with $\vec v = (0.6, 0, 0)$ and $R$ the rotation by $\pi/2$ about $z$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda)_{\mu\nu} = (\Lambda e_\mu)\cdot(\Lambda e_\nu)$, so the condition is the orthonormality of the columns; for rows apply it to $\Lambda^T \in O(1, 3)$
(@exr-sr-lg-inverse). The product has columns $(1.25, 0.75, 0, 0)$, $(0, 0, 1, 0)$, $(-0.75, -1.25, 0, 0)$, $(0, 0, 0, 1)$, which are
orthonormal:

{{< sage exr-sr-lg-columns >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Lorentz group is not compact, unlike $O(4)$. The third exercise exhibits unbounded sequences of elements. Compactness is what distinguishes the representation theory of the two groups, as @sec-sr-wigner-classification will show.

::: {#exr-sr-lg-noncompact}
#### The Lorentz group is not compact

Show that $\{B(\tanh n\,\hat x) : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$ has no convergent subsequence in $GL(4, \mathbb{R})$, and conclude that $O(1, 3)$ is not compact. Why is $O(4)$
compact?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$B^0{}_0 = \cosh n \to \infty$, so no subsequence is bounded, let alone convergent. A compact subset of the matrices is bounded. $O(4)$
is closed and bounded, since $\Lambda^T\Lambda = 1$ forces every entry to have modulus at most $1$; $O(1, 3)$ is closed but not bounded, because
$\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda = \eta$ only controls the differences $(\Lambda^0{}_0)^2 - \sum_i(\Lambda^i{}_0)^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

Being a group is not yet being a Lie group. The theorem below shows that $O(1, 3)$ is a smooth submanifold of the
matrices, of dimension six, with an explicit tangent space at the identity; the proof uses the regular value theorem
rather than the general closed-subgroup theorem quoted in @def-matrix-lie-group.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-sr-lorentz-lie}
#### The Lorentz group is a Lie group

$O(1, 3)$ is a closed subgroup of $GL(4, \mathbb{R})$ and a submanifold of dimension $6$; it is a matrix Lie group (@def-matrix-lie-group) whose Lie
algebra (@def-lie-algebra-of-group) is
$$
\mathfrak{so}(1, 3) = \{X \in \mathfrak{gl}(4, \mathbb{R}) : X^T\eta + \eta X = 0\} = \{X : \eta X \text{ is antisymmetric}\} .
$$ {#eq-sr-lorentz-algebra}

*Proof.* Let $\mathrm{Sym}$ be the $10$-dimensional space of symmetric $4 \times 4$ matrices and $F : GL(4, \mathbb{R}) \to \mathrm{Sym}$, $F(\Lambda) = \Lambda^T\eta\Lambda$. $F$ is
continuous, so $O(1, 3) = F^{-1}(\eta)$ is closed. Its derivative at $\Lambda$ is $dF_\Lambda(X) = X^T\eta\Lambda + \Lambda^T\eta X$. For $\Lambda \in O(1, 3)$ and any $S \in \mathrm{Sym}$, the
matrix $X = \tfrac12\Lambda\eta S$ gives $\Lambda^T\eta X = \tfrac12\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda\eta S = \tfrac12S$ and $X^T\eta\Lambda = (\Lambda^T\eta X)^T = \tfrac12S$, so $dF_\Lambda(X) = S$: $dF_\Lambda$ is surjective at every point of
$F^{-1}(\eta)$. By the regular value theorem $O(1, 3)$ is a submanifold of dimension $16 - 10 = 6$, with tangent space $\ker dF_\Lambda$; at $\Lambda = 1$
this is $\{X : X^T\eta + \eta X = 0\}$. Multiplication and inversion are restrictions of the smooth operations of $GL(4, \mathbb{R})$, so $O(1, 3)$ is a Lie
group. Finally, if $X^T\eta + \eta X = 0$ then $\frac{d}{dt}(e^{tX})^T\eta e^{tX} = (e^{tX})^T(X^T\eta + \eta X)e^{tX} = 0$, so $e^{tX} \in O(1, 3)$ for all $t$, and conversely
differentiating $(e^{tX})^T\eta e^{tX} = \eta$ at $t = 0$ gives the condition: the tangent space is the Lie algebra of @def-lie-algebra-of-group.
$X^T\eta + \eta X = 0$ says $(\eta X)^T = -\eta X$. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The dimension can be read off the Lie algebra. The first example counts the free entries and names them. The count agrees with the dimension found in the theorem.

::: {#exm-sr-lie-count}
#### Six parameters

$\eta X = A$ antisymmetric means $X = \eta A$, and antisymmetric $4 \times 4$ matrices have $6$ entries: three in the block $A_{ij}$ and three in
$A_{0i}$. In terms of an infinitesimal transformation $\Lambda = 1 + \omega$ with $\omega^\mu{}_\nu$ small, the condition is $\omega_{\mu\nu} = -\omega_{\nu\mu}$
[@maggiore2023electrodynamics, eq. (7.86)]: three rotation angles $\omega_{ij}$ and three rapidities $\omega_{0i}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A basis of the Lie algebra is chosen once for the whole chapter. The second example writes it down, with the sign
convention of @sec-conventions-lie for rotations.

::: {#exm-sr-lie-basis}
#### Rotation and boost generators

Let $(J_i)^j{}_k = -\epsilon_{ijk}$ with all other entries zero, so that $J_3$ has $(J_3)^1{}_2 = -1$, $(J_3)^2{}_1 = 1$, and let $K_i$ have $(K_i)^0{}_i = (K_i)^i{}_0 = 1$
and all other entries zero. Then $\eta J_i$ and $\eta K_i$ are antisymmetric, so the six matrices lie in $\mathfrak{so}(1, 3)$, and they are independent.
$e^{\theta J_3}$ is the rotation by $\theta$ about $z$ (counterclockwise, active) and $e^{\eta K_1} = B(\tanh\eta\,\hat x)$ is the active boost along $x$. With
$(M^{\mu\nu})^\alpha{}_\beta = \eta^{\mu\alpha}\delta^\nu_\beta - \eta^{\nu\alpha}\delta^\mu_\beta$, $J_i = \tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}M^{jk}$ and $K_i = M^{0i}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

Every element of the Lie algebra generates a one-parameter subgroup. The third example exponentiates a combination of a
boost and a rotation about the same axis.

::: {#exm-sr-lie-loxodromic}
#### A boost and a rotation about one axis

$K_3$ and $J_3$ commute, since $K_3$ acts on $(t, z)$ and $J_3$ on $(x, y)$. Hence $e^{\eta K_3 + \theta J_3} = e^{\eta K_3}e^{\theta J_3}$, a boost along $z$ and a rotation about
$z$, for all $\eta$, $\theta$: a one-parameter subgroup in which the observer spins while it accelerates. Such elements are called
**loxodromic**.
:::

The identity follows from $\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda\eta = \eta\eta = 1$ as in the proof; the computation confirms it exactly with rational entries $\gamma = 2/\sqrt3$:

The tangent space at a point other than the identity is a translate of the Lie algebra. The second exercise proves it.

::: {#exr-sr-tangent-translate}
#### Tangent spaces are translates

Show that the tangent space of $O(1, 3)$ at $\Lambda$ is $\{\Lambda X : X \in \mathfrak{so}(1, 3)\}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$dF_\Lambda(\Lambda X) = X^T\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda + \Lambda^T\eta\Lambda X = X^T\eta + \eta X$, which vanishes exactly when $X \in \mathfrak{so}(1, 3)$. Since left multiplication by $\Lambda$ is a linear
isomorphism, $\ker dF_\Lambda = \Lambda\,\mathfrak{so}(1, 3)$, of dimension $6$.
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

The same proof works for every signature. The third exercise computes the dimension of $O(p, q)$ and its relation to
the rotation groups.

::: {#exr-sr-opq-dimension}
#### The groups $O(p, q)$

Adapt the proof to $O(p, q) = \{\Lambda : \Lambda^T\eta_{p,q}\Lambda = \eta_{p,q}\}$ with $\eta_{p,q} = \operatorname{diag}(1_p, -1_q)$, and show that its dimension is $n(n - 1)/2$ with $n = p + q$,
the same as $O(n)$. What are the dimensions of $O(1, 4)$, the Lorentz group of five-dimensional Minkowski space, and of $O(2, 3)$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Only $\eta^2 = 1$ was used, so the proof applies verbatim: the dimension is $n^2 - n(n + 1)/2 = n(n - 1)/2$, and the Lie algebra is
$\{X : \eta_{p,q}X \text{ antisymmetric}\}$. For $n = 5$ all of $O(5)$, $O(1, 4)$ and $O(2, 3)$ have dimension $10$; $O(1, 4)$ is both the Lorentz group of
five-dimensional Minkowski space and the isometry group of four-dimensional de Sitter space, and $O(2, 3)$ that of anti-de
Sitter space.
:::

The defining condition constrains the determinant and the time component. The proposition below gives the two facts
that the classification of components needs [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Sec. 7.3.1].

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sr-det-lambda}
#### Determinant and time component

For every $\Lambda \in O(1, 3)$, $\det\Lambda = \pm1$ and
$$
(\Lambda^0{}_0)^2 = 1 + \sum_{i=1}^3(\Lambda^i{}_0)^2 = 1 + \sum_{i=1}^3(\Lambda^0{}_i)^2 \geq 1 ,
$$
so either $\Lambda^0{}_0 \geq 1$ or $\Lambda^0{}_0 \leq -1$.

*Proof.* Taking determinants in $\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda = \eta$ gives $(\det\Lambda)^2\det\eta = \det\eta$, and $\det\eta = -1 \neq 0$, so $(\det\Lambda)^2 = 1$. The $(0, 0)$ entry of
$\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda = \eta$ is $(\Lambda^0{}_0)^2 - \sum_i(\Lambda^i{}_0)^2 = 1$: the first column $\Lambda e_0$ is a unit vector. Since $\Lambda^T \in O(1, 3)$ (@exr-sr-lg-inverse), the same
applied to $\Lambda^T$ gives $(\Lambda^0{}_0)^2 - \sum_i(\Lambda^0{}_i)^2 = 1$. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The time component has a physical meaning. The first example identifies it with a Lorentz factor. The interpretation explains why the bound $|\Lambda^0{}_0| \geq 1$ is the relativistic statement that speeds stay below that of light.

::: {#exm-sr-lambda00-gamma}
#### $\Lambda^0{}_0$ is a Lorentz factor

$\Lambda e_0$ is the four-velocity of the observer obtained by moving an observer at rest with $\Lambda$, up to sign, and $\Lambda^0{}_0 = e_0\cdot\Lambda e_0$
is the Lorentz factor of the relative motion when $\Lambda$ is orthochronous (@exm-sr-gamma-bound). For $B(\vec v)$ it is $\gamma$; for a rotation it is $1$; for
$T$ it is $-1$: the image of the rest vector is past-directed.
:::

The two conditions are necessary but far from sufficient. The second example shows a matrix that satisfies both and is
not a Lorentz transformation.

::: {#exm-sr-lambda00-not-sufficient}
#### Necessary, not sufficient

$\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(1, 2, 1/2, 1)$ has determinant $1$ and $\Lambda^0{}_0 = 1$, with $\Lambda^i{}_0 = 0$, but $\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(1, -4, -1/4, -1) \neq \eta$: it is not in
$O(1, 3)$. The full condition is ten equations, of which the proposition uses one and the determinant.
:::

two equal sums for a composite transformation.

For $\Lambda = B(0.6\hat x)R_z(\pi/2)$ of @exr-sr-lg-columns, $\Lambda^0{}_0 = 1.25$, the first column $(1.25, 0.75, 0, 0)$ has $\sum_i(\Lambda^i{}_0)^2 = 0.5625$ and the
first row $(1.25, 0, -0.75, 0)$ has $\sum_i(\Lambda^0{}_i)^2 = 0.5625$; both equal $1.25^2 - 1$. The column and the row point in different spatial
directions, $\hat x$ and $-\hat y$, because of the rotation.

When $|\Lambda^0{}_0| = 1$ the matrix leaves the time axis alone. The first exercise proves that it is then a rotation, possibly composed
with $P$ or $T$.

::: {#exr-sr-lambda00-one}
#### When the time component is $\pm1$

Show that if $\Lambda \in O(1, 3)$ has $\Lambda^0{}_0 = \pm1$, then $\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(\pm1, R)$ with $R \in O(3)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By the proposition, $\sum_i(\Lambda^i{}_0)^2 = \sum_i(\Lambda^0{}_i)^2 = 0$, so the first row and column vanish off the diagonal. The remaining $3 \times 3$ block $R$
satisfies $-R^TR = -1$, so $R \in O(3)$.
:::

The bound $\Lambda^0{}_0 \geq 1$ for an orthochronous matrix is a special case of the reverse Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. The second
exercise derives it so.

::: {#exr-sr-lambda00-cs}
#### The bound from the reverse Cauchy-Schwarz inequality

Show that if $\Lambda$ is orthochronous then $\Lambda e_0$ is a future-directed unit timelike vector, and derive $\Lambda^0{}_0 \geq 1$ from
@prp-sr-reverse-inequalities.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\Lambda e_0\cdot\Lambda e_0 = e_0\cdot e_0 = 1$ and its time component $\Lambda^0{}_0$ is positive, so $\Lambda e_0$ is a unit future timelike vector. Then $\Lambda^0{}_0 = e_0\cdot\Lambda e_0 \geq
|e_0||\Lambda e_0| = 1$ by part 4 of @prp-sr-reverse-inequalities, with equality exactly when $\Lambda e_0 = e_0$.
:::

The discrete invariants $\det\Lambda$ and $\operatorname{sign}\Lambda^0{}_0$ cannot change along a continuous path of Lorentz matrices. The theorem below
shows that they are the only obstruction: the Lorentz group has exactly four connected components, as $O(1, 1)$ had in
@prp-sr-o11. The proof of connectedness constructs the boost that carries the rest vector to a given four-velocity.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-sr-four-components}
#### The four components of the Lorentz group

The map $\sigma(\Lambda) = (\det\Lambda, \operatorname{sign}\Lambda^0{}_0)$ is a continuous surjective homomorphism $O(1, 3) \to \{\pm1\} \times \{\pm1\}$, and its four fibres
$$
L^\uparrow_+ = SO^+(1, 3), \qquad L^\uparrow_- = P\,SO^+(1, 3), \qquad L^\downarrow_- = T\,SO^+(1, 3), \qquad L^\downarrow_+ = PT\,SO^+(1, 3)
$$
are the connected components of $O(1, 3)$. $SO^+(1, 3)$ is the identity component, a normal subgroup, and $O(1, 3)/SO^+(1, 3) \cong \mathbb{Z}_2 \times
\mathbb{Z}_2$.

*Proof.* *Homomorphism.* The determinant is multiplicative. For the sign, $(\Lambda\Lambda')^0{}_0 = \Lambda^0{}_0\Lambda'^0{}_0 + \sum_i\Lambda^0{}_i\Lambda'^i{}_0$, and by the
Cauchy-Schwarz inequality in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and @prp-sr-det-lambda,
$$
\Bigl|\sum_i\Lambda^0{}_i\Lambda'^i{}_0\Bigr| \leq \sqrt{(\Lambda^0{}_0)^2 - 1}\sqrt{(\Lambda'^0{}_0)^2 - 1} < |\Lambda^0{}_0||\Lambda'^0{}_0| ,
$$
so $(\Lambda\Lambda')^0{}_0$ has the sign of $\Lambda^0{}_0\Lambda'^0{}_0$. *Continuity and surjectivity.* $\det$ and $\Lambda^0{}_0$ are continuous and take values in $\{\pm1\}$
and $(-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)$, so $\sigma$ is locally constant; $\sigma(1) = (1, 1)$, $\sigma(P) = (-1, 1)$, $\sigma(T) = (-1, -1)$, $\sigma(PT) = (1, -1)$. Hence the four fibres
are non-empty, open and closed, and no connected set meets two of them; since $\sigma$ is a homomorphism with kernel $SO^+(1, 3)$, the fibres
are the cosets listed. *Connectedness of $SO^+(1, 3)$.* Let $\Lambda \in SO^+(1, 3)$ and $u = \Lambda e_0 = \gamma(1, \vec v)$, a unit future timelike vector
(@exr-sr-lambda00-cs). The boost $B(\vec v)$ of @eq-sr-boost-matrix has $B(\vec v)e_0 = u$, so $R = B(\vec v)^{-1}\Lambda$ fixes $e_0$; by @exr-sr-lambda00-one, $R = \operatorname{diag}(1,
R_3)$ with $R_3 \in O(3)$, and $\det R_3 = \det\Lambda/\det B = 1$. The path $s \mapsto B(\tanh(s\eta)\hat v)\exp(sA)$, $s \in [0, 1]$, where $\eta = \operatorname{artanh}|\vec v|$
and $A$ is an antisymmetric matrix with $e^A = R_3$ (every rotation is a rotation by some angle about some axis, @prp-rotation-subgroup),
joins $1$ to $\Lambda$ inside $SO^+(1, 3)$. So $SO^+(1, 3)$ is path-connected, and each coset, its image under a homeomorphism $\Lambda \mapsto D\Lambda$, is
connected. The quotient by the kernel is the image $\{\pm1\} \times \{\pm1\}$. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Each component has a physical meaning. The first example lists representatives and the transformations of physics in
each. The table connects the abstract components with symmetries that physics tests.

::: {#exm-sr-components-table}
#### The components and their physics

$L^\uparrow_+$ contains the rotations and boosts, the transformations between observers that can be realised physically. $L^\uparrow_-$
contains $P$ and the reflections in one plane, $\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, 1, 1) = P\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -1, -1)$; $L^\downarrow_-$ contains $T$; $L^\downarrow_+$ contains $PT = -1$.
The weak interaction is not invariant under $P$, and the $CPT$ theorem of quantum field theory states that $PT$ together with
charge conjugation is always a symmetry.
:::

Subgroups of the Lorentz group that contain $SO^+(1, 3)$ correspond to subgroups of the quotient. The third example lists

::: {#exm-sr-components-subgroups}
#### Groups between $SO^+(1, 3)$ and $O(1, 3)$

The subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$ are the trivial one, the three of order two and the whole group, so the subgroups of $O(1, 3)$ containing
$SO^+(1, 3)$ are $SO^+(1, 3)$, the proper group $SO(1, 3) = L^\uparrow_+ \cup L^\downarrow_+$, the orthochronous group $O^\uparrow(1, 3) = L^\uparrow_+ \cup L^\uparrow_-$, the group
$L^\uparrow_+ \cup L^\downarrow_-$ generated by $T$, and $O(1, 3)$.

The theorem says no continuous family of Lorentz transformations connects the identity to a reflection. The second

#### No path from the identity to parity

Show directly that there is no continuous path $\Lambda(s)$ in $O(1, 3)$ with $\Lambda(0) = 1$ and $\Lambda(1) = P$, and that there is one with $\Lambda(0) = 1$ and $\Lambda(1) =

by $\pi$ about $z$, joined to $1$ by $R_z(s\pi)$.

The three non-identity components are cosets, but they can be written with any representative. The third exercise
shows that a reflection in a single plane can replace $P$.

::: {#exr-sr-plane-reflection}
#### Any reflection will do

Show that $L^\uparrow_- = M\,SO^+(1, 3)$ for $M = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, 1, 1)$, and that $M$ and $P$ are conjugate in $O(1, 3)$ only up to a rotation: $P = M R_x(\pi)$.

$MR_x(\pi) = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1) = P$.

### The polar decomposition

The proof of the theorem split a proper orthochronous transformation into a boost and a rotation. This third step makes
that splitting precise and unique, after characterising the boosts among all Lorentz transformations.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-sr-pure-boost}
#### Pure boost

A **pure boost** is a matrix $B(\vec v)$ of @eq-sr-boost-matrix, for some $|\vec v| < 1$; equivalently, for the unit future timelike vector $u =
\gamma(1, \vec v)$, the element $B_u$ of $SO^+(1, 3)$ that sends $e_0$ to $u$ and acts as the identity on the vectors orthogonal to both $e_0$
and $u$. The pure boosts are exactly the elements of $SO^+(1, 3)$ that are symmetric and positive definite as real matrices
(@exr-sr-symmetric-boost).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
![The polar decomposition along the one-parameter subgroup $\Lambda(s) = \exp(s(K_1 + J_3))$. Left: the rapidity $\operatorname{arcosh}\Lambda^0{}_0$ of its
boost part and the angle of its rotation part. Right: the spatial direction $\vec v/|\vec v|$ of the boost part, which turns as $s$
grows because boosts and rotations do not commute. Generated by `figures/sr-polar.sage`.](figures/sr-polar.svg){#fig-sr-polar width=90%}

A pure boost is determined by the four-velocity it produces. The first example checks this and finds the inverse. Both facts follow from the form of the first column.

::: {#exm-sr-pure-boost-inverse}
#### The image of the rest vector determines the boost

$B(\vec v)e_0 = \gamma(1, \vec v) = u$, the first column, so two pure boosts with the same image of $e_0$ have the same velocity and are equal.
The inverse is $B(\vec v)^{-1} = \eta B(\vec v)^T\eta = \eta B(\vec v)\eta$ (@exr-sr-lg-inverse), which changes the sign of the mixed entries $\gamma\vec v$
and keeps the others: $B(\vec v)^{-1} = B(-\vec v)$, the pure boost that brings $u$ back to $e_0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A pure boost has a simple spectrum. The second example computes it: the eigenvalues are the Doppler factors along the
boost and $1$ across it.

::: {#exm-sr-pure-boost-spectrum}
#### Eigenvalues of a pure boost

$B(\vec v)$ acts as $L(\eta)$ in the plane of $e_0$ and $\hat v$ and as the identity on the two directions perpendicular to $\hat v$. Its eigenvalues are
$e^\eta$, $e^{-\eta}$ (eigenvectors $(1, \pm\hat v)$, the light rays along $\pm\hat v$) and $1$, $1$. As a symmetric matrix with positive eigenvalues it is
**positive definite** in the Euclidean sense, which is the property used in the polar decomposition.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Pure boosts are exponentials of boost generators. The third example identifies the generator. The generator is a unit combination of the $K_i$ along the velocity, scaled by the rapidity, and the series can be summed in closed form.

::: {#exm-sr-pure-boost-exp}
#### A pure boost is an exponential

With $\hat n = \hat v$ and $\eta = \operatorname{artanh}|\vec v|$, $B(\vec v) = \exp(\eta\,\hat n\cdot\vec K)$, where $\hat n\cdot\vec K = \sum_in_iK_i$. Indeed $N = \hat n\cdot\vec K$ has $N^3 = N$, so
$e^{\eta N} = 1 + N\sinh\eta + N^2(\cosh\eta - 1)$, whose entries are those of @eq-sr-boost-matrix with $\gamma = \cosh\eta$, $\gamma|\vec v| = \sinh\eta$
(@exr-sr-boost-exp).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The characterisation of pure boosts by symmetry is the bridge to linear algebra. The first exercise proves it. Symmetry alone is not enough, and the exercise also finds the counterexample.

::: {#exr-sr-symmetric-boost}
#### Pure boosts are the symmetric elements

Show that a symmetric, positive definite $\Lambda \in SO^+(1, 3)$ is a pure boost, and that the rotation by $\pi$ about the $z$-axis is symmetric
but not a pure boost.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Let $u = \Lambda e_0 = \gamma(1, \vec v)$ and $R = B(\vec v)^{-1}\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(1, R_3)$ as in the proof of @thm-sr-four-components, so that $\Lambda = BR$. With
$M = 1 + (\gamma - 1)\hat v\hat v^T$, the blocks of $\Lambda$ are $\Lambda^0{}_i = \gamma(R_3^T\vec v)_i$, $\Lambda^i{}_0 = \gamma v^i$ and $MR_3$. Symmetry gives $R_3^T\vec v = \vec v$, so $R_3$
fixes $\hat v$ and commutes with $M$, and $MR_3 = (MR_3)^T = R_3^TM$ gives $R_3 = R_3^T$, that is $R_3^2 = 1$: $R_3$ is the identity or a rotation by $\pi$ about
an axis (about $\hat v$ if $\vec v \neq 0$). In the second case a spatial vector $w \perp \hat v$ with $R_3w = -w$ gives $\Lambda(0, w) = B(0, -w) = (0, -w)$,
an eigenvalue $-1$, so $\Lambda$ is not positive definite. Hence $R_3 = 1$ and $\Lambda = B$. The rotation $\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, 1)$ is symmetric with
eigenvalues $1, -1, -1, 1$: symmetric but not positive definite.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

Conjugating a boost by a rotation turns its direction. The second exercise proves the formula used in the Wigner
rotation.

::: {#exr-sr-boost-conjugate}
#### Rotating a boost

Show that $RB(\vec v)R^{-1} = B(R\vec v)$ for every rotation $R = \operatorname{diag}(1, R_3)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$RB(\vec v)R^{-1}$ is in $SO^+(1, 3)$, symmetric and positive definite (conjugation by the orthogonal matrix $R = (R^T)^{-1}$ keeps
both properties) and sends $e_0$ to $RB(\vec v)e_0 = R\gamma(1, \vec v) = \gamma(1, R_3\vec v)$. By
@exr-sr-symmetric-boost it is a pure boost, and by @exm-sr-pure-boost-inverse it is the one with velocity $R_3\vec v$. Directly: $R_3\hat v\hat v^TR_3^T =
(R_3\hat v)(R_3\hat v)^T$ in @eq-sr-boost-matrix.
:::

$N = \cos\phi K_1 + \sin\phi K_2$ satisfies $N^3 = N$, and the exponential series sums to $1 + N\sinh\eta + N^2(\cosh\eta - 1)$, which matches @eq-sr-boost-matrix
entry by entry:

{{< sage exr-sr-boost-exp >}}

The theorem below is the Lorentzian version of the polar decomposition of an invertible matrix into a positive definite
symmetric matrix and an orthogonal one. Its existence part was the heart of the proof of @thm-sr-four-components; the new
content is uniqueness and the formula for the boost.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-sr-polar}
#### Polar decomposition of a Lorentz transformation

Every $\Lambda \in SO^+(1, 3)$ can be written uniquely as $\Lambda = BR$ with $B$ a pure boost and $R = \operatorname{diag}(1, R_3)$, $R_3 \in SO(3)$, and uniquely as $\Lambda =
R'B'$ in the opposite order; then $R' = R$, $B' = R^{-1}BR$, $B = B_{\Lambda e_0}$, and $B$ is the unique positive definite symmetric square root of $\Lambda\Lambda^T$.

*Proof.* *Existence:* $B = B_u$ with $u = \Lambda e_0$ and $R = B^{-1}\Lambda$, as in the proof of @thm-sr-four-components. *Uniqueness:* if $B_1R_1 = B_2R_2$, then
$B_1e_0 = B_1R_1e_0 = B_2R_2e_0 = B_2e_0$, since rotations fix $e_0$; a pure boost is determined by the image of $e_0$ (@exm-sr-pure-boost-inverse), so $B_1 =
B_2$ and then $R_1 = R_2$. *Other order:* $\Lambda = BR = R(R^{-1}BR)$ and $R^{-1}BR$ is a pure boost (@exr-sr-boost-conjugate); uniqueness of $\Lambda = R'B'$
follows from that of $\Lambda^{-1} = B'^{-1}R'^{-1}$, which is of the first form. *Square root:* $\Lambda\Lambda^T = BRR^TB^T = B^2$, because $R^T = R^{-1}$ and $B^T = B$;
$B$ is symmetric and positive definite (@exm-sr-pure-boost-spectrum), and a positive definite symmetric matrix has exactly one positive
definite symmetric square root (diagonalise it in an orthonormal basis and take positive roots of the eigenvalues). $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For a single boost the decomposition is trivial; it becomes informative for products. The first example decomposes a
transformation given as a rotation followed by a boost along a different axis.

::: {#exm-sr-polar-numbers}
#### A decomposition in numbers

$\Lambda = R_z(\pi/2)B(0.6\hat x)$ is a boost along $x$ followed by a rotation. Its polar decomposition $\Lambda = BR$ has $B = R_z(\pi/2)B(0.6\hat x)R_z(\pi/2)^{-1} =
B(0.6\hat y)$ and $R = R_z(\pi/2)$: $\Lambda e_0 = (1.25, 0, 0.75, 0)$ is the velocity $0.6\hat y$, as the formula $B = B_{\Lambda e_0}$ says.
:::

$\Lambda = B(0.7\hat y)B(0.6\hat x)$ has $\Lambda e_0 = (1.75, 0.75, 1.225, 0)$ (to three decimals), so its boost part has velocity $(0.429, 0.700, 0)$ of
magnitude $0.821$; its rotation part is a rotation about $z$ by $0.271\,$rad, the Wigner rotation of @thm-sr-wigner-angle. A product of two
boosts is not a boost.

The square-root formula works for any element. The third example applies it to a rotation, where it gives the trivial
boost.

::: {#exm-sr-polar-rotation}
#### The square root for a rotation

For $\Lambda = R$, $\Lambda\Lambda^T = 1$ and its positive square root is $1$: $B = 1$, as $\Lambda e_0 = e_0$ requires. For $T$, outside $SO^+(1, 3)$, the
formula again gives $B = 1$, and $B^{-1}T = T$ is not a rotation: the decomposition into a boost and a rotation is special to the
identity component, and the other components need the extra factor $P$, $T$ or $PT$ of @thm-sr-four-components.

Pure boosts do not form a subgroup, as the second example of the theorem showed. The second exercise proves that this
happens for every pair of non-collinear boosts.

::: {#exr-sr-boosts-not-subgroup}
#### Boosts do not form a subgroup

Show that $B(\vec v_2)B(\vec v_1)$ is symmetric only if $\vec v_1$ and $\vec v_2$ are parallel (or one is zero).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(B_2B_1)^T = B_1B_2$, so the product is symmetric if and only if $B_1B_2 = B_2B_1$, which implies $B_2u_1 = B_1u_2$ with $u_k = B_ke_0 =
\gamma_k(1, \vec v_k)$. Write $\vec v_k = v_k\hat v_k$ and $c = \hat v_1\cdot\hat v_2$. The spatial parts are $\gamma_1(\gamma_2\vec v_2 + \vec v_1 + (\gamma_2 - 1)v_1c\,\hat v_2)$ and
$\gamma_2(\gamma_1\vec v_1 + \vec v_2 + (\gamma_1 - 1)v_2c\,\hat v_1)$; if $\hat v_1$, $\hat v_2$ are independent their difference vanishes only if the coefficients
of $\hat v_1$ and $\hat v_2$ do: $\gamma_1(1 - \gamma_2)v_1 = \gamma_2(\gamma_1 - 1)v_2c$ and $\gamma_2(\gamma_1 - 1)v_2 = -\gamma_1(\gamma_2 - 1)v_1c$. With $a = \gamma_2(\gamma_1 - 1)v_2 > 0$ and $b =
\gamma_1(\gamma_2 - 1)v_1 > 0$ these read $b = -ac$ and $a = -bc$, so $a = ac^2$ and $c^2 = 1$: the velocities are parallel after all.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The decomposition is a homeomorphism, and it computes the topology of the group. The third exercise draws the
consequence for loops.

::: {#exr-sr-topology}
#### The topology of $SO^+(1, 3)$

Show that $\Lambda \mapsto (\Lambda e_0, R)$ is a homeomorphism from $SO^+(1, 3)$ onto $H \times SO(3)$, where $H$ is the unit future hyperboloid, homeomorphic to
$\mathbb{R}^3$. Conclude that $SO^+(1, 3)$ has the same fundamental group as $SO(3)$, namely $\mathbb{Z}_2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The map is continuous, with continuous inverse $(u, R) \mapsto B_uR$, since $B_u$ depends continuously on $u$ (@eq-sr-boost-matrix with $\vec v = \vec u/u^0$); it
is bijective by @thm-sr-polar. $H$ is homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^3$ by $u \mapsto \vec u$, which is contractible, so $\pi_1(SO^+(1, 3)) = \pi_1(SO(3)) = \mathbb{Z}_2$
(@exm-cover-su2): a rotation by $2\pi$ is a loop that cannot be shrunk, and its lift to $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ ends at $-1$ (@thm-sr-double-cover).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

### The Lorentz algebra and the exponential map

The fourth step passes to the Lie algebra. The six generators of @exm-sr-lie-basis close under commutators, and their
brackets encode how infinitesimal rotations and boosts compose; @fig-sr-boost-commutator shows the most important
bracket at work, two boosts producing a rotation.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-sr-lorentz-algebra}
#### Lorentz algebra

The **Lorentz algebra** $\mathfrak{so}(1, 3)$ is the Lie algebra @eq-sr-lorentz-algebra of $O(1, 3)$, with the bracket $[X, Y] = XY - YX$ and the basis
$J_i$, $K_i$ of @exm-sr-lie-basis, in which
$$
[J_i, J_j] = \epsilon_{ijk}J_k, \qquad [J_i, K_j] = \epsilon_{ijk}K_k, \qquad [K_i, K_j] = -\epsilon_{ijk}J_k .
$$ {#eq-sr-lorentz-brackets}
Equivalently the $M^{\mu\nu}$ satisfy $[M^{\mu\nu}, M^{\rho\sigma}] = \eta^{\nu\rho}M^{\mu\sigma} - \eta^{\mu\rho}M^{\nu\sigma} - \eta^{\nu\sigma}M^{\mu\rho} + \eta^{\mu\sigma}M^{\nu\rho}$, the relations @eq-lorentz-spinor
of the spinor generators. In a unitary representation $U$ the **Hermitian generators** are $\hat J_i = i\,dU(J_i)$ and $\hat K_i = i\,dU(K_i)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
![Two boosts make a rotation. Left: the group commutator $C(\epsilon) = e^{\epsilon K_1}e^{\epsilon K_2}e^{-\epsilon K_1}e^{-\epsilon K_2}$ of two boosts with rapidity $\epsilon$ is
a rotation about $z$ (its boost part is of higher order), with angle (dots) approaching $-\epsilon^2$ (line), the rotation $e^{-\epsilon^2J_3}$ that
@eq-sr-lorentz-brackets predicts. Right: the same for two rotations, whose commutator approaches $e^{\epsilon^2J_3}$. Generated by
`figures/sr-boost-commutator.sage`.](figures/sr-boost-commutator.svg){#fig-sr-boost-commutator width=90%}

The brackets can be checked by multiplying $4 \times 4$ matrices. The first example computes the bracket of two boosts by hand,
because its sign is the origin of the Thomas-Wigner rotation.

::: {#exm-sr-boost-bracket}
#### The bracket of two boosts

$K_1$ has entries $(0, 1)$ and $(1, 0)$ equal to $1$, and $K_2$ entries $(0, 2)$ and $(2, 0)$. Then $K_1K_2$ has the single non-zero entry
$(K_1K_2)^1{}_2 = (K_1)^1{}_0(K_2)^0{}_2 = 1$ and $K_2K_1$ the entry $(2, 1)$ equal to $1$, so $[K_1, K_2]$ has $(1, 2)$ entry $1$ and $(2, 1)$ entry $-1$:
it is $-J_3$. Boosts do not close among themselves; their commutator is a rotation, with the sign opposite to that of
rotations, $[J_1, J_2] = J_3$.
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The bracket $[J_i, K_j] = \epsilon_{ijk}K_k$ says that the boost generators form a vector under rotations. The second example
interprets it at the group level.

::: {#exm-sr-boost-vector}
#### Boost generators form a vector

Differentiating $R\,e^{\eta K_j}R^{-1} = e^{\eta RK_jR^{-1}}$ and using @exr-sr-boost-conjugate gives $RK_jR^{-1} = \sum_k(R_3)_{kj}K_k$: the boost along $R_3\hat e_j$. Its
infinitesimal form for $R = e^{\theta J_i}$ is $[J_i, K_j] = \epsilon_{ijk}K_k$, the same law as $[J_i, J_j] = \epsilon_{ijk}J_k$ for the rotation generators
themselves and as $(J_i)\vec x$ for an ordinary vector.
:::

The covariant parameters $\omega_{\mu\nu}$ of an infinitesimal transformation and the angles and rapidities are related by the
basis change $J_i = \tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}M^{jk}$, $K_i = M^{0i}$. The third example spells it out.

::: {#exm-sr-omega-parameters}
#### Angles and rapidities from $\omega_{\mu\nu}$

$\tfrac12\omega_{\mu\nu}M^{\mu\nu} = \omega_{01}M^{01} + \omega_{02}M^{02} + \omega_{03}M^{03} + \omega_{12}M^{12} + \omega_{13}M^{13} + \omega_{23}M^{23} = \vec\zeta\cdot\vec K + \vec\theta\cdot\vec J$ with
rapidities $\zeta_i = \omega_{0i}$ and angles $\theta_1 = \omega_{23}$, $\theta_2 = \omega_{31}$, $\theta_3 = \omega_{12}$. So $\exp(\tfrac12\omega_{\mu\nu}M^{\mu\nu})$ with only $\omega_{01} = -\omega_{10} =
\zeta$ is the active boost along $x$ with rapidity $\zeta$, and its spinor version $\exp(\tfrac12\omega_{\mu\nu}S^{\mu\nu})$ (@def-lorentz-generators) is the same
transformation on spinors.
:::

An invariant inner product on the algebra distinguishes compact from non-compact directions. The second exercise
computes the trace form and finds that it is indefinite, unlike that of $\mathfrak{so}(4)$.

::: {#exr-sr-trace-form}
#### The trace form is indefinite

Compute $\operatorname{tr}(XY)$ on the basis $J_i$, $K_i$ in the $4 \times 4$ representation, and compare with $\mathfrak{so}(4)$, whose generators are the real
antisymmetric $4 \times 4$ matrices. Conclude that $\mathfrak{so}(1, 3)$ and $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ are not isomorphic as real Lie algebras, using that the Killing form
(@def-killing-form) of a simple or semisimple algebra is a fixed multiple of the trace form in any faithful irreducible
representation of each simple factor.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\operatorname{tr}(J_iJ_j) = -2\delta_{ij}$, $\operatorname{tr}(K_iK_j) = +2\delta_{ij}$, $\operatorname{tr}(J_iK_j) = 0$: signature $(3, 3)$. For antisymmetric matrices $\operatorname{tr}(A^2) = -\sum A_{ij}^2 < 0$,
so the trace form of $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ is negative definite. The Killing forms are $2\operatorname{tr}$ for both (they equal $(n - 2)\operatorname{tr}$ for $\mathfrak{so}(p, q)$,
$n = 4$), so they have different signatures and no isomorphism exists. The negative directions $J_i$ generate the compact
rotations; the positive ones the non-compact boosts.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The group commutator of two small boosts is computed in @fig-sr-boost-commutator. The third exercise derives its leading
term from the brackets.

::: {#exr-sr-group-commutator}
#### Small boosts around a square

Show that $e^{\epsilon K_1}e^{\epsilon K_2}e^{-\epsilon K_1}e^{-\epsilon K_2} = 1 + \epsilon^2[K_1, K_2] + O(\epsilon^3) = 1 - \epsilon^2J_3 + O(\epsilon^3)$. What does an observer who performs the four
boosts in turn find at the end?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Expanding each exponential to second order, the first-order terms cancel and the second-order terms leave $\epsilon^2(K_1K_2 - K_2K_1)$. By
@exm-sr-boost-bracket this is $-\epsilon^2J_3$. The observer is back at rest (the boost part is $O(\epsilon^3)$) but rotated by $-\epsilon^2$ about $z$: a closed loop of
boosts produces a rotation, the infinitesimal Thomas-Wigner rotation of @sec-sr-thomas-wigner.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The brackets @eq-sr-lorentz-brackets mix rotations and boosts. Over the complex numbers they can be untangled into two
commuting copies of one simple algebra, and this is the origin of the two labels $(j_1, j_2)$ of the representations.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sr-complexification}
#### The complexified Lorentz algebra

In the complexification $\mathfrak{so}(1, 3)_{\mathbb{C}} = \mathfrak{so}(1, 3) \otimes \mathbb{C}$ put $A_i = \tfrac12(J_i + iK_i)$ and $B_i = \tfrac12(J_i - iK_i)$. Then
$$
[A_i, A_j] = \epsilon_{ijk}A_k, \qquad [B_i, B_j] = \epsilon_{ijk}B_k, \qquad [A_i, B_j] = 0 ,
$$
so $\mathfrak{so}(1, 3)_{\mathbb{C}} = \operatorname{span}(A_i) \oplus \operatorname{span}(B_i)$ is a direct sum of two commuting ideals (@def-direct-sum-algebras), each isomorphic to
$\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{C})$, the traceless complex $2 \times 2$ matrices, by $A_i \mapsto -\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_i$. Complex conjugation of the coefficients exchanges $A_i$ and
$B_i$.

*Proof.* With @eq-sr-lorentz-brackets and $[K_i, J_j] = -[J_j, K_i] = \epsilon_{ijk}K_k$:
$[A_i, A_j] = \tfrac14([J_i, J_j] + i[J_i, K_j] + i[K_i, J_j] - [K_i, K_j]) = \tfrac14\epsilon_{ijk}(J_k + iK_k + iK_k + J_k) = \epsilon_{ijk}A_k$; the same computation with $i \to -i$
gives $[B_i, B_j] = \epsilon_{ijk}B_k$; and $[A_i, B_j] = \tfrac14([J_i, J_j] - i[J_i, K_j] + i[K_i, J_j] + [K_i, K_j]) = \tfrac14\epsilon_{ijk}(J_k - iK_k + iK_k - J_k) = 0$. The six
$A_i$, $B_i$ are a complex basis since $J_i = A_i + B_i$, $K_i = -i(A_i - B_i)$. The matrices $T_i = -\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_i$ satisfy $[T_i, T_j] = \epsilon_{ijk}T_k$ (from $[\sigma_i,
\sigma_j] = 2i\epsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k$) and are a complex basis of $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{C})$, so $A_i \mapsto T_i$ is an isomorphism. Conjugation fixes $J_i$, $K_i$ and
sends $i$ to $-i$, hence $A_i \leftrightarrow B_i$. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Representations of $\mathfrak{so}(1, 3)_{\mathbb{C}}$ are pairs of representations of $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{C})$. The first example takes the smallest non-trivial one
on the first factor and finds which way its boosts act.

::: {#exm-sr-left-weyl}
#### The left-handed Weyl representation

Represent $A_i$ by $-\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_i$ and $B_i$ by $0$. Then $J_i = A_i + B_i \mapsto -\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_i$ and $K_i = -i(A_i - B_i) \mapsto -\tfrac12\sigma_i$: rotations act by $e^{-i\theta\hat n\cdot\vec\sigma/2}$
and the boost of rapidity $\eta$ along $\hat n$ by $e^{-\eta\hat n\cdot\vec\sigma/2}$. These are the matrices acting on the upper two components, those with $\gamma_5 =
-1$, of a Dirac spinor in the Weyl representation of @exm-gamma-weyl when $\Lambda = e^{\eta K_1}$ (@exr-sr-weyl-blocks).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Exchanging the roles of the two factors exchanges the sign of the boosts. The second example gives the other Weyl
representation.

::: {#exm-sr-right-weyl}
#### The right-handed Weyl representation

Represent $A_i$ by $0$ and $B_i$ by $-\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_i$: $J_i \mapsto -\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_i$ again but $K_i \mapsto +\tfrac12\sigma_i$, so boosts act by $e^{+\eta\hat n\cdot\vec\sigma/2}$. The two
representations agree on rotations and differ on boosts by $\eta \to -\eta$, which is the action of parity; this is why a
parity-invariant theory of spin one-half needs both, as the Dirac equation does. They are the lower two components of a
Weyl-representation Dirac spinor.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The defining representation itself must be some pair. The third example identifies it by computing the two Casimir
operators $\sum_iA_i^2$ and $\sum_iB_i^2$, which take the value $-j(j + 1)$ on the spin-$j$ representation in this anti-Hermitian
normalisation.

::: {#exm-sr-vector-pair}
#### The four-vector representation is $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$

On $\mathbb{C}^4$ with the matrices $A_i$, $B_i$ built from $J_i$, $K_i$, a direct computation gives $\sum_iA_i^2 = \sum_iB_i^2 = -\tfrac34\cdot1$ (@exr-sr-ab-casimirs), the
value $-j(j + 1)$ for $j = \tfrac12$. The four-vectors therefore carry spin $\tfrac12$ under each factor, the representation $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$ of
@def-sr-j1j2; under rotations alone, $\tfrac12 \otimes \tfrac12 = 0 \oplus 1$, the time component and the three space components.
:::

The same splitting works for $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ over the reals (@prp-so4-split), but not for $\mathfrak{so}(1, 3)$. The second exercise explains the
difference.

::: {#exr-sr-why-complex}
#### Why the splitting needs complex numbers

For $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ the combinations $\tfrac12(L_{23} \pm L_{14})$ (and cyclic) are real and split the algebra into $\mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus \mathfrak{su}(2)$. Show that
for $\mathfrak{so}(1, 3)$ the real combinations $\tfrac12(J_i \pm K_i)$ do not close, and explain the role of the sign in $[K_i, K_j] = -\epsilon_{ijk}J_k$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[\tfrac12(J_1 + K_1), \tfrac12(J_2 + K_2)] = \tfrac14(J_3 + K_3 + K_3 - J_3) = \tfrac12K_3$, which is not of the form $\tfrac12(J_3 + K_3)$: the combination does not close.
For $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ the analogous bracket of the "boost" generators is $+\epsilon_{ijk}J_k$, and $\tfrac12(J \pm K)$ close; for the Lorentz algebra the minus sign
requires $K \to iK$, which is possible only over $\mathbb{C}$. The real Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(1, 3)$ is in fact simple, and isomorphic to $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{C})$
regarded as a real Lie algebra of dimension six.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Conjugation exchanges the two factors, so it exchanges the two labels of a representation. The third exercise draws the
consequence for the Weyl spinors.

::: {#exr-sr-conjugate-weyl}
#### Conjugating a Weyl spinor

Show that if $\psi$ transforms in the left-handed representation of @exm-sr-left-weyl, then $\sigma_2\psi^*$ transforms in the right-handed one.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Under the group element with parameters $\vec\theta$, $\vec\zeta$, $\psi \mapsto M\psi$ with $M = e^{-i\vec\theta\cdot\vec\sigma/2 - \vec\zeta\cdot\vec\sigma/2}$. Then $\sigma_2\psi^* \mapsto \sigma_2M^*\psi^* =
(\sigma_2M^*\sigma_2)\sigma_2\psi^*$, and $\sigma_2\vec\sigma^*\sigma_2 = -\vec\sigma$ gives $\sigma_2M^*\sigma_2 = e^{-i\vec\theta\cdot\vec\sigma/2 + \vec\zeta\cdot\vec\sigma/2}$, the right-handed matrix. This is the charge
conjugation of @def-dq-charge-conjugate in two-component form, and it is why one Weyl spinor suffices for a Majorana fermion
(@def-dq-majorana-fermion).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The exponential map sends the Lie algebra into the group, and one may ask whether it reaches every element. For compact
connected groups it does (@def-exponential-map). The group $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$, the exponential of $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{C})$ and soon the double cover of the Lorentz
group, is not compact, and the theorem below shows that it is not reached: some of its elements lie on no one-parameter
subgroup.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-sr-exp-sl2c}
#### The exponential of $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ is not surjective

Let $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ be the complex $2 \times 2$ matrices of determinant $1$, with Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{C})$. An element $A \in SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ is of the form $e^X$
with $X \in \mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{C})$ if and only if $\operatorname{tr}A \neq -2$ or $A = -1$. In particular
$$
A_0 = -\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}
$$
is not the exponential of any traceless matrix, and lies on no one-parameter subgroup of $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$.

*Proof.* Let $X \in \mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{C})$, with eigenvalues $\pm\lambda$. If $\lambda \neq 0$, $X$ is diagonalisable, $X = Q\operatorname{diag}(\lambda, -\lambda)Q^{-1}$, and $e^X = Q\operatorname{diag}(e^\lambda, e^{-\lambda})Q^{-1}$
is diagonalisable. If $\lambda = 0$, $X$ is nilpotent, $X^2 = 0$ by the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, and $e^X = 1 + X$ has trace $2$. Now let $\operatorname{tr}A = -2$, so both
eigenvalues of $A$ are $-1$. If $A = e^X$, the case $\lambda = 0$ is excluded by the trace, so $A$ is diagonalisable with both eigenvalues $-1$,
that is $A = -1$. Hence $A_0$, which has trace $-2$ but is not $-1$, is not an exponential, and since a one-parameter subgroup through
$A_0$ would give $A_0 = e^{tX}$ for some $t$, there is none. Conversely, $-1 = e^{i\pi\sigma_3}$; if $\operatorname{tr}A \neq \pm2$ the eigenvalues $\mu, 1/\mu$ are distinct, $A =
Q\operatorname{diag}(\mu, 1/\mu)Q^{-1}$, and $A = e^X$ with $X = Q\operatorname{diag}(\log\mu, -\log\mu)Q^{-1}$ for any branch of the logarithm; if $\operatorname{tr}A = 2$, either $A = 1 = e^0$ or $A = 1 +
N$ with $N = A - 1$ nilpotent (its eigenvalues are $0$), and $A = e^N$. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

The element $-1$ is an exponential although it has trace $-2$. The first example shows the one-parameter subgroups through
it.

::: {#exm-sr-minus-one}
#### $-1$ lies on rotations

$e^{-i\theta\sigma_3/2}$ is the lift of the rotation by $\theta$ about $z$ (@thm-sr-double-cover); at $\theta = 2\pi$ it is $-1$. Every one-parameter subgroup
$e^{-i\theta\hat n\cdot\vec\sigma/2}$ passes through $-1$ at $\theta = 2\pi$: the sign of a spinor under a full turn (@exm-sr-field-spinor).
:::

Unipotent elements, those of trace $2$ other than the identity, are exponentials of nilpotent matrices. The second example
gives them, and their images in the Lorentz group, the null rotations, reappear in the little group of a photon.

::: {#exm-sr-unipotent}
#### Unipotent elements

$\begin{pmatrix}1 & a \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix} = \exp\begin{pmatrix}0 & a \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ for every complex $a$, since the nilpotent matrix squares to zero. These form a
one-parameter group in $a$, isomorphic to $(\mathbb{C}, +)$. The obstruction of the theorem is the sign: $-\begin{pmatrix}1 & a \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ is
not an exponential for $a \neq 0$.
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The logarithm of a diagonalisable element is far from unique. The third example shows the freedom for a diagonal
element with a negative eigenvalue.

::: {#exm-sr-log-diag}
#### Logarithms of a diagonal element

$A = \operatorname{diag}(-2, -\tfrac12)$ has trace $-\tfrac52 \neq -2$, so it is an exponential: $A = e^X$ with $X = \operatorname{diag}(\ln2 + i\pi(2k + 1), -\ln2 - i\pi(2k + 1))$ for any
integer $k$. In $SL(2, \mathbb{R})$ no real traceless $X$ works (@exr-sr-sl2r), so the answer depends on whether complex generators are allowed.
:::

::: {#exr-sr-exp-closed-form}
#### A closed form for $e^X$

For $X \in \mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{C})$ with $\lambda^2 = -\det X$, show that $e^X = \cosh\lambda\cdot1 + \frac{\sinh\lambda}{\lambda}X$ (with $\sinh\lambda/\lambda = 1$ at $\lambda = 0$), and deduce that $\operatorname{tr}e^X = 2\cosh\lambda$.
Check the formula with Sage on a random complex traceless matrix.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By Cayley-Hamilton $X^2 = -\det X\cdot1 = \lambda^21$, so the even powers are $\lambda^{2k}1$ and the odd ones $\lambda^{2k}X$; summing the series gives the formula. The
trace follows from $\operatorname{tr}X = 0$:

{{< sage exr-sr-exp-closed-form >}}

The closed form gives the theorem again in a few lines. The second exercise asks for this proof. It replaces the diagonalisation argument by a computation of the trace.

::: {#exr-sr-exp-trace-proof}
#### The theorem from the closed form

Using @exr-sr-exp-closed-form, show that if $e^X$ has trace $-2$ then $e^X = -1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$2\cosh\lambda = -2$ forces $\lambda = i\pi(2k + 1)$, so $\lambda \neq 0$ and $\sinh\lambda = 0$; then $e^X = \cosh\lambda\cdot1 = -1$. The non-exponential element $A_0$ of the theorem
has trace $-2$ and is not $-1$.
:::

The real group $SL(2, \mathbb{R})$ has an even smaller image of the exponential. The third exercise finds an element outside it with a
different trace.

::: {#exr-sr-sl2r}
#### The exponential of $SL(2, \mathbb{R})$

Show that a real traceless $X$ has $\operatorname{tr}e^X \geq -2$, and conclude that $\operatorname{diag}(-2, -\tfrac12) \in SL(2, \mathbb{R})$ is not $e^X$ for any real traceless $X$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For real $X$, $\lambda^2 = -\det X$ is real: either $\lambda$ is real and $\operatorname{tr}e^X = 2\cosh\lambda \geq 2$, or $\lambda = i\mu$ and $\operatorname{tr}e^X = 2\cos\mu \in [-2, 2]$. The trace of
$\operatorname{diag}(-2, -\tfrac12)$ is $-\tfrac52 < -2$, so it is not an exponential, although its square, $\operatorname{diag}(4, \tfrac14)$, is.
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

### $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ and the spinor representations

The fifth step realises the Lorentz group through $2 \times 2$ complex matrices. Four-vectors become Hermitian matrices, and
$SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ acts on them by conjugation; the resulting map onto $SO^+(1, 3)$ is two-to-one, and its source is the group on which
the spinors live. @fig-sr-j1j2 previews the representations that this produces.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-sr-double-cover}
#### $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ is the double cover of the Lorentz group

With $\sigma_0 = 1$ and the Pauli matrices $\sigma_i$, the map $x \mapsto X(x) = x^\mu\sigma_\mu = \begin{pmatrix}t + z & x - iy \\ x + iy & t - z\end{pmatrix}$ is a linear isomorphism from
$\mathbb{R}^4$ onto the Hermitian $2 \times 2$ matrices, with $\det X(x) = x\cdot x$. For $A \in SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ define $\Lambda(A)$ by
$$
X(\Lambda(A)x) = AX(x)A^\dagger .
$$ {#eq-sr-sl2c-action}
Then $A \mapsto \Lambda(A)$ is a surjective homomorphism of Lie groups $SL(2, \mathbb{C}) \to SO^+(1, 3)$ with kernel $\{1, -1\}$, a double cover
(@def-covering-homomorphism). Explicitly $\Lambda(e^{\eta\hat n\cdot\vec\sigma/2}) = e^{\eta\hat n\cdot\vec K}$ is the active pure boost of rapidity $\eta$ along $\hat n$, and $\Lambda(e^{-i\theta\hat n\cdot\vec\sigma/2}) =
e^{\theta\hat n\cdot\vec J}$ is the rotation by $\theta$ about $\hat n$.

*Proof.* *Isomorphism.* A Hermitian matrix has real diagonal and conjugate off-diagonal entries, four real parameters; $x \mapsto X(x)$ is
linear and injective, hence bijective, and $\det X = (t + z)(t - z) - (x - iy)(x + iy) = x\cdot x$. *Lorentz.* $AXA^\dagger$ is Hermitian and
$\det(AXA^\dagger) = |\det A|^2\det X = \det X$, so $\Lambda(A)$ is a linear map preserving the Minkowski form: $\Lambda(A) \in O(1, 3)$. It is a homomorphism,
$X(\Lambda(AB)x) = ABX(x)B^\dagger A^\dagger = X(\Lambda(A)\Lambda(B)x)$, and its entries are quadratic polynomials in those of $A$, $\bar A$, so it is smooth.
*Image in $SO^+(1, 3)$.* $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ is connected: every $A$ has the polar form $A = HU$ with $H = (AA^\dagger)^{1/2}$ positive Hermitian of determinant $1$
and $U = H^{-1}A \in SU(2)$; $H = e^h$ with $h$ Hermitian traceless, and $s \mapsto e^{sh}U_s$, with $U_s$ a path from $1$ to $U$ in $SU(2) \cong S^3$, joins $1$ to $A$.
The image of a connected group under a continuous homomorphism lies in the identity component, $SO^+(1, 3)$ (@thm-sr-four-components).
*The two families.* For $A = e^{-i\theta\sigma_3/2} = \operatorname{diag}(e^{-i\theta/2}, e^{i\theta/2})$, $AXA^\dagger$ multiplies the off-diagonal entry $x - iy$ by $e^{-i\theta}$, which is the
rotation $(x, y) \mapsto (x\cos\theta - y\sin\theta, x\sin\theta + y\cos\theta)$ and fixes $t$, $z$; for $A = e^{\eta\sigma_3/2} = \operatorname{diag}(e^{\eta/2}, e^{-\eta/2})$, $AXA^\dagger$ multiplies
$t + z$ by $e^\eta$ and $t - z$ by $e^{-\eta}$, the boost along $z$ of @exm-sr-rapidity-lightcone, read actively. A general axis follows by conjugating with a
rotation, using the homomorphism property and @exr-sr-boost-conjugate. *Surjectivity.* By @thm-sr-polar every element of $SO^+(1, 3)$ is a
boost times a rotation, and both are in the image. *Kernel.* If $AXA^\dagger = X$ for all Hermitian $X$, then $X = 1$ gives $AA^\dagger = 1$, so $AX = XA$ for all
Hermitian $X$, hence for all complex matrices $X + iY$; $A$ is then a multiple of the identity (@thm-schur), $A = \lambda1$ with $\lambda^2 = \det A = 1$.
*Covering.* A homomorphism of Lie groups with discrete kernel has injective differential; both groups have dimension $6$, so the
differential is an isomorphism of Lie algebras and $\Lambda$ is a local diffeomorphism, a covering with two sheets. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

$(2j_1 + 1)(2j_2 + 1)$, and its label the spins it contains under rotations, $|j_1 - j_2|, \dots, j_1 + j_2$. Squares with $j_1 + j_2$ integer

The boosts were checked in the proof only along $z$. The first example computes the boost along $x$ in components, as an

::: {#exm-sr-cover-boost-x}
#### A boost along $x$

$A = e^{\eta\sigma_1/2} = \cosh\tfrac\eta2 + \sigma_1\sinh\tfrac\eta2$. For $X = t + x\sigma_1 + y\sigma_2 + z\sigma_3$, using $\sigma_1\sigma_2\sigma_1 = -\sigma_2$, $\sigma_1\sigma_3\sigma_1 = -\sigma_3$, $AXA^\dagger =
(t\cosh\eta + x\sinh\eta) + (t\sinh\eta + x\cosh\eta)\sigma_1 + y\sigma_2 + z\sigma_3$: the active boost along $x$ with rapidity $\eta$, $e^{\eta K_1}$. The matrix $A$ is Hermitian and
positive, as a pure boost should be.
:::

The kernel contains $-1$, and the path of rotations shows how it is reached. The second example follows the lift of a full
turn.

::: {#exm-sr-cover-loop}
#### A full turn lifts to an open path

The rotations $R_z(\theta)$, $0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi$, form a closed loop in $SO^+(1, 3)$. Their lifts $e^{-i\theta\sigma_3/2}$ start at $1$ and end at $-1$: the loop does
not lift to a loop, so it cannot be contracted in $SO^+(1, 3)$ (@exr-sr-topology). Going around twice, $0 \leq \theta \leq 4\pi$, lifts to a closed loop.
:::

Elements of $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ that are neither Hermitian nor unitary give the remaining transformations. The third example
computes the image of a unipotent element, a **null rotation**, which fixes a light ray.

::: {#exm-sr-null-rotation}
#### A null rotation

For $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & a \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ with $a$ real, @eq-sr-sl2c-action gives $t' - z' = t - z$, $x' = x + a(t - z)$, $y' = y$ and $t' + z' = t + z + 2ax + a^2(t - z)$,
that is
$$
t' = t + ax + \tfrac{a^2}{2}(t - z), \qquad x' = x + a(t - z), \qquad z' = z + ax + \tfrac{a^2}{2}(t - z) .
$$
It fixes $k = (1, 0, 0, 1)$, it is neither a boost nor a rotation, and its generator is $K_1 - J_2$ (@exr-sr-null-rotation-exp).
:::

::: {#exr-sr-cover-numeric}
#### The covering map by computer

With Sage, implement $A \mapsto \Lambda(A)$ through $\Lambda^\mu{}_\nu = \tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(\sigma_\mu A\sigma_\nu A^\dagger)$, which extracts the components $x^\mu = \tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(\sigma_\mu X)$
of a Hermitian matrix $X$ ($\mu = 0, \dots, 3$, no metric involved). Check on random $A, B \in SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ that $\Lambda(A) \in SO^+(1, 3)$, $\Lambda(AB) = \Lambda(A)\Lambda(B)$ and $\Lambda(-A) = \Lambda(A)$.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Since $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma_\mu\sigma_\nu) = 2\delta_{\mu\nu}$, the components of a Hermitian $X$ are $\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(\sigma_\mu X)$, and the column $\nu$ of $\Lambda(A)$ is the image of $\sigma_\nu$. All
checks pass to machine precision:

{{< sage exr-sr-cover-numeric >}}

Parity is not in the image, but it has a simple description on Hermitian matrices. The second exercise finds it.

::: {#exr-sr-parity-hermitian}
#### Parity on Hermitian matrices

Show that $X \mapsto \sigma_2X^T\sigma_2$ sends $X(t, \vec x)$ to $X(t, -\vec x)$, and explain why it is not of the form $X \mapsto AXA^\dagger$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sigma_2\sigma_i^T\sigma_2 = -\sigma_i$ for each $i$ (for $i = 1, 3$, $\sigma_i^T = \sigma_i$ anticommutes with $\sigma_2$; for $i = 2$, $\sigma_2^T = -\sigma_2$) and $\sigma_2\sigma_2 = 1$, so $t + \vec x\cdot\vec\sigma \mapsto t -
\vec x\cdot\vec\sigma$: parity. Every $X \mapsto AXA^\dagger$ is in $SO^+(1, 3)$ by the theorem, while $P$ has determinant $-1$. The map is $X \mapsto \det X\cdot X^{-1}$, the
adjugate.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

$SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ is the universal cover, not just a double cover. The third exercise proves that it is simply connected.

::: {#exr-sr-sl2c-simply-connected}
#### $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ is simply connected

Show that the polar decomposition $A = HU$ of the proof is a homeomorphism $SL(2, \mathbb{C}) \to \mathcal{H} \times SU(2)$, where $\mathcal{H}$ is the set of positive
Hermitian matrices of determinant $1$, and that $\mathcal{H} \cong \mathbb{R}^3$, $SU(2) \cong S^3$. Conclude that $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ is simply connected.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$H = (AA^\dagger)^{1/2}$ and $U = H^{-1}A$ depend continuously on $A$, and $(H, U) \mapsto HU$ is continuous; uniqueness of the polar decomposition makes them
inverse. $\mathcal{H} = \{e^h : h \text{ Hermitian traceless}\}$ and $h \mapsto e^h$ is a homeomorphism from $\mathbb{R}^3$ (the matrices $h = \vec a\cdot\vec\sigma$). $SU(2)$ is the
unit sphere $|a|^2 + |b|^2 = 1$ in $\mathbb{C}^2$ (@exm-cover-su2). Both factors are simply connected, so their product is.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The covering map turns the failure of @thm-sr-exp-sl2c into a success downstairs. Since $A$ and $-A$ have the same image, an
element of $SO^+(1, 3)$ is an exponential as soon as one of its two lifts is.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sr-exp-surjective}
#### Every proper orthochronous Lorentz transformation is an exponential

The exponential map $\mathfrak{so}(1, 3) \to SO^+(1, 3)$ is surjective, but not injective.

*Proof.* Let $\Lambda \in SO^+(1, 3)$ and $A$ a lift, $\Lambda = \Lambda(A)$ (@thm-sr-double-cover). If $\operatorname{tr}A \neq -2$ or $A = -1$, then $A = e^X$ by @thm-sr-exp-sl2c; otherwise $\operatorname{tr}(-A) =
2$ and $-A = e^X$. In both cases $\Lambda = \Lambda(\pm A) = \Lambda(e^X) = e^{d\Lambda(X)}$, where $d\Lambda : \mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{C}) \to \mathfrak{so}(1, 3)$ is the differential, an isomorphism of real Lie
algebras, and $\Lambda(e^X) = e^{d\Lambda(X)}$ because both sides are one-parameter subgroups with the same velocity. It is not injective because $e^{2\pi J_3} = 1 =
e^0$. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The non-exponential element $A_0$ of @thm-sr-exp-sl2c has an image that is an exponential. The first example finds it. The example shows concretely how the sign ambiguity of the lift rescues surjectivity.

::: {#exm-sr-a0-image}
#### The image of $A_0$

$\Lambda(A_0) = \Lambda(-A_0) = \Lambda\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, the null rotation of @exm-sr-null-rotation with $a = 1$, and it equals $e^{K_1 - J_2}$. In $SO^+(1, 3)$ it lies on
the one-parameter subgroup $e^{s(K_1 - J_2)}$, whose lift through $1$ ends at $-A_0$, not at $A_0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Elements that boost and rotate about the same axis are exponentials of commuting generators. The second example gives the
logarithm explicitly.

::: {#exm-sr-loxodromic-log}
#### Logarithm of a loxodromic element

$\Lambda = e^{\eta K_3}e^{\theta J_3}$ is $e^{\eta K_3 + \theta J_3}$, since the generators commute (@exm-sr-lie-loxodromic). Its lift is $e^{(\eta - i\theta)\sigma_3/2} = \operatorname{diag}(e^{(\eta - i\theta)/2}, e^{-(\eta - i\theta)/2})$,
with trace $2\cosh\tfrac{\eta - i\theta}{2}$; boost and rotation combine into one complex rapidity $\eta - i\theta$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The exponential map of $SO^+(1, 3)$ hits every element, but many generators hit the same one. The third example lists the
generators that exponentiate to the identity among the rotations.

::: {#exm-sr-exp-kernel}
#### Generators with trivial exponential

$e^{\theta\hat n\cdot\vec J} = 1$ exactly when $\theta \in 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$, for every axis $\hat n$: a whole family of spheres of radius $2\pi k$ in the rotation generators maps to the
identity. In $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ the lifts $e^{-i\theta\hat n\cdot\vec\sigma/2}$ equal $(-1)^k$ there, so only the spheres with $k$ even map to $1$ upstairs.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise finds the generator of a given transformation, a boost followed by a rotation about the boost axis. The two factors commute, which makes the logarithm easy to guess.

::: {#exr-sr-find-log}
#### Finding a generator

Find $X \in \mathfrak{so}(1, 3)$ with $e^X = B(0.6\hat x)R_x(\pi/2)$, and check with Sage.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$B(0.6\hat x) = e^{\ln2K_1}$ (@exm-sr-rapidity-ln2) and $R_x(\pi/2) = e^{(\pi/2)J_1}$, and $K_1$, $J_1$ commute, so $X = \ln2K_1 + \tfrac\pi2J_1$:

{{< sage exr-sr-find-log >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The generator of the null rotation was announced in @exm-sr-null-rotation. The second exercise verifies it. The nilpotency of the generator makes the exponential series stop after three terms.

::: {#exr-sr-null-rotation-exp}
#### The generator of a null rotation

Show that $N = K_1 - J_2$ satisfies $N^3 = 0$, compute $e^{aN} = 1 + aN + \tfrac{a^2}{2}N^2$, and compare with the matrix of @exm-sr-null-rotation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
From the matrices of @exm-sr-lie-basis, $K_1$ exchanges $e_0$ and $e_1$, and $J_2$ sends $e_3 \mapsto e_1$, $e_1 \mapsto -e_3$. So $N$ sends $e_0 \mapsto e_1$,
$e_1 \mapsto e_0 + e_3$, $e_3 \mapsto -e_1$, $e_2 \mapsto 0$; then $N^2$ sends $e_0 \mapsto e_0 + e_3$, $e_3 \mapsto -(e_0 + e_3)$ and kills $e_1$, $e_2$, and $N^3 = 0$ because
$N(e_0 + e_3) = 0$. In particular $e^{aN}e_0 = (1 + \tfrac{a^2}{2}, a, 0, \tfrac{a^2}{2})$, the first column of the null rotation, and the other columns agree
as well:

{{< sage exr-sr-null-rotation-exp >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The exponential map of $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ failed at the elements of trace $-2$. The third exercise counts the exceptions downstairs, where
there are none.

::: {#exr-sr-trace-minus-two}
#### Elements of trace $-2$

Describe the set of $A \in SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ with $\operatorname{tr}A = -2$, $A \neq -1$, and its image in $SO^+(1, 3)$. Show that the image consists of the null rotations
(conjugates of @exm-sr-null-rotation), all of which are exponentials.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Such $A$ have the single eigenvalue $-1$ and are not diagonalisable, so $A = -Q\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}Q^{-1}$ by the Jordan form. Their images are
$\Lambda(Q)\Lambda\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\Lambda(Q)^{-1}$, conjugates of a null rotation, equal to $\Lambda(Q)e^{N}\Lambda(Q)^{-1} = e^{\Lambda(Q)N\Lambda(Q)^{-1}}$: exponentials.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The representations of $\mathfrak{so}(1, 3)$ follow from @prp-sr-complexification: a representation of the complexified algebra is a pair of
commuting representations of $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{C})$, and the irreducible finite-dimensional ones are labelled by two spins
[@boudreau2018applied, Sec. 14.3; @bekaert2006unitary, Sec. 1.1]. Since $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ is simply connected (@exr-sr-sl2c-simply-connected),
each integrates to a representation of the group.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-sr-j1j2}
#### Representation labelled by two spins

For $j_1, j_2 \in \{0, \tfrac12, 1, \tfrac32, \dots\}$ let $S^{(j)}_i$ be the Hermitian spin-$j$ matrices of @def-spin-j and $T^{(j)}_i = -iS^{(j)}_i$. The **representation
$(j_1, j_2)$** of $\mathfrak{so}(1, 3)$ on $\mathbb{C}^{2j_1 + 1} \otimes \mathbb{C}^{2j_2 + 1}$ is
$$
A_i \mapsto T^{(j_1)}_i \otimes 1, \qquad B_i \mapsto 1 \otimes T^{(j_2)}_i, \qquad\text{that is}\qquad J_i \mapsto T^{(j_1)}_i \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes T^{(j_2)}_i, \quad K_i \mapsto
-i\bigl(T^{(j_1)}_i \otimes 1 - 1 \otimes T^{(j_2)}_i\bigr) ,
$$
of dimension $(2j_1 + 1)(2j_2 + 1)$, together with the representation of $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ it integrates to. Under rotations it decomposes as $j_1 \otimes j_2 = |j_1 -
j_2| \oplus \dots \oplus (j_1 + j_2)$ (@def-clebsch-gordan), and it descends to $SO^+(1, 3)$ exactly when $j_1 + j_2$ is an integer.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The two smallest representations are the Weyl spinors of @exm-sr-left-weyl and @exm-sr-right-weyl. The first example writes their
group action through $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ and relates them to the Dirac spinor.

::: {#exm-sr-weyl-group}
#### Weyl and Dirac spinors

For $A \in SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ covering $\Lambda$, a right-handed spinor $(0, \tfrac12)$ transforms as $\psi_R \mapsto A\psi_R$ and a left-handed one $(\tfrac12, 0)$ as $\psi_L \mapsto
(A^\dagger)^{-1}\psi_L$: for $A = e^{\eta\sigma_1/2}$ the boost matrices are $e^{\pm\eta\sigma_1/2}$, for $A = e^{-i\theta\sigma_3/2}$ both get $e^{-i\theta\sigma_3/2}$. A Dirac spinor $\psi = (\psi_L, \psi_R)$
transforms in $(\tfrac12, 0) \oplus (0, \tfrac12)$, by the block-diagonal matrix $\exp(\tfrac12\omega_{\mu\nu}S^{\mu\nu})$ of @def-lorentz-generators in the Weyl representation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The defining action @eq-sr-sl2c-action of $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ on Hermitian matrices is a tensor product of the two Weyl representations.
The second example shows how a four-vector is built from spinors.

::: {#exm-sr-vector-from-spinors}
#### A four-vector from a spinor

For a right-handed spinor $\psi_R$, the matrix $X = \psi_R\psi_R^\dagger$ is Hermitian with $\det X = 0$, and $X \mapsto A\psi_R\psi_R^\dagger A^\dagger = AXA^\dagger$: the four-vector $x^\mu =
\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(\sigma_\mu X) = \tfrac12\psi_R^\dagger\sigma_\mu\psi_R$ is null and transforms as a vector. In general $X$ transforms in $(0, \tfrac12) \otimes \overline{(0, \tfrac12)} = (0, \tfrac12) \otimes
(\tfrac12, 0) = (\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$, the four-vector representation of @exm-sr-vector-pair. This is the construction of @blennow2022relativity [Problem
1.35] and of the four-momentum of a Weyl spinor in @boudreau2018applied [eq. (14.9)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The six components of an antisymmetric tensor split into two complex three-vectors, as in @boudreau2018applied [eq. (14.15)].
The third example identifies them for the electromagnetic field.

::: {#exm-sr-field-pair}
#### The field strength is $(1, 0) \oplus (0, 1)$

For the field tensor $F^{\mu\nu}$ of @def-field-strength-abelian, the complex vectors $\vec E - i\vec B$ and $\vec E + i\vec B$ transform separately: under rotations as
vectors, and under the active boost $e^{\eta K_1}$ by the complex rotations $e^{-i\eta L_1}$ and $e^{+i\eta L_1}$, where $L_1$ is the rotation generator of
@sec-conventions-lie (@exr-sr-field-complex). So $\vec E - i\vec B$ carries $(1, 0)$ and $\vec E + i\vec B$ carries $(0, 1)$, and $(\vec E \pm i\vec B)^2 = E^2 - B^2 \pm 2i\vec E\cdot\vec B$
gives the two invariants of @prp-sr-field-invariants.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The first exercise checks the block structure of the Dirac spinor representation claimed in @exm-sr-weyl-group. It ties the abstract representations to the explicit gamma matrices of @exm-gamma-weyl.

::: {#exr-sr-weyl-blocks}
#### The blocks of the spinor representation

With Sage, compute $\exp(\zeta S^{01})$ and $\exp(\theta S^{12})$ in the Weyl representation and identify the blocks with $(A^\dagger)^{-1}$ and $A$ for $A = e^{\zeta\sigma_1/2}$
and $A = e^{-i\theta\sigma_3/2}$. Check that the boost $e^{\zeta S^{01}}$ covers $e^{\zeta K_1}$, that is $S^{-1}\gamma^\mu S = (e^{\zeta K_1})^\mu{}_\nu\gamma^\nu$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The upper block, on which $\gamma_5 = -1$, is $e^{-\zeta\sigma_1/2} = (A^\dagger)^{-1}$ and the lower block is $e^{\zeta\sigma_1/2} = A$; for rotations both blocks are $e^{-i\theta\sigma_3/2}$, and
the covariance identity holds:

{{< sage exr-sr-weyl-blocks >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The spin content of a representation follows from the Clebsch-Gordan rule. The second exercise applies it to the field
of a spin-$\tfrac32$ particle.

::: {#exr-sr-rarita-schwinger}
#### The vector-spinor

The field $\psi_\mu$ of a spin-$\tfrac32$ particle carries a vector index and a Dirac index: $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12) \otimes ((\tfrac12, 0) \oplus (0, \tfrac12))$. Decompose it into
irreducible $(j_1, j_2)$ and give the dimensions and the spins under rotations.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(\tfrac12, \tfrac12) \otimes (\tfrac12, 0) = (1 \oplus 0, \tfrac12) = (1, \tfrac12) \oplus (0, \tfrac12)$, of dimensions $6 + 2$, and similarly $(\tfrac12, 1) \oplus (\tfrac12, 0)$. In total $16 = 6 + 2 + 6 + 2$.
$(1, \tfrac12)$ contains spins $\tfrac32 \oplus \tfrac12$; the spin-$\tfrac32$ particle uses $(1, \tfrac12) \oplus (\tfrac12, 1)$, and the conditions $\gamma^\mu\psi_\mu = 0$, $\partial^\mu\psi_\mu = 0$
remove the spin-$\tfrac12$ parts.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The third exercise verifies the transformation of $\vec E \pm i\vec B$ claimed in @exm-sr-field-pair, which fixes which combination is
$(1, 0)$ in the conventions of this chapter. It also asks why such finite-dimensional representations cannot be unitary.

::: {#exr-sr-field-complex}
#### $\vec E \pm i\vec B$ under a boost

With $F^{i0} = E^i$ and $F^{ij} = -\epsilon_{ijk}B^k$, transform $F^{\mu\nu} \mapsto \Lambda^\mu{}_\alpha\Lambda^\nu{}_\beta F^{\alpha\beta}$ by $\Lambda = e^{\eta K_1}$ and check with Sage that $\vec E - i\vec B \mapsto e^{-i\eta L_1}(\vec E - i\vec B)$
and $\vec E + i\vec B \mapsto e^{i\eta L_1}(\vec E + i\vec B)$, where $(L_1)_{jk} = -\epsilon_{1jk}$. Why are finite-dimensional representations like these never unitary,
except the trivial one?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The computation confirms both laws. In $(j_1, j_2)$ the rotation generators are anti-Hermitian but the boost generators $K_i = -i(T \otimes 1 - 1 \otimes T)$ are
Hermitian, so $e^{\eta K_i}$ is Hermitian and positive, not unitary; more generally a non-trivial finite-dimensional unitary representation of a
non-compact simple group cannot exist [@bekaert2006unitary, Sec. 1.3], which is why the unitary representations of
@sec-sr-wigner-classification are infinite-dimensional:

{{< sage exr-sr-field-complex >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
