### The Thomas-Wigner rotation {#sec-sr-thomas-wigner}

The sixth step returns to physics. Two boosts in different directions compose to a boost followed by a rotation
(@exm-sr-polar-two-boosts): an observer who accelerates first along $x$ and then along $y$, without ever rotating in her own
frame, ends up rotated relative to an observer who reaches the same velocity with a single boost. The rotation is
named after Thomas, who found its consequence for the electron in an atom in 1926, and Wigner, who identified it as the
little-group transformation of @sec-sr-wigner-classification; @fig-sr-wigner shows its size. The derivation follows
@odonnell2011wigner [Secs. 4-5].

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-sr-wigner-rotation}
#### Wigner rotation

For velocities $\vec v_1$, $\vec v_2$ with $|\vec v_k| < 1$, the product of active pure boosts $B(\vec v_2)B(\vec v_1)$ (first $B(\vec v_1)$, then $B(\vec v_2)$) has
the polar decomposition (@thm-sr-polar)
$$
B(\vec v_2)B(\vec v_1) = B(\vec u)\,W(\vec v_2, \vec v_1) ,
$$ {#eq-sr-wigner-def}
where $\vec u = \vec v_1 \oplus \vec v_2$ is the **composite velocity**, the velocity of $B(\vec v_2)B(\vec v_1)e_0$, and the rotation $W(\vec v_2, \vec v_1)$ is the
**Wigner rotation** of the pair.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
![The size of the Wigner rotation. Left: the angle $\Omega$ of $W(\vec v_2, \vec v_1)$ against the angle $\theta$ between the two velocities, for equal
speeds $0.5$, $0.9$, $0.99$ and $0.9999$; as the speeds approach $c$, $\Omega$ approaches $\theta$ (dashed). Right: the Thomas precession per revolution
$2\pi(\gamma - 1)$ of a gyroscope on a circular orbit, against the speed. Generated by `figures/sr-wigner.sage`.](figures/sr-wigner.svg){#fig-sr-wigner width=95%}

Collinear boosts produce no rotation. The first example checks this from the definition, recovering the composition of
collinear velocities. This is the case in which the composition law of @prp-sr-velocity-addition is exact.

::: {#exm-sr-wigner-collinear}
#### Collinear boosts

If $\vec v_1 = v_1\hat n$ and $\vec v_2 = v_2\hat n$, both boosts act in the plane of $e_0$ and $\hat n$ and commute, $B(\vec v_2)B(\vec v_1) = B((v_1 \oplus v_2)\hat n)$ with $v_1
\oplus v_2 = (v_1 + v_2)/(1 + v_1v_2)$ (@exr-sr-boost-group). The product is already a pure boost, and $W = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Perpendicular boosts give the simplest non-trivial case. The second example computes the composite velocity, which is
already asymmetric in the two boosts.

::: {#exm-sr-wigner-perpendicular}
#### Perpendicular boosts

For $\vec v_1 = 0.6\hat x$ and $\vec v_2 = 0.7\hat y$, $B(\vec v_1)e_0 = (1.25, 0.75, 0, 0)$ and $B(\vec v_2)$ multiplies $t$ and $y$ by $\gamma_2 = 1.400$: $B(\vec v_2)B(\vec v_1)e_0 \approx
(1.750, 0.750, 1.225, 0)$, so $\vec u = (0.6/\gamma_2, 0.7, 0) \approx (0.429, 0.700, 0)$, with $|\vec u| \approx 0.821$. The other order gives $\vec u' = (0.6, 0.7/\gamma_1, 0) = (0.6,
0.56, 0)$, of the same magnitude and a different direction (@exr-sr-wigner-reversed).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Reversing the order of the boosts reverses the rotation. The third example derives this from transposition, as in
@odonnell2011wigner [eqs. (38)-(40)].

::: {#exm-sr-wigner-reverse}
#### The reverse order

Pure boosts are symmetric and rotations orthogonal, so transposing @eq-sr-wigner-def gives $B(\vec v_1)B(\vec v_2) = W^TB(\vec u) = W^{-1}B(\vec u) = B(W^{-1}\vec u)W^{-1}$
(@exr-sr-boost-conjugate): $W(\vec v_1, \vec v_2) = W(\vec v_2, \vec v_1)^{-1}$ and $\vec v_2 \oplus \vec v_1 = W^{-1}(\vec v_1 \oplus \vec v_2)$. The two composite velocities have the same magnitude, and
the angle between them is the angle of the Wigner rotation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The composite velocity has a closed form, Einstein's rule for adding velocities in arbitrary directions. The first
exercise derives it.

::: {#exr-sr-composite-velocity}
#### Einstein's addition of velocities

Show that
$$
\vec v_1 \oplus \vec v_2 = \frac{\vec v_2 + \vec v_1/\gamma_2 + (1 - 1/\gamma_2)(\hat v_2\cdot\vec v_1)\hat v_2}{1 + \vec v_1\cdot\vec v_2} ,
$$
and that its Lorentz factor is $\gamma_1\gamma_2(1 + \vec v_1\cdot\vec v_2)$. Check the formula numerically against the matrices.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$B(\vec v_1)e_0 = \gamma_1(1, \vec v_1)$, and @eq-sr-boost-matrix gives $B(\vec v_2)\gamma_1(1, \vec v_1) = \gamma_1\bigl(\gamma_2(1 + \vec v_2\cdot\vec v_1),\ \gamma_2\vec v_2 + \vec v_1 + (\gamma_2 - 1)(\hat v_2\cdot\vec v_1)\hat v_2\bigr)$.
Dividing the spatial part by the time part gives the formula, and the time part is the Lorentz factor:

{{< sage exr-sr-composite-velocity >}}
:::

#### The angle between the two composite velocities

rotation $B(\vec u)^{-1}B(\vec v_2)B(\vec v_1)$, about $+\hat z$:

{{< sage exr-sr-wigner-reversed >}}

The Wigner rotation is trivial only for collinear boosts. The third exercise proves the converse of the first example
without computing the angle.

::: {#exr-sr-wigner-trivial}
#### When the rotation is trivial

Show that $W(\vec v_2, \vec v_1) = 1$ if and only if $B(\vec v_1)$ and $B(\vec v_2)$ commute, and conclude with @exr-sr-boosts-not-subgroup that this happens only for
parallel (or zero) velocities.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $W = 1$, $B(\vec v_2)B(\vec v_1) = B(\vec u)$ is symmetric, so it equals its transpose $B(\vec v_1)B(\vec v_2)$. Conversely, commuting symmetric
positive definite matrices can be diagonalised in one orthonormal basis, so their product is again symmetric and positive
definite; it is then a pure boost (@exr-sr-symmetric-boost), and $W = 1$ by the uniqueness in @thm-sr-polar. Commuting boosts have
parallel velocities by @exr-sr-boosts-not-subgroup.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

The theorem below computes the Wigner rotation exactly. The computation is done in $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$, where boosts are the matrices
$e^{\xi\hat n\cdot\vec\sigma/2} = \cosh\tfrac\xi2 + \sinh\tfrac\xi2\,\hat n\cdot\vec\sigma$ and rotations $e^{-i\Omega\hat m\cdot\vec\sigma/2} = \cos\tfrac\Omega2 - i\sin\tfrac\Omega2\,\hat m\cdot\vec\sigma$
(@thm-sr-double-cover), and products reduce to the identity $(\vec a\cdot\vec\sigma)(\vec b\cdot\vec\sigma) = \vec a\cdot\vec b + i(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec\sigma$
[@odonnell2011wigner, Sec. 5].

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-sr-wigner-angle}
#### The Wigner angle

Let $\vec v_1$, $\vec v_2$ be non-zero with rapidities $\xi_k = \operatorname{artanh}|\vec v_k|$, directions $\hat n_k$ and angle $\theta \in [0, \pi]$ between them, $\cos\theta = \hat n_1\cdot\hat n_2$.
Then $W(\vec v_2, \vec v_1)$ is the rotation by the angle $\Omega \in [0, \pi)$ about the axis $\hat n_1 \times \hat n_2$, with
$$
\tan\frac\Omega2 = \frac{\sin\theta}{\coth\frac{\xi_1}{2}\coth\frac{\xi_2}{2} + \cos\theta} ,
$$ {#eq-sr-wigner-tan}
equivalently, with $\gamma = \gamma_1\gamma_2(1 + \vec v_1\cdot\vec v_2)$ the Lorentz factor of $\vec v_1 \oplus \vec v_2$,
$$
1 + \cos\Omega = \frac{(1 + \gamma_1 + \gamma_2 + \gamma)^2}{(1 + \gamma_1)(1 + \gamma_2)(1 + \gamma)} .
$$ {#eq-sr-wigner-cos}

*Proof.* Let $c_k = \cosh\tfrac{\xi_k}{2}$, $s_k = \sinh\tfrac{\xi_k}{2}$ and $\hat B_k = c_k + s_k\hat n_k\cdot\vec\sigma$, so that $\Lambda(\hat B_k) = B(\vec v_k)$. The product is
$$
\hat B_2\hat B_1 = \alpha + \vec\beta\cdot\vec\sigma + i\vec g\cdot\vec\sigma, \qquad \alpha = c_1c_2 + s_1s_2\cos\theta, \quad \vec\beta = c_1s_2\hat n_2 + s_1c_2\hat n_1, \quad \vec g = s_1s_2\,\hat n_2\times\hat n_1 .
$$
By the polar decomposition in $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ (@exr-sr-sl2c-simply-connected), $\hat B_2\hat B_1 = \hat W\hat H$ with $\hat W = \cos\tfrac\Omega2 - i\sin\tfrac\Omega2\,\hat m\cdot\vec\sigma \in SU(2)$
and $\hat H = C + S\hat h\cdot\vec\sigma$ positive Hermitian, $C = \cosh\tfrac\zeta2$, $S = \sinh\tfrac\zeta2$. Then $\Lambda(\hat W)$ is the rotation by $\Omega$ about $\hat m$ and $\Lambda(\hat H)$ a pure
boost, and $B(\vec v_2)B(\vec v_1) = \Lambda(\hat W)\Lambda(\hat H)$; by @thm-sr-polar the rotation in this order equals the rotation in @eq-sr-wigner-def, so $W =
\Lambda(\hat W)$. Expanding with the product identity, writing $c = \cos\tfrac\Omega2$, $s = \sin\tfrac\Omega2$,
$$
\hat W\hat H = (cC - isS\,\hat m\cdot\hat h) + (cS\,\hat h + sS\,\hat m\times\hat h)\cdot\vec\sigma - isC\,\hat m\cdot\vec\sigma .
$$
The matrices $1, \sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3$ are a basis over $\mathbb{C}$, so the coefficients agree. The coefficient of $1$ gives $cC = \alpha$ and $sS\,\hat m\cdot\hat h = 0$; the
imaginary part of the coefficient of $\vec\sigma$ gives $sC\,\hat m = -\vec g = s_1s_2\,\hat n_1\times\hat n_2$. If $\sin\theta = 0$ then $s = 0$ and $W = 1$. Otherwise $\hat m$ is
the unit vector along $\hat n_1\times\hat n_2$ with $sC = s_1s_2\sin\theta > 0$, and $\alpha > 0$ (since $c_1c_2 > s_1s_2$) gives $c > 0$, so $\Omega \in (0, \pi)$ and $\tan\tfrac\Omega2 =
s/c = s_1s_2\sin\theta/\alpha$; dividing by $s_1s_2$ gives @eq-sr-wigner-tan. For @eq-sr-wigner-cos: $1 + \cos\Omega = 2c^2 = 2\alpha^2/C^2$; $\Lambda(\hat H)$ and $B(\vec u) =
W\Lambda(\hat H)W^{-1}$ have the same rapidity $\zeta$, so $\cosh\zeta = \gamma$ and $C^2 = \tfrac12(1 + \gamma)$; and with $\sinh\xi_k = 2s_kc_k$, $4c_k^2 = 1 + \gamma_k$,
$$
1 + \gamma_1 + \gamma_2 + \gamma = (1 + \gamma_1)(1 + \gamma_2) + \sinh\xi_1\sinh\xi_2\cos\theta = 4c_1c_2(c_1c_2 + s_1s_2\cos\theta) = 4c_1c_2\alpha ,
$$
where $\gamma = \cosh\xi_1\cosh\xi_2 + \sinh\xi_1\sinh\xi_2\cos\theta$ was used. Substituting $\alpha$ and $C^2$ gives @eq-sr-wigner-cos. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The perpendicular boosts of @exm-sr-wigner-perpendicular give the first numerical value. The first example evaluates
@eq-sr-wigner-tan for them. The perpendicular case makes $\cos\theta = 0$ and the formula particularly simple.

::: {#exm-sr-wigner-numbers}
#### The angle for $0.6\hat x$ and $0.7\hat y$

$\xi_1 = \ln2$ gives $\coth\tfrac{\xi_1}{2} = \frac{e^{\xi_1} + 1}{e^{\xi_1} - 1} = 3$, and $\xi_2 = \operatorname{artanh}0.7$ gives $\coth\tfrac{\xi_2}{2} = 2.4487$. With $\theta = \pi/2$, $\tan\tfrac\Omega2 = 1/(3 \cdot
2.4487) = 0.1361$, so $\Omega = 0.2706\,$rad $= 15.5°$ about $\hat x\times\hat y = \hat z$: the observer who boosted along $x$ and then along $y$ is turned
counterclockwise relative to one boosted directly to $\vec u$. This is the rotation found numerically in @exr-sr-polar-compute.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

For small velocities the rotation is of second order. The second example extracts the leading term, which is the
Lorentzian echo of the bracket $[K_1, K_2] = -J_3$.

::: {#exm-sr-wigner-small}
#### Small velocities

For $\xi_k \ll 1$, $\coth\tfrac{\xi_k}{2} \approx 2/\xi_k$, so $\tan\tfrac\Omega2 \approx \tfrac14\xi_1\xi_2\sin\theta$ and $\Omega \approx \tfrac12|\vec v_1\times\vec v_2|$ (in units $c = 1$; $\tfrac{1}{2c^2}|\vec v_1\times\vec v_2|$ in
general). Two boosts of $30\,$km/s at right angles produce a rotation of $5 \times 10^{-9}\,$rad. The second-order size matches the group
commutator of @exr-sr-group-commutator.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In the opposite limit the rotation becomes as large as the angle between the boosts. The third example takes both speeds
to the speed of light, the regime of @fig-sr-wigner.

::: {#exm-sr-wigner-ultra}
#### Ultrarelativistic boosts

As $\xi_1, \xi_2 \to \infty$, $\coth\tfrac{\xi_k}{2} \to 1$ and $\tan\tfrac\Omega2 \to \frac{\sin\theta}{1 + \cos\theta} = \tan\tfrac\theta2$: $\Omega \to \theta$. For every finite speed $\coth\tfrac{\xi_1}{2}\coth\tfrac{\xi_2}{2} > 1$,
so $\Omega < \theta$. Two perpendicular boosts close to $c$ produce a rotation close to $90°$.
:::

With Sage, for $100$ random pairs of velocities, compute $W = B(\vec u)^{-1}B(\vec v_2)B(\vec v_1)$, its angle and axis, and compare with @eq-sr-wigner-tan,
@eq-sr-wigner-cos and the axis $\hat n_1\times\hat n_2$.

The literature quotes the Wigner angle in several equivalent forms. The second exercise derives Stapp's formula for $\sin\Omega$
[@odonnell2011wigner, eq. (21)].

::: {#exr-sr-stapp}
#### Stapp's formula

Show that
$$
\sin\Omega = \frac{\gamma_1\gamma_2|\vec v_1||\vec v_2|(1 + \gamma_1 + \gamma_2 + \gamma)}{(1 + \gamma_1)(1 + \gamma_2)(1 + \gamma)}\sin\theta .
$$
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sin\Omega = 2sc = 2(s_1s_2\sin\theta/C)(\alpha/C) = 4s_1s_2\alpha\sin\theta/(1 + \gamma)$. With $\alpha = (1 + \gamma_1 + \gamma_2 + \gamma)/(4c_1c_2)$ this is $s_1s_2(1 + \gamma_1 + \gamma_2 +
\gamma)\sin\theta/(c_1c_2(1 + \gamma))$, and $s_k/c_k = \tanh\tfrac{\xi_k}{2} = \sinh\xi_k/(1 + \cosh\xi_k) = \gamma_k|\vec v_k|/(1 + \gamma_k)$ gives the formula:

{{< sage exr-sr-stapp >}}
:::

The bound $\Omega < \theta$ has a geometric meaning on the hyperboloid of velocities. The third exercise connects the Wigner angle
with the triangle of @exr-sr-velocity-triangle.

::: {#exr-sr-wigner-defect}
#### The Wigner angle as an angular defect

For unit future timelike $a$, $b$ let $P_{a \to b}$ be the pure boost in the plane of $a$ and $b$ that sends $a$ to $b$. With $w = B(\vec v_2)e_0$ and $u =
B(\vec v_2)B(\vec v_1)e_0$, show that $B(\vec v_2)B(\vec v_1) = P_{w \to u}P_{e_0 \to w}$, so that $W(\vec v_2, \vec v_1) = P_{u \to e_0}P_{w \to u}P_{e_0 \to w}$ is the rotation produced by
the closed loop of pure boosts around the triangle $e_0wu$ on the hyperboloid of velocities. Check numerically for $\vec v_1 = 0.6\hat x$,
$\vec v_2 = 0.7\hat y$ that $\Omega$ equals $\pi$ minus the sum of the angles of this triangle.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$B(\vec v_2) = P_{e_0 \to w}$, and $B(\vec v_2)B(\vec v_1)B(\vec v_2)^{-1}$ is symmetric positive definite in the frame obtained by applying $B(\vec v_2)$, sending
$w$ to $u$: it is $P_{w \to u}$. Hence $B(\vec v_2)B(\vec v_1) = P_{w \to u}P_{e_0 \to w}$, and $P_{u \to e_0} = B(\vec u)^{-1}$ gives the loop. The angle of the rotation equals the
area of the hyperbolic triangle, $\pi$ minus its angle sum, which is $0.2706$; for the triangle $e_0$, $B(\vec v_1)e_0$, $u$ the defect would be
$0.3238$, which is not the Wigner angle:

{{< sage exr-sr-wigner-defect >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A particle moving on a curve undergoes a continuous sequence of small boosts, each in its own rest frame, and the Wigner
rotations accumulate. A gyroscope carried by the particle, on which no torque acts, keeps its axes fixed in the frame
obtained by composing these boosts, the **Fermi-Walker frame**; relative to the frame obtained from the laboratory by a
single pure boost, it turns. The proposition gives the rate.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sr-thomas}
#### Thomas precession

Let a particle move with laboratory velocity $\vec v(t)$ and acceleration $\vec a = d\vec v/dt$, and let $F(t)$ be its Fermi-Walker frame, defined by
$F(t + dt) = F(t)B(\delta\vec w)$ where $\delta\vec w$ is the velocity increment measured in the frame $F(t)$. Write $F(t) = B(\vec v(t))R(t)$ with $R(t)$ a rotation.
Then $R$ turns with the angular velocity
$$
\vec\omega_T = \frac{\gamma^2}{\gamma + 1}\,\vec a\times\vec v ,
$$ {#eq-sr-thomas}
that is, a vector with fixed components in $F$ has components in the boosted laboratory frame $B(\vec v)$ that rotate with $\vec\omega_T$.

*Proof.* $F(t + dt) = B(\vec v)RB(\delta\vec w) = B(\vec v)B(\delta\vec w')R$ with $\delta\vec w' = R\delta\vec w$ (@exr-sr-boost-conjugate). By @eq-sr-wigner-def, $B(\vec v)B(\delta\vec w') =
B(\vec v + d\vec v)W$, where $\vec v + d\vec v = \delta\vec w' \oplus \vec v$ and $W = W(\vec v, \delta\vec w')$; so $R(t + dt) = WR(t)$. By @thm-sr-wigner-angle with $\vec v_1 = \delta\vec w'$, $\vec v_2 = \vec v$,
$W$ rotates about $\delta\hat w'\times\hat v$ by $\Omega$ with $\tan\tfrac\Omega2 = \sin\theta/(\coth\tfrac{\xi_1}{2}\coth\tfrac{\xi_2}{2} + \cos\theta)$, $\xi_1 = |\delta\vec w'|$. To first order,
$\coth\tfrac{\xi_1}{2} \approx 2/\xi_1$ and $\Omega \approx |\delta\vec w'|\sin\theta\tanh\tfrac{\xi_2}{2}$, with $\tanh\tfrac{\xi_2}{2} = \gamma v/(1 + \gamma)$; as a vector, $\vec\Omega = \frac{\gamma}{1 + \gamma}\delta\vec w'\times\vec v$.
The composite-velocity formula of @exr-sr-composite-velocity, with the small velocity first, gives to first order $d\vec v_\perp = \delta\vec w'_\perp/\gamma$ for the
components perpendicular to $\vec v$; only these enter the cross product, so $\delta\vec w'\times\vec v = \gamma\,d\vec v\times\vec v$ and $\vec\Omega = \frac{\gamma^2}{1 + \gamma}d\vec v\times\vec v$. Dividing by $dt$
gives @eq-sr-thomas. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On a circular orbit the precession accumulates at a constant rate. The first example computes the angle per revolution,
which @fig-sr-wigner plots.

::: {#exm-sr-thomas-circle}
#### Precession on a circle

For uniform circular motion with speed $v$ and radius $r$, $|\vec a\times\vec v| = v^3/r$ and the period is $2\pi r/v$, so the angle per revolution is
$\frac{\gamma^2}{\gamma + 1}\frac{v^3}{r}\frac{2\pi r}{v} = 2\pi\frac{\gamma^2v^2}{\gamma + 1} = 2\pi(\gamma - 1)$, using $\gamma^2v^2 = \gamma^2 - 1$. Since $\vec a\times\vec v$ is opposite to the orbital angular velocity,
the gyroscope turns backwards relative to the orbit.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The historical application is the spin of the electron in an atom. The second example shows how the Thomas term halves
the spin-orbit coupling.

::: {#exm-sr-thomas-hydrogen}
#### The Thomas half

For $v \ll c$, $\vec\omega_T \approx \tfrac{1}{2c^2}\vec a\times\vec v$. An electron in the electric field $\vec E$ of a nucleus has $\vec a = -e\vec E/m$ and sees, in its rest
frame, the magnetic field $\vec B' \approx -\vec v\times\vec E/c^2$. A magnetic moment with $g = 2$ precesses about $\vec B'$ with angular velocity of magnitude
$\frac{e}{mc^2}|\vec v\times\vec E|$, while the Thomas precession has magnitude $\frac{e}{2mc^2}|\vec v\times\vec E|$ and the opposite sense. The net precession, and
with it the spin-orbit energy, is half of the naive value: this factor $\tfrac12$, missing before Thomas, brought the fine structure into
agreement with experiment, and the Dirac equation contains it automatically (@thm-dq-fw-hamiltonian).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Acceleration along the velocity produces no precession. The third example records this case, which is why the effect is
absent in linear accelerators.

::: {#exm-sr-thomas-linear}
#### No precession in linear motion

If $\vec a \parallel \vec v$, $\vec a\times\vec v = 0$ and $\vec\omega_T = 0$: successive boosts are collinear and their Wigner rotations vanish (@exm-sr-wigner-collinear). A
particle accelerated along a straight line, as in @prp-sr-hyperbolic-motion, keeps its spin direction fixed relative to the boosted
laboratory axes.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The definition of the Fermi-Walker frame by infinitesimal boosts is equivalent to the Fermi-Walker transport equation
$dS^\mu/d\tau = -(a\cdot S)u^\mu$ for a spatial vector $S \perp u$, with $a = du/d\tau$. The first exercise integrates it numerically for a circular orbit
and finds the angle of @exm-sr-thomas-circle.

::: {#exr-sr-fermi-walker}
#### A gyroscope on a circle by computer

With $v = 0.8$ ($\gamma = 5/3$), integrate the Fermi-Walker equation for one revolution starting from $S = (0, 1, 0, 0)$ at a point where $\vec v \parallel \hat y$, and
express the final $S$ in the frame $B(\vec v)$. Compare the angle with $-2\pi(\gamma - 1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The equation keeps $S\cdot u = 0$ and $S\cdot S$ fixed. After one revolution the components of $S$ in the boosted frame are turned by $-4\pi/3 \equiv
2\pi/3$ about $+\hat z$, that is by $2\pi(\gamma - 1)$ clockwise, opposite to the orbit:

{{< sage exr-sr-fermi-walker >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The angle $2\pi(\gamma - 1)$ has a geometric meaning. The second exercise shows that it is the area enclosed by the orbit's
velocities on the hyperboloid of @exr-sr-velocity-space, as the defect of @exr-sr-wigner-defect suggested.

::: {#exr-sr-thomas-area}
#### Precession equals enclosed area

On a circular orbit the four-velocity runs around the circle $\chi = \xi$ (the rapidity) on the hyperboloid with metric $d\chi^2 + \sinh^2\chi\,d\phi^2$
in the plane of the orbit. Compute the area of the disk $\chi \leq \xi$ and compare with $2\pi(\gamma - 1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The area is $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\xi\sinh\chi\,d\chi\,d\phi = 2\pi(\cosh\xi - 1) = 2\pi(\gamma - 1)$. The Thomas precession per revolution is the holonomy of the hyperbolic plane,
of curvature $-1$, around the loop of velocities: parallel transport around a loop turns a vector by the enclosed area.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The effect is small in atoms and large in storage rings. The third exercise estimates it for the electron in the ground
state of hydrogen in the Bohr model.

::: {#exr-sr-thomas-bohr}
#### Thomas precession in the Bohr atom

With $v = \alpha c$ ($\alpha \approx 1/137$) and $r = 0.529 \times 10^{-10}\,$m, compute $\omega_T$ and compare it with the orbital angular velocity.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$v = 2.19 \times 10^6\,$m/s, $a = v^2/r = 9.0 \times 10^{22}\,$m/s$^2$, and $\omega_T \approx av/(2c^2) = 1.1 \times 10^{12}\,$rad/s. The orbital angular velocity is
$v/r = 4.1 \times 10^{16}\,$rad/s, so $\omega_T/\omega = \tfrac12\alpha^2 \approx 2.7 \times 10^{-5}$: a fine-structure effect, of relative size $\alpha^2$:

{{< sage exr-sr-thomas-bohr >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

::::

### The Poincaré group

The seventh step adds translations. The isometries of Minkowski spacetime are the maps that preserve the interval between
every pair of events; they include the Lorentz transformations about any origin and the translations, and they form the
group that replaces the Galilean group [@bekaert2006unitary, Sec. 1.2]. @fig-sr-poincare shows that its translations and
boosts do not commute.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-sr-poincare-group}
#### Poincaré group

The **Poincaré group** is the set of maps $x \mapsto \Lambda x + a$ of $\mathbb{R}^4$ with $\Lambda \in SO^+(1, 3)$ and $a \in \mathbb{R}^4$, written $(\Lambda, a)$, with the composition
$$
(\Lambda_2, a_2)(\Lambda_1, a_1) = (\Lambda_2\Lambda_1, a_2 + \Lambda_2a_1) ,
$$
the semidirect product $ISO^+(1, 3) = \mathbb{R}^4 \rtimes SO^+(1, 3)$; it is the matrix Lie group of the $5 \times 5$ matrices $\begin{pmatrix}\Lambda & a \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$. Allowing
$\Lambda \in O(1, 3)$ gives the full group $IO(1, 3)$, and replacing $\Lambda$ by $A \in SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ acting through $\Lambda(A)$ gives its double cover.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
![Translations and boosts do not commute. A square of events (black) is translated by $a = (0, 1)$ and boosted by $L(0.6)$ in
the two orders: boost after translation (blue) and translation after boost (orange). The two images differ by the
translation $L(0.6)a - a$, as the composition law requires. Generated by `figures/sr-poincare.sage`.](figures/sr-poincare.svg){#fig-sr-poincare width=60%}

The matrix form makes the composition law automatic. The first example multiplies two matrices and reads off the law. The $5 \times 5$ representation is faithful, so nothing is lost by working with it.

::: {#exm-sr-poincare-matrix}
#### The composition law from matrices

$\begin{pmatrix}\Lambda_2 & a_2 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\Lambda_1 & a_1 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}\Lambda_2\Lambda_1 & \Lambda_2a_1 + a_2 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, and acting on $(x, 1)$ the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}\Lambda & a \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$
gives $(\Lambda x + a, 1)$. The inverse is $(\Lambda, a)^{-1} = (\Lambda^{-1}, -\Lambda^{-1}a)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The translations form a normal subgroup and the Lorentz group a subgroup that is not normal. The second example
identifies Minkowski spacetime as a coset space of the Poincaré group.

::: {#exm-sr-poincare-coset}
#### Minkowski spacetime as a coset space

The Poincaré group acts transitively on $\mathbb{R}^4$, and the stabiliser of the origin is $\{(\Lambda, 0)\} \cong SO^+(1, 3)$. By the orbit-stabiliser bijection
(@def-stabiliser), Minkowski spacetime is the coset space $ISO^+(1, 3)/SO^+(1, 3)$ (@def-coset-space), the Lorentzian analogue of $\mathbb{R}^3 = ISO(3)/SO(3)$.
The translations are normal: $(\Lambda, 0)(1, a)(\Lambda, 0)^{-1} = (1, \Lambda a)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The dimension of the Poincaré group is the largest possible for a group of isometries in four dimensions. The third example
counts it and compares with the Galilean group.

::: {#exm-sr-poincare-dimension}
#### Ten parameters

Four translations and six Lorentz parameters give $\dim ISO^+(1, 3) = 10 = 4 \cdot 5/2$, the maximal dimension of an isometry group in four
dimensions (@def-maximally-symmetric, @exm-maximal-minkowski). The Galilean group also has ten parameters (time and space translations, rotations, Galilean
boosts) and arises from the Poincaré group in the limit $c \to \infty$ (@exr-sr-poincare-algebra-limit).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the group axioms in the semidirect product form. Associativity is the only axiom that needs a short computation.

::: {#exr-sr-poincare-axioms}
#### The group axioms

Verify that the composition law is associative, that $(1, 0)$ is the identity, and that $(\Lambda^{-1}, -\Lambda^{-1}a)$ is the inverse of $(\Lambda, a)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$((\Lambda_3, a_3)(\Lambda_2, a_2))(\Lambda_1, a_1) = (\Lambda_3\Lambda_2\Lambda_1, a_3 + \Lambda_3a_2 + \Lambda_3\Lambda_2a_1)$, and the other bracketing gives $(\Lambda_3\Lambda_2\Lambda_1, a_3 + \Lambda_3(a_2 + \Lambda_2a_1))$, the
same. $(\Lambda, a)(\Lambda^{-1}, -\Lambda^{-1}a) = (1, a - a) = (1, 0)$, and the identity is clear.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Every isometry of Minkowski spacetime is a Poincaré transformation, possibly with a reflection. The second exercise proves
the affine case.

::: {#exr-sr-isometries-affine}
#### Affine isometries

Show that an affine map $x \mapsto Lx + a$ preserves the interval of every pair of events if and only if $L \in O(1, 3)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The difference of the images of $x$ and $y$ is $L(x - y)$, so the condition is $L(x - y)\cdot L(x - y) = (x - y)\cdot(x - y)$ for all displacements: $L$ preserves the
quadratic form, hence by polarisation the bilinear form, $L^T\eta L = \eta$. (That every interval-preserving map is affine is a theorem of the
same kind as the Mazur-Ulam theorem; it is not needed here.)
:::

The Lie algebra of the Poincaré group extends the Lorentz algebra by four commuting translation generators. In the
$5 \times 5$ representation the translation generator $P_\mu$ is the matrix with a single $1$ in row $\mu$ of the last column, so that $e^{a^\mu P_\mu}$
is the translation by $a$, and $P^\mu = \eta^{\mu\nu}P_\nu$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sr-poincare-algebra}
#### The Poincaré algebra

The Lie algebra $\mathfrak{iso}(1, 3)$ has the basis $M^{\mu\nu}$ (embedded in the upper-left block) and $P^\mu$, with
$$
[M^{\mu\nu}, M^{\rho\sigma}] = \eta^{\nu\rho}M^{\mu\sigma} - \eta^{\mu\rho}M^{\nu\sigma} - \eta^{\nu\sigma}M^{\mu\rho} + \eta^{\mu\sigma}M^{\nu\rho}, \qquad [M^{\mu\nu}, P^\rho] = \eta^{\nu\rho}P^\mu - \eta^{\mu\rho}P^\nu, \qquad [P^\mu, P^\nu] = 0 .
$$ {#eq-sr-poincare-brackets}
The translations span an abelian ideal, and $\mathfrak{iso}(1, 3) = \mathbb{R}^4 \rtimes \mathfrak{so}(1, 3)$. In a unitary representation the Hermitian generators $\hat P^\mu = -i\,dU(P^\mu)$
and $\hat M^{\mu\nu} = i\,dU(M^{\mu\nu})$ (so that $\hat J_i = \tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}\hat M^{jk}$ and $\hat K_i = \hat M^{0i}$ are those of @def-sr-lorentz-algebra) satisfy
$[\hat M^{\mu\nu}, \hat P^\rho] = i(\eta^{\nu\rho}\hat P^\mu - \eta^{\mu\rho}\hat P^\nu)$, and translations act as $U(1, a) = e^{ia_\mu\hat P^\mu}$; with these signs rotations are $e^{-i\theta\hat n\cdot\hat{\vec J}}$
and spatial translations $e^{-i\vec a\cdot\hat{\vec P}}$, as in quantum mechanics.

*Proof.* For a matrix group the bracket is the commutator of matrices. The Lorentz relations hold in the upper-left block by
@def-sr-lorentz-algebra. The matrix of $P_\rho$ sends the last basis vector to $e_\rho$ and kills the others, and $M^{\mu\nu}$ kills the last basis vector,
so $[M^{\mu\nu}, P_\rho] = M^{\mu\nu}P_\rho$, the generator that sends the last basis vector to $M^{\mu\nu}e_\rho = (M^{\mu\nu})^\alpha{}_\rho e_\alpha = \eta^{\mu\alpha}\delta^\nu_\rho e_\alpha - \eta^{\nu\alpha}\delta^\mu_\rho e_\alpha$:
$[M^{\mu\nu}, P_\rho] = \delta^\nu_\rho P^\mu - \delta^\mu_\rho P^\nu$, and raising $\rho$ gives the stated bracket. Two translation generators multiply to zero in both orders.
For the Hermitian generators, $[\hat M^{\mu\nu}, \hat P^\rho] = (i)(-i)[dU(M^{\mu\nu}), dU(P^\rho)] = dU([M^{\mu\nu}, P^\rho]) = \eta^{\nu\rho}dU(P^\mu) - \eta^{\mu\rho}dU(P^\nu)$, and
$dU(P^\mu) = i\hat P^\mu$ gives the factor $i$; and $e^{a^\mu P_\mu} = e^{a_\mu P^\mu}$ is represented by $e^{a_\mu dU(P^\mu)} = e^{ia_\mu\hat P^\mu}$. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In terms of the three-dimensional generators the brackets have a familiar reading. The first example writes them with the
energy $H = P^0$ and the momentum $P^i$.

::: {#exm-sr-poincare-3d}
#### Energy, momentum, rotations and boosts

From @eq-sr-poincare-brackets with $J_i = \tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}M^{jk}$, $K_i = M^{0i}$: $[J_i, P^0] = 0$ (energy is a scalar under rotations), $[J_i, P^j] = \epsilon_{ijk}P^k$
(momentum is a vector), $[K_i, P^0] = -P^i$ and $[K_i, P^j] = -\delta_{ij}P^0$ (boosts mix energy and momentum). For example $[K_1, P^1] = [M^{01}, P^1] = \eta^{11}P^0 -
\eta^{01}P^1 = -P^0$.
:::

The algebra acts on functions of spacetime by differential operators. The second example gives the realisation that
quantum field theory uses for scalar fields.

::: {#exm-sr-poincare-differential}
#### Differential operators

On functions, the active transformation $(\Lambda, a)\cdot f(x) = f(\Lambda^{-1}(x - a))$ has the generators $dU(P_\mu) = -\partial_\mu$ and $dU(M^{\mu\nu}) = x^\mu\partial^\nu -
x^\nu\partial^\mu$, which satisfy @eq-sr-poincare-brackets (@exr-sr-differential-brackets). The Hermitian momentum is $\hat P^\mu = -i\,dU(P^\mu) = i\partial^\mu$, so that
$\hat P^\mu e^{-ip\cdot x} = p^\mu e^{-ip\cdot x}$: the familiar $\hat E = i\partial_t$ and $\hat{\vec p} = -i\nabla$ of wave mechanics. Likewise $\hat J_3 = i\,dU(J_3) = -i(x\partial_y - y\partial_x)$,
the orbital angular momentum $L_z$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Lorentz algebra is semisimple but the Poincaré algebra is not. The third example identifies the obstruction, which
is the abelian ideal of translations.

::: {#exm-sr-poincare-not-semisimple}
#### Not semisimple

The translations $P^\mu$ span an abelian ideal, since $[M, P] \subset \operatorname{span}(P)$ and $[P, P] = 0$; a semisimple Lie algebra has no non-zero abelian ideals,
so $\mathfrak{iso}(1, 3)$ is not semisimple. Its Killing form vanishes on the translations. This is why its Casimir operators are not quadratic
forms in all generators, as for $\mathfrak{su}(2)$, but are built from $P^\mu$ and the Pauli-Lubanski vector.
:::

The differential operators of the second example are the form in which the algebra appears in field theory. The second
exercise checks one of their brackets.

::: {#exr-sr-differential-brackets}
#### The algebra on functions

Show that $\mathcal{P}^\mu = -\partial^\mu$ and $\mathcal{M}^{\mu\nu} = x^\mu\partial^\nu - x^\nu\partial^\mu$ satisfy $[\mathcal{M}^{\mu\nu}, \mathcal{P}^\rho] = \eta^{\nu\rho}\mathcal{P}^\mu - \eta^{\mu\rho}\mathcal{P}^\nu$ on smooth
functions, and derive $\mathcal{M}^{\mu\nu}$ from the action $f \mapsto f\circ\Lambda^{-1}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[x^\mu\partial^\nu, -\partial^\rho]f = -x^\mu\partial^\nu\partial^\rho f + \partial^\rho(x^\mu\partial^\nu f) = \eta^{\rho\mu}\partial^\nu f$, so $[\mathcal{M}^{\mu\nu}, \mathcal{P}^\rho] = \eta^{\rho\mu}\partial^\nu - \eta^{\rho\nu}\partial^\mu = \eta^{\nu\rho}\mathcal{P}^\mu -
\eta^{\mu\rho}\mathcal{P}^\nu$. For the derivation, $\frac{d}{dt}f(e^{-tM^{\mu\nu}}x)|_{t=0} = -(M^{\mu\nu}x)^\alpha\partial_\alpha f = -(x^\nu\partial^\mu - x^\mu\partial^\nu)f$, using $(M^{\mu\nu}x)^\alpha = \eta^{\mu\alpha}x^\nu -
\eta^{\nu\alpha}x^\mu$. The map from the algebra to differential operators is a homomorphism, as it must be for a left action.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The Galilean algebra is a limit of the Poincaré algebra. The third exercise performs the contraction. The contraction explains why the Galilean group is an approximation to the Poincaré group at low speeds.

::: {#exr-sr-poincare-algebra-limit}
#### The Galilean limit of the algebra

Restore $c$ by $P^0 = H/c$ and $K_i = cG_i$, where $H$ generates time translations in units of time and $G_i$ Galilean boosts. Show that as $c \to \infty$ the
brackets become $[G_i, P^j] = -\delta_{ij}H/c^2 \to 0$ and $[G_i, G_j] = -\epsilon_{ijk}J_k/c^2 \to 0$, while $[G_i, H] = -P^i$ survives: the Galilean algebra without
central extension.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[K_i, P^j] = -\delta_{ij}P^0$ becomes $c[G_i, P^j] = -\delta_{ij}H/c$, so $[G_i, P^j] = -\delta_{ij}H/c^2$; $[K_i, K_j] = -\epsilon_{ijk}J_k$ becomes $[G_i, G_j] = -\epsilon_{ijk}J_k/c^2$; $[K_i, P^0] = -P^i$ becomes $[G_i,
H] = -P^i$, unchanged. As $c \to \infty$ boosts commute with each other and with momenta: the Galilean algebra. (In quantum mechanics the
mass appears as a central term $[G_i, P^j] \propto \delta_{ij}m$, the remnant of $-\delta_{ij}H/c^2$ with $H \approx mc^2$.)
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

In a unitary representation the momentum operators can be diagonalised together, but the Lorentz generators do not commute
with them. One more vector operator is needed to describe the spin of a state of definite momentum, and it is built from
both [@bekaert2006unitary, Sec. 1.2].

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-sr-pauli-lubanski}
#### Pauli-Lubanski vector

In a unitary representation of the Poincaré group with Hermitian generators $\hat P^\mu$, $\hat M^{\mu\nu}$, the **Pauli-Lubanski vector** is
$$
\hat W_\mu = \tfrac12\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\hat M^{\nu\rho}\hat P^\sigma , \qquad \epsilon_{0123} = 1 .
$$ {#eq-sr-pauli-lubanski}
The order of the factors does not matter, since $[\hat M^{\nu\rho}, \hat P^\sigma]$ is a combination of $\eta^{\rho\sigma}$ and $\eta^{\nu\sigma}$, which vanish against $\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In the rest frame of a massive state the Pauli-Lubanski vector is the spin. The first example computes it, with the
Hermitian rotation generators $\hat J_i = \tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}\hat M^{jk}$.

::: {#exm-sr-pl-rest}
#### The rest frame

On a state with $\hat P^\mu = (m, 0, 0, 0)$, $\hat W_0 = \tfrac12\epsilon_{0ijk}\hat M^{ij}\hat P^k = 0$ and $\hat W_i = \tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk0}\hat M^{jk}m = -\tfrac12m\epsilon_{ijk}\hat M^{jk} = -m\hat J_i$, since $\epsilon_{ijk0} =
-\epsilon_{0ijk}$. So $\hat W^\mu = (0, m\hat{\vec J})$ and $\hat W_\mu\hat W^\mu = -m^2\hat{\vec J}^2$: on a particle of spin $s$, $-m^2s(s + 1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Pauli-Lubanski vector is orthogonal to the momentum. The second example proves it from the antisymmetry of $\epsilon$. The orthogonality removes one of the four components.

::: {#exm-sr-pl-orthogonal}
#### $\hat W\cdot\hat P = 0$

$\hat W_\mu\hat P^\mu = \tfrac12\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\hat M^{\nu\rho}\hat P^\sigma\hat P^\mu$, and $\hat P^\sigma\hat P^\mu$ is symmetric in $\sigma\mu$ (the momenta commute) while $\epsilon$ is antisymmetric: the sum
vanishes. In the rest frame this says $\hat W^0 = 0$; in general it leaves three independent components, the spin.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For a massless state there is no rest frame. The third example computes $\hat W$ for the standard light-like momentum, where it
involves a rotation and two null rotations.

::: {#exm-sr-pl-massless}
#### A light-like momentum

On a state with $\hat P^\mu = k^\mu = (\kappa, 0, 0, \kappa)$, a computation like that of the first example gives $\hat W^0 = \hat W^3 = \kappa\hat J_3$, $\hat W_1 = -\kappa(\hat J_1 +
\hat K_2)$ and $\hat W_2 = \kappa(\hat K_1 - \hat J_2)$ (@exr-sr-pl-components). The combinations $K_1 - J_2$ and $K_2 + J_1$ generate the null rotations that fix $k$
(@exm-sr-a0-image); on states on which they act trivially, $\hat W^\mu = \hat J_3k^\mu$: the Pauli-Lubanski vector is the helicity times the momentum.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The components in the third example require bookkeeping of signs of $\epsilon$. The first exercise does it by computer, treating
$\hat M^{\nu\rho}$ as formal symbols.

::: {#exr-sr-pl-components}
#### Components of $\hat W$ by computer

With Sage, compute $\hat W_\mu = \tfrac12\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\hat M^{\nu\rho}k^\sigma$ for $k = (m, 0, 0, 0)$ and for $k = (\kappa, 0, 0, \kappa)$, with $\hat M^{\nu\rho} = -\hat M^{\rho\nu}$ formal and $\hat J_i = \tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}\hat M^{jk}$,
$\hat K_i = \hat M^{0i}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For the rest momentum $\hat W_\mu = (0, -m\hat J_1, -m\hat J_2, -m\hat J_3)$; for the light-like one $\hat W_\mu = (\kappa\hat J_3, -\kappa(\hat J_1 + \hat K_2), \kappa(\hat K_1 - \hat J_2), -\kappa\hat J_3)$,
so $\hat W^0 = \hat W^3 = \kappa\hat J_3$:

{{< sage exr-sr-pl-components >}}
:::

Under parity the momentum is a vector and the Pauli-Lubanski vector an axial vector. The second exercise shows the
consequence for massless particles.

::: {#exr-sr-pl-parity}
#### Parity reverses helicity

Under parity $\hat P^0 \to \hat P^0$, $\hat P^i \to -\hat P^i$, $\hat J_i \to \hat J_i$, $\hat K_i \to -\hat K_i$. Show that $\hat W^0 \to -\hat W^0$ and $\hat W^i \to \hat W^i$, and conclude that parity maps a massless
state with $\hat W = \lambda\hat P$ to one with $\hat W = -\lambda\hat P$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\hat W^0 = \hat{\vec J}\cdot\hat{\vec P}$ (from $\hat W_0 = \tfrac12\epsilon_{0ijk}\hat M^{ij}\hat P^k = \hat J_k\hat P^k$), which changes sign; $\hat W^i = \hat P^0\hat J_i + (\hat{\vec K}\times\hat{\vec P})_i$ up to the ordering, which does not.
So $\hat W$ is an axial vector, and $\hat W = \lambda\hat P$ becomes $(-\hat W^0, \hat W^i) = \lambda(\hat P^0, -\hat P^i)$, that is $\hat W' = -\lambda\hat P'$: helicity $\lambda \to -\lambda$. A
parity-invariant massless particle, such as the photon, needs both helicities $\pm\lambda$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For massless particles both $\hat P^2$ and $\hat W^2$ vanish on the helicity states, and this forces proportionality. The third
exercise proves it with the geometry of null vectors.

::: {#exr-sr-pl-proportional}
#### $\hat W$ is proportional to $\hat P$

On a state of definite light-like momentum $k$, suppose $\hat W^\mu$ acts as a real vector $w^\mu$ (a common eigenvector) with $w\cdot w = 0$. Show that
$w = \lambda k$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$w\cdot k = 0$ by @exm-sr-pl-orthogonal and $k\cdot k = w\cdot w = 0$. Two orthogonal null vectors are parallel (@exr-sr-null-orthogonal), so $w = \lambda k$ (or $w = 0$, $\lambda = 0$).
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Operators that commute with every generator are constant on irreducible representations, by Schur's lemma (@thm-schur, whose
infinite-dimensional version holds for unitary representations). The theorem below shows that the Poincaré algebra has two
such operators, and their values are the mass and the spin.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-sr-casimirs}
#### The Casimir operators $\hat P^2$ and $\hat W^2$

$\hat P^2 = \hat P_\mu\hat P^\mu$ and $\hat W^2 = \hat W_\mu\hat W^\mu$ commute with all $\hat P^\rho$ and $\hat M^{\rho\sigma}$. On a representation of a single massive particle of spin
$s$ they take the values $m^2$ and $-m^2s(s + 1)$; on a massless helicity representation both vanish.

*Proof.* Write $[\hat M^{\mu\nu}, \hat V^\rho] = i(\eta^{\nu\rho}\hat V^\mu - \eta^{\mu\rho}\hat V^\nu)$ for an operator $\hat V$ that transforms as a vector; $\hat P$ does so by
@prp-sr-poincare-algebra. For such $\hat V$, $[\hat M^{\mu\nu}, \hat V_\rho\hat V^\rho] = [\hat M^{\mu\nu}, \hat V_\rho]\hat V^\rho + \hat V_\rho[\hat M^{\mu\nu}, \hat V^\rho] = i(\hat V^\mu\hat V^\nu - \hat V^\nu\hat V^\mu + \hat V^\nu\hat V^\mu -
\hat V^\mu\hat V^\nu) = 0$, after lowering the index in the first term. *$\hat P^2$:* it commutes with $\hat P^\rho$ since momenta commute, and with $\hat M$ by the
identity. *$\hat W^2$ and translations:* $[\hat P^\alpha, \hat W_\mu] = \tfrac12\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}[\hat P^\alpha, \hat M^{\nu\rho}]\hat P^\sigma$ is a combination of terms $\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\hat P^\nu\hat P^\sigma$ and
$\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\hat P^\rho\hat P^\sigma$, which vanish by antisymmetry; so $\hat W_\mu$, and $\hat W^2$, commute with $\hat P^\alpha$. *$\hat W^2$ and Lorentz generators:* $\hat W$ transforms as a
vector. Indeed, $\hat M^{\nu\rho}$ and $\hat P^\sigma$ transform as tensors, so $[\hat M^{\alpha\beta}, \hat W_\mu]$ is $\tfrac12$ times the sum of four terms in which one index of
$\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}$ is acted on by the infinitesimal Lorentz transformation; for $X \in \mathfrak{so}(1, 3)$, $\epsilon_{\lambda\nu\rho\sigma}X^\lambda{}_\mu + \epsilon_{\mu\lambda\rho\sigma}X^\lambda{}_\nu + \epsilon_{\mu\nu\lambda\sigma}X^\lambda{}_\rho +
\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\lambda}X^\lambda{}_\sigma = (\operatorname{tr}X)\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} = 0$ (the infinitesimal form of $\det\Lambda\,\epsilon = \epsilon$, with $\operatorname{tr}X = 0$ because $\eta X$ is antisymmetric), so the three
contracted indices can be traded for the free one, which gives the vector law for $\hat W$. The identity then shows that $\hat W^2$
commutes with $\hat M$. *Values:* in the rest frame $\hat P^2 = m^2$ and $\hat W^2 = -m^2\hat{\vec J}^2 = -m^2s(s + 1)$ (@exm-sr-pl-rest); since both are invariant, these
values hold on the whole representation. For helicity states $\hat P^2 = k^2 = 0$ and $\hat W = \lambda\hat P$ gives $\hat W^2 = \lambda^2\hat P^2 = 0$. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first Casimir is the mass. The first example evaluates it on plane waves and on a particle with given energy and
momentum.

::: {#exm-sr-casimir-mass}
#### The mass as an eigenvalue

On the plane wave $e^{-ip\cdot x}$ the momentum is $\hat p^\mu = i\partial^\mu$ (@exm-sr-poincare-differential), so $\hat P^2 = -\Box$ has the eigenvalue $p\cdot p = E^2 - \vec p^2$; for
an electron this is $m_e^2 = (0.511\,\mathrm{MeV})^2$ in every frame (@def-sr-four-momentum). The condition $\hat P^2 = m^2$ on wave functions is the
Klein-Gordon equation $(\Box + m^2)\phi = 0$ (@def-klein-gordon).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The second Casimir is the spin. The second example evaluates it for a spin-one-half particle and compares it with the
square of the angular momentum, which is not invariant.

::: {#exm-sr-casimir-spin}
#### The spin as an eigenvalue

For an electron $\hat W^2 = -m_e^2 \cdot \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac32 = -\tfrac34m_e^2$. The total angular momentum $\hat{\vec J}^2$ is not a Casimir: it includes orbital angular
momentum and does not commute with the boosts (@exr-sr-j2-not-casimir), so it is not a label of the particle; $-\hat W^2/\hat P^2$ is, and
equals $s(s + 1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Massless particles have both Casimirs zero, so these do not distinguish them. The third example shows that helicity takes
over the role of spin.

::: {#exm-sr-casimir-massless}
#### Massless particles

For the photon $\hat P^2 = \hat W^2 = 0$, and the representations are told apart by the helicity $\lambda$ in $\hat W = \lambda\hat P$, an invariant because both sides are
vectors: $\lambda = \pm1$ for the photon, $\pm2$ for the graviton, and $-\tfrac12$ for a left-handed massless neutrino.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the commutation of $\hat P^2$ with the Lorentz generators in the explicit form of the proof. The calculation is the proof of the theorem in a single instance.

::: {#exr-sr-p2-invariant}
#### $\hat P^2$ commutes with the Lorentz generators

Using $[\hat M^{\mu\nu}, \hat P^\rho] = i(\eta^{\nu\rho}\hat P^\mu - \eta^{\mu\rho}\hat P^\nu)$, compute $[\hat K_1, \hat P^2]$ explicitly in components.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[\hat K_1, \hat P^0] = -i\hat P^1$ and $[\hat K_1, \hat P^1] = -i\hat P^0$ (from the bracket with $\mu\nu = 01$), and $\hat K_1$ commutes with $\hat P^2$, $\hat P^3$. With $\hat P^2 = (\hat P^0)^2 -
(\hat P^1)^2 - \dots$: $[\hat K_1, (\hat P^0)^2] = -i(\hat P^1\hat P^0 + \hat P^0\hat P^1)$ and $[\hat K_1, (\hat P^1)^2] = -i(\hat P^0\hat P^1 + \hat P^1\hat P^0)$, which cancel in the difference.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The angular momentum squared is a Casimir of the rotation algebra but not of the Lorentz algebra. The second exercise
shows this in the four-vector representation.

::: {#exr-sr-j2-not-casimir}
#### $\vec J^2$ is not invariant under boosts

In the $4 \times 4$ representation, compute $[K_1, J_1^2 + J_2^2 + J_3^2]$ and show it is non-zero. Which quadratic combinations of $J$ and $K$
commute with all generators?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The commutator is a non-zero matrix. The invariant combinations are $\vec J^2 - \vec K^2 = 2(\vec A^2 + \vec B^2)$ and $\vec J\cdot\vec K = -i(\vec A^2 - \vec B^2)$, the Casimirs
of the two factors of @prp-sr-complexification; on four-vectors they equal $-3$ and $0$:

{{< sage exr-sr-j2-not-casimir >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The third exercise shows that two states related by a Poincaré transformation have the same Casimir values, which is the
group-level meaning of the theorem. The argument works for any unitary representation in which momenta transform as vectors.

::: {#exr-sr-casimir-group}
#### Invariance under the group

Using $U(\Lambda)\hat P^\mu U(\Lambda)^{-1} = (\Lambda^{-1})^\mu{}_\nu\hat P^\nu$ for Lorentz transformations, show that $U(\Lambda)\hat P^2U(\Lambda)^{-1} = \hat P^2$, and that a state $U(\Lambda)|\psi\rangle$ has the same mass as
$|\psi\rangle$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$U\hat P_\mu\hat P^\mu U^{-1} = \eta_{\mu\alpha}(\Lambda^{-1})^\alpha{}_\beta(\Lambda^{-1})^\mu{}_\nu\hat P^\beta\hat P^\nu = \eta_{\beta\nu}\hat P^\beta\hat P^\nu = \hat P^2$, by the defining property of $\Lambda^{-1} \in O(1, 3)$. If $\hat P^2|\psi\rangle =
m^2|\psi\rangle$, then $\hat P^2U|\psi\rangle = U\hat P^2|\psi\rangle = m^2U|\psi\rangle$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Wigner's classification {#sec-sr-wigner-classification}

The last step classifies the unitary irreducible representations of the Poincaré group, the possible elementary particles
of a relativistic quantum theory. A state of definite momentum $p$ can be moved to any other momentum on the orbit of $p$, so
the representation is determined by what happens to a single standard momentum, and only the transformations that fix it
matter. Wigner's method of 1939, reviewed in @bekaert2006unitary [Sec. 3], builds the representation from these. @fig-sr-orbits
shows the orbits.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-sr-little-group}
#### Little group

For a four-momentum $k$, the **little group** of $k$ is its stabiliser (@def-stabiliser) in $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$, $G_k = \{A : \Lambda(A)k = k\}$, or its image $\{\Lambda \in
SO^+(1, 3) : \Lambda k = k\}$. Little groups of momenta on the same orbit are conjugate: $G_{\Lambda(A)k} = AG_kA^{-1}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
![Orbits of the Lorentz group in momentum space, with one spatial dimension suppressed. The two sheets of the mass
hyperboloid $p^2 = m^2$ (blue), the light cone $p^2 = 0$ (orange) and the one-sheeted hyperboloid $p^2 = -\mu^2$ of tachyonic
momenta (green). The marked points are the standard momenta $(m, 0, 0)$, $(\kappa, 0, \kappa)$ and $(0, 0, \mu)$. Generated by
`figures/sr-orbits.sage`.](figures/sr-orbits.svg){#fig-sr-orbits width=70%}

The rest momentum of a massive particle is fixed by rotations only. The first example checks this, which makes the spin
of a massive particle an ordinary spin.

::: {#exm-sr-little-massive}
#### A particle at rest

For $k = (m, 0, 0, 0)$, $X(k) = m\cdot1$ and $AX(k)A^\dagger = mAA^\dagger$, so $G_k = \{A : AA^\dagger = 1\} = SU(2)$; its image is the rotation group $SO(3)$
(@exr-sr-lambda00-one). The spin of a massive particle is its behaviour under these rotations.
:::

A spacelike momentum has a non-compact little group. The second example identifies it as the Lorentz group of one lower
dimension.

::: {#exm-sr-little-tachyonic}
#### A spacelike momentum

For $k = (0, 0, 0, \mu)$ the transformations fixing $k$ act on the orthogonal complement, spanned by $e_0$, $e_1$, $e_2$ with the form $\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1)$: the
little group is $SO^+(1, 2)$, the Lorentz group of three-dimensional Minkowski space. In $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$, $X(k) = \mu\sigma_3$ and $G_k = \{A : A\sigma_3A^\dagger = \sigma_3\} =
SU(1, 1)$, isomorphic to $SL(2, \mathbb{R})$.
:::

The zero momentum is fixed by everything. The third example notes what this means physically. It is the degenerate end of the classification.

::: {#exm-sr-little-zero}
#### Zero momentum

For $k = 0$ the little group is all of $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$, and a representation with zero momentum is a representation of the Lorentz group on which
translations act trivially. The vacuum, invariant under everything, is the trivial one; the others are infinite-dimensional
(@exr-sr-field-complex) and describe no particle.
:::

The conjugacy statement of the definition is a special case of @def-stabiliser. The first exercise proves it directly. Only the homomorphism property of $\Lambda$ is needed.

::: {#exr-sr-little-conjugate}
#### Conjugate little groups

Show that $G_{\Lambda(A)k} = AG_kA^{-1}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$B \in G_{\Lambda(A)k}$ iff $\Lambda(B)\Lambda(A)k = \Lambda(A)k$ iff $\Lambda(A^{-1}BA)k = k$ iff $A^{-1}BA \in G_k$, using that $\Lambda$ is a homomorphism.
:::

The little group of the rest momentum in $SO^+(1, 3)$ follows from @exr-sr-lambda00-one as well. The second exercise derives it from
the polar decomposition instead.

::: {#exr-sr-little-polar}
#### The rest momentum and the polar decomposition

Show with @thm-sr-polar that $\Lambda \in SO^+(1, 3)$ fixes $e_0$ if and only if its boost part is trivial.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\Lambda = BR$ with $B = B_{\Lambda e_0}$. If $\Lambda e_0 = e_0$, then $B = B_{e_0} = 1$ and $\Lambda = R$ is a rotation. Conversely rotations fix $e_0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The little group of a spacelike momentum contains boosts. The third exercise exhibits one and checks that it fixes $k$.

::: {#exr-sr-little-tachyon-boost}
#### A boost that fixes a spacelike momentum

Show that the boosts along $x$ and $y$ and the rotations about $z$ fix $k = (0, 0, 0, \mu)$, and that they generate a three-dimensional group.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e^{\eta K_1}$ and $e^{\eta K_2}$ act only on $(t, x)$ and $(t, y)$, and $e^{\theta J_3}$ on $(x, y)$; all leave $z$ unchanged and $k$ has only a $z$-component. The
generators $K_1$, $K_2$, $J_3$ close: $[K_1, K_2] = -J_3$, $[J_3, K_1] = K_2$, $[J_3, K_2] = -K_1$, the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(1, 2)$ of dimension three.
:::

The orbits and the little groups of all standard momenta are collected in the proposition below. The massless case is the
interesting one: its little group is not a rotation group but the group of motions of a Euclidean plane [@bekaert2006unitary,
Sec. 3.2].

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sr-little-groups}
#### Orbits and little groups

The orbits of $SO^+(1, 3)$ on $\mathbb{R}^4$ are: the origin; for each $m > 0$ the two sheets $p^2 = m^2$, $\pm p^0 > 0$; the two half-cones $p^2 = 0$, $\pm p^0 > 0$; and
for each $\mu > 0$ the hyperboloid $p^2 = -\mu^2$. The little groups in $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ of the standard momenta are $SU(2)$ for $(m, 0, 0, 0)$; $SU(1, 1)$ for $(0, 0, 0,
\mu)$; $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ for $0$; and for $k = (\kappa, 0, 0, \kappa)$
$$
G_k = \Bigl\{g(\phi, w) = \begin{pmatrix}e^{-i\phi/2} & e^{-i\phi/2}w \\ 0 & e^{i\phi/2}\end{pmatrix} : \phi \in \mathbb{R}/4\pi\mathbb{Z}, w \in \mathbb{C}\Bigr\}, \qquad g(\phi_1, w_1)g(\phi_2, w_2) = g(\phi_1 + \phi_2,
e^{i\phi_2}w_1 + w_2) ,
$$
a double cover of the Euclidean group $ISO(2)$ of the plane $\mathbb{C}$, with Lie algebra spanned by $J_3$, $E_1 = K_1 - J_2$, $E_2 = K_2 + J_1$ and brackets
$[E_1, E_2] = 0$, $[J_3, E_1] = E_2$, $[J_3, E_2] = -E_1$.

*Proof.* *Orbits.* Lorentz transformations preserve $p^2$, and orthochronous ones the sign of $p^0$ for $p^2 \geq 0$, $p \neq 0$ (@exm-sr-time-orientation). On each
set, transitivity: a timelike $p$ with $p^0 > 0$ is $mB_ue_0$ with $u = p/m$; a null $p = (E, E\hat n)$ is $R\,e^{\ln(E/\kappa)K_3}k$ with $R$ a rotation taking $\hat z$
to $\hat n$; a spacelike $p$ is first boosted to $p^0 = 0$ (@prp-sr-simultaneity) and then rotated to $(0, 0, 0, \mu)$; negative energies follow with $-1$.
*Little groups.* By @eq-sr-sl2c-action, $A \in G_k$ iff $AX(k)A^\dagger = X(k)$. For $X = m1$ this is $AA^\dagger = 1$; for $X = \mu\sigma_3$, $A\sigma_3A^\dagger = \sigma_3$ with $\det A = 1$, which
defines $SU(1, 1)$. For $k = (\kappa, 0, 0, \kappa)$, $X(k) = \operatorname{diag}(2\kappa, 0)$; with $A = \begin{pmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{pmatrix}$, $AX(k)A^\dagger = 2\kappa\begin{pmatrix}|a|^2 & a\bar c \\ c\bar a &
|c|^2\end{pmatrix}$, which equals $X(k)$ iff $|a| = 1$ and $c = 0$; then $d = 1/a$, and writing $a = e^{-i\phi/2}$, $b = e^{-i\phi/2}w$ gives $g(\phi, w)$. The product is
$g(\phi_1, w_1)g(\phi_2, w_2) = \operatorname{diag}(e^{-i\phi_1/2}, e^{i\phi_1/2})N(w_1)\operatorname{diag}(e^{-i\phi_2/2}, e^{i\phi_2/2})N(w_2)$ with $N(w) = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1 & w \\ 0 & 1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, and
moving the diagonal matrix to the left conjugates $N(w_1)$ into $N(e^{i\phi_2}w_1)$. This is the law of rotations by $\phi$ (mod $2\pi$ for the image, mod $4\pi$
upstairs) and translations by $w$ of the plane. The Lie algebra: $e^{-i\phi\sigma_3/2}$ covers $e^{\phi J_3}$, and $N(w)$ covers $e^{(\operatorname{Re}w)E_1 + (\operatorname{Im}w)E_2}$ by
@exm-sr-null-rotation and @exr-sr-null-rotation-exp (and its analogue for imaginary $w$); the brackets follow from @eq-sr-lorentz-brackets:
$[E_1, E_2] = [K_1, K_2] + [K_1, J_1] - [J_2, K_2] - [J_2, J_1] = -J_3 + 0 - 0 + J_3 = 0$, $[J_3, E_1] = K_2 + J_1 = E_2$, $[J_3, E_2] = -K_1 + J_2 = -E_1$. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The null rotations of the massless little group have a direct physical effect. The first example shows that they shift the
polarisation vector of a light wave by a multiple of its wave vector, which is a gauge transformation.

::: {#exm-sr-little-gauge}
#### Null rotations are gauge transformations

The null rotation of @exm-sr-null-rotation sends $e_1$ to the second column of its matrix, $(a, 1, 0, a) = e_1 + ak$ with $k = (1, 0, 0, 1)$. A plane
wave $A^\mu = \epsilon^\mu e^{-ik\cdot x}$ with $\epsilon = e_1$ is mapped to one with $\epsilon = e_1 + ak$, and $A^\mu \to A^\mu + ak^\mu e^{-ik\cdot x} = A^\mu + \partial^\mu(iae^{-ik\cdot x})$ is a gauge
transformation (@def-field-strength-abelian): the field strength is unchanged. This is why a massless vector particle has only
two physical polarisations.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The orbit of the electron is a mass shell. The second example describes the states of an electron in this language.

::: {#exm-sr-little-electron}
#### The states of an electron

An electron has momentum on the sheet $p^2 = m_e^2$, $p^0 > 0$, a copy of the hyperboloid of velocities of @exr-sr-velocity-space. Its little group
$SU(2)$ acts on the spin states $|{\uparrow}\rangle$, $|{\downarrow}\rangle$ of the electron at rest; a state of momentum $p$ is defined by applying the standard boost
$B_{p/m}$ to the rest states. The positron, with the same mass and spin, lives on the same orbit in a different representation of the
internal symmetries.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The composition law of the massless little group mixes rotations and translations as the Euclidean group of the plane
does. The third example compares the two laws.

::: {#exm-sr-little-euclidean}
#### The Euclidean group of the plane

The map $T_{(\phi, w)}(z) = e^{-i\phi}(z + w)$ of the complex plane, a translation by $w$ followed by a rotation by $-\phi$, satisfies $T_{(\phi_1, w_1)}\circ
T_{(\phi_2, w_2)}(z) = e^{-i(\phi_1 + \phi_2)}(z + w_2 + e^{i\phi_2}w_1) = T_{(\phi_1 + \phi_2, e^{i\phi_2}w_1 + w_2)}(z)$: the law of @prp-sr-little-groups. So $g(\phi, w) \mapsto T_{(\phi, w)}$ is a
homomorphism onto the Euclidean group of the plane, $\mathbb{C} \rtimes U(1)$, with kernel $\{g(0, 0), g(2\pi, 0)\} = \{1, -1\}$: the little group is its double cover.
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

Transitivity on the light cone uses a rotation and a boost along the standard direction. The second exercise constructs
them for a given photon momentum.

::: {#exr-sr-cone-transitive}
#### Reaching any light-like momentum

Find $\Lambda \in SO^+(1, 3)$ with $\Lambda k = p$ for $k = (1, 0, 0, 1)$ and $p = (5, 3, 0, 4)$.

$(3/5, 0, 4/5)$: $(5, 0, 0, 5) \mapsto (5, 3, 0, 4)$:

{{< sage exr-sr-cone-transitive >}}

The massless little group has a three-dimensional orbit structure of its own. The third exercise shows that its rotation
part is what remains when the translations act trivially.

::: {#exr-sr-little-quotient}
#### Dividing out the translations

Show that the translations $\{g(0, w)\}$ form a normal subgroup of $G_k$ and that the quotient is $U(1)$, with $\phi$ defined modulo $4\pi$. What are the
one-dimensional unitary representations of $G_k$ that are trivial on the translations?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$g(\phi, w)g(0, w')g(\phi, w)^{-1}$ has angle $\phi + 0 - \phi = 0$, so it is a translation: the subgroup is normal, and $g(\phi, w) \mapsto \phi$ is a homomorphism onto
$\mathbb{R}/4\pi\mathbb{Z}$ with this kernel. Its unitary characters are $e^{-i\lambda\phi}$ with $e^{-4\pi i\lambda} = 1$, that is $\lambda \in \tfrac12\mathbb{Z}$: the helicities of
@thm-sr-wigner-classification.
:::

**Sage.** Pending.

Wigner's construction defines a representation of the whole group from a representation of the little group. A state of
momentum $p$ is obtained from a state of the standard momentum $k$ by a chosen transformation $A_p$; any other transformation
moves it to a state of momentum $\Lambda p$, up to a little-group transformation that acts on the internal label. The theorem below
states the construction for wave functions on the orbit [@bekaert2006unitary, Sec. 3.1, eqs. (9)-(13)].

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-sr-induced}
#### Wigner's induced representation

Let $k = (m, 0, 0, 0)$ with $m > 0$ or $k = (\kappa, 0, 0, \kappa)$, let $\mathcal{O}$ be its orbit with the measure $d\mu(p) = d^3p/(2p^0)$, let $D$ be a unitary representation of
$G_k$ on a Hilbert space $V$, and choose for each $p \in \mathcal{O}$ an $A_p \in SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ with $\Lambda(A_p)k = p$, depending measurably on $p$. On $\mathcal{H} = L^2(\mathcal{O}, d\mu;
V)$ define, for $(A, a)$ in the double cover of the Poincaré group, with $\Lambda = \Lambda(A)$,
$$
(U(A, a)\psi)(p) = e^{ip\cdot a}\,D\bigl(W(A, p)\bigr)\,\psi(\Lambda^{-1}p), \qquad W(A, p) = A_p^{-1}AA_{\Lambda^{-1}p} \in G_k .
$$ {#eq-sr-induced}
Then $U$ is a unitary representation, the momentum operators act by multiplication, $\hat P^\mu\psi(p) = p^\mu\psi(p)$, and $\hat P^2 = k^2$.

*Proof.* *Little group:* $\Lambda(W(A, p))k = \Lambda(A_p)^{-1}\Lambda(A)\Lambda^{-1}p = \Lambda(A_p)^{-1}p = k$. *Homomorphism:* for the Lorentz part, with $q = \Lambda(A)^{-1}p$,
$(U(A)U(B)\psi)(p) = D(A_p^{-1}AA_q)D(A_q^{-1}BA_{\Lambda(B)^{-1}q})\psi(\Lambda(B)^{-1}q) = D(A_p^{-1}ABA_{\Lambda(AB)^{-1}p})\psi(\Lambda(AB)^{-1}p) = (U(AB)\psi)(p)$, since $D$ is a representation and
the factors $A_q$ cancel. For translations $U(1, a)$ multiplies by $e^{ip\cdot a}$, so translations compose, and $(U(A)U(1, a)U(A)^{-1}\psi)(p) =
e^{i(\Lambda^{-1}p)\cdot a}\psi(p) = e^{ip\cdot(\Lambda a)}\psi(p)$, because the Minkowski product is invariant: $U(A)U(1, a)U(A)^{-1} = U(1, \Lambda a)$, which with $U(A, a) =
U(1, a)U(A)$ is the semidirect product law of @def-sr-poincare-group. *Unitarity:* $D$ is unitary and $d\mu$ is invariant (@exr-sr-invariant-measure),
so $\|U(A)\psi\|^2 = \int\|\psi(\Lambda^{-1}p)\|^2d\mu(p) = \int\|\psi(q)\|^2d\mu(\Lambda q) = \|\psi\|^2$; $U(A)$ is invertible with inverse $U(A^{-1})$. *Momentum:* $U(1, a) =
e^{ia_\mu\hat P^\mu}$ (@prp-sr-poincare-algebra) and $U(1, a)$ multiplies by $e^{ia_\mu p^\mu}$. On $\mathcal{O}$, $p^2 = k^2$. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For a spinless massive particle the little-group representation is trivial. The first example identifies the
representation with positive-energy solutions of the Klein-Gordon equation.

::: {#exm-sr-induced-scalar}
#### Spin zero

With $D = 1$, $(U(A, a)\psi)(p) = e^{ip\cdot a}\psi(\Lambda^{-1}p)$. The function $\phi(x) = \int d\mu(p)\,\psi(p)e^{-ip\cdot x}$ satisfies $(\Box + m^2)\phi = 0$ and contains only
positive frequencies; under $U$ it transforms as a scalar field, $\phi \mapsto \phi(\Lambda^{-1}(x - a))$ (@def-sr-field-transformation). The quantum field of
@sec-quantisation is built from such wave functions.
:::

For a massive particle with spin, the little-group element $W(A, p)$ is a rotation, and for boosts it is the Wigner rotation of
@thm-sr-wigner-angle. The second example shows this, which is the reason for the name.

::: {#exm-sr-induced-spin}
#### Spin and the Wigner rotation

Choose $A_p$ to be the lift of the pure boost $B_{p/m}$. For a rotation $A = R$, $W(R, p) = B_{p/m}^{-1}RB_{R^{-1}p/m} = R$ by @exr-sr-boost-conjugate: spin rotates as
at rest. For a boost $A$ covering $B(\vec w)$, with $q = \Lambda^{-1}p$, $W = B_{p/m}^{-1}B(\vec w)B_{q/m}$, and since $B(\vec w)B_{q/m} = B_{p/m}W(\vec w, \vec v_q)$ by
@eq-sr-wigner-def, $W(A, p)$ is the Wigner rotation of the pair: a boosted electron has its spin turned by the Wigner angle.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For massless particles the helicity representation of the little group is a phase. The third example writes the
resulting transformation law.

::: {#exm-sr-induced-helicity}
#### Helicity states

With $D(g(\phi, w)) = e^{-i\lambda\phi}$, @eq-sr-induced becomes $(U(A)\psi)(p) = e^{-i\lambda\phi(A, p)}\psi(\Lambda^{-1}p)$, where $\phi(A, p)$ is the angle of the little-group element
$W(A, p)$: a photon state is multiplied by a phase and moved to the new momentum, and its helicity $\lambda$ never changes under Lorentz
transformations. The null-rotation part of $W$ drops out, which is the group-theoretical form of gauge invariance
(@exm-sr-little-gauge).
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The invariance of the measure was used for unitarity. The first exercise proves it. The invariance of this measure is what makes the induced representations unitary.

::: {#exr-sr-invariant-measure}
#### The invariant measure

Show that $d^3p/(2p^0)$ on $p^2 = m^2$, $p^0 > 0$ equals $d^4p\,\delta(p^2 - m^2)\theta(p^0)$, and deduce its invariance. Check with Sage that the Jacobian of the map $\vec p \mapsto \vec p'$
induced by a boost along $x$ is $p'^0/p^0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Integrating $\delta(p_0^2 - E^2)$ over $p^0 > 0$ with $E = \sqrt{\vec p^2 + m^2}$ gives $1/(2E)$, so $\int d^4p\,\delta(p^2 - m^2)\theta(p^0)f = \int\frac{d^3p}{2E}f$. The left side is
invariant, because $d^4p$ is ($|\det\Lambda| = 1$), $p^2$ is, and orthochronous transformations keep $p^0 > 0$. The Jacobian computation confirms
$d^3p'/p'^0 = d^3p/p^0$:

{{< sage exr-sr-invariant-measure >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

::: {#exr-sr-induced-wigner}
#### The little-group element in numbers

For $m = 1$, $p = (\cosh1, \sinh1, 0, 0)$ and the boost $B(0.8\hat y)$, compute $W = B_p^{-1}B(0.8\hat y)B_{q}$ with $q = B(0.8\hat y)^{-1}p$ and compare its angle with
@eq-sr-wigner-tan for the pair $(\vec v_q, 0.8\hat y)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$W$ is a rotation about $\hat z$ by the angle given by @eq-sr-wigner-tan with $\vec v_1 = \vec v_q$ and $\vec v_2 = 0.8\hat y$:

{{< sage exr-sr-induced-wigner >}}

The choice of the standard transformations $A_p$ is arbitrary. The third exercise shows that another choice gives an
equivalent representation.

::: {#exr-sr-induced-choice}
#### Changing the standard boosts

Let $A'_p = A_ph(p)$ with $h(p) \in G_k$. Show that $(V\psi)(p) = D(h(p))^{-1}\psi(p)$ intertwines the representations built with $A_p$ and with $A'_p$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$W'(A, p) = h(p)^{-1}A_p^{-1}AA_{q}h(q) = h(p)^{-1}W(A, p)h(q)$ with $q = \Lambda^{-1}p$. Then $(VU(A)\psi)(p) = D(h(p))^{-1}D(W(A, p))\psi(q) = D(W'(A, p))D(h(q))^{-1}\psi(q) =
(U'(A)V\psi)(p)$; $V$ is unitary because $D$ is, so the two representations are unitarily equivalent.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

The construction turns each unitary representation of a little group into one of the Poincaré group. Wigner's theorem
lists the outcome. Its proof below establishes the little-group data and the values of the Casimir operators; that every
unitary irreducible representation arises in this way, and that irreducible little-group representations give irreducible
ones, is Mackey's theory of induced representations, which we cite [@bekaert2006unitary, Sec. 3.1].

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-sr-wigner-classification}
#### Wigner's classification

The unitary irreducible representations of the double cover of $ISO^+(1, 3)$ with momenta on one orbit of @prp-sr-little-groups are, up to
equivalence:

1. **Massive**, $p^2 = m^2 > 0$, $p^0 > 0$: induced from the spin-$s$ representation of $SU(2)$, $s \in \{0, \tfrac12, 1, \dots\}$, with $\hat P^2 = m^2$, $\hat W^2 = -m^2s(s + 1)$
   and $2s + 1$ states for each momentum.
2. **Massless with helicity**, $p^2 = 0$, $p^0 > 0$: induced from $D(g(\phi, w)) = e^{-i\lambda\phi}$, $\lambda \in \tfrac12\mathbb{Z}$, with $\hat P^2 = 0$, $\hat W = \lambda\hat P$ and one state for
   each momentum.
3. **Massless with continuous spin**: induced from a representation in which the translations $w$ act non-trivially; it is
   infinite-dimensional for each momentum, with $\hat W^2 = -\rho^2 < 0$.
4. **Tachyonic**, $p^2 < 0$, little group $SU(1, 1)$, and **zero momentum**, little group $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$: all non-trivial ones infinite-dimensional
   for each momentum.

The same list with $p^0 < 0$ completes the classification.

*Proof.* (1) $SU(2)$ is compact, so its unitary irreducible representations are finite-dimensional, and they are the spin-$s$
representations (@def-spin-j, with $e^{-2\pi i\hat J_3} = (-1)^{2s}$ allowed since $-1 \in SU(2)$). The Casimir values were computed in @thm-sr-casimirs. (2) If the
normal subgroup of translations $\{g(0, w)\}$ acts trivially, $D$ is a representation of the quotient $\mathbb{R}/4\pi\mathbb{Z}$ (@exr-sr-little-quotient), and its
irreducible unitary representations are the characters $e^{-i\lambda\phi}$, $\lambda \in \tfrac12\mathbb{Z}$. On the standard states $\hat J_3 = \lambda$, because $g(\phi, 0)$ covers the rotation
$e^{\phi J_3}$, represented by $e^{-i\phi\hat J_3}$; the generators $E_1$, $E_2$ act as zero, so by @exm-sr-pl-massless $\hat W = \lambda k$ there, and by covariance $\hat W = \lambda\hat P$
on the whole representation. (3) If the translations act non-trivially, the joint spectrum of the commuting Hermitian generators
$\hat E_1$, $\hat E_2$ is invariant under the rotations generated by $\hat J_3$, so in an irreducible representation it is a circle of some radius
$r > 0$, and square-integrable functions on a circle form an infinite-dimensional space; at the standard momentum $\hat W^0 = \hat W^3$ and
$\hat W^2 = -(\hat W_1^2 + \hat W_2^2) = -\kappa^2(\hat E_1^2 + \hat E_2^2) = -\kappa^2r^2$ (@exm-sr-pl-massless), a negative constant $-\rho^2$. (4) $SU(1, 1)$ and $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ are non-compact
simple groups, whose non-trivial unitary representations are infinite-dimensional [@bekaert2006unitary, Sec. 1.3]. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The particles of the Standard Model fall into the first two classes. The first example places some of them. Each known particle occupies one entry of the classification.

::: {#exm-sr-classification-particles}
#### Particles in the classification

The electron, the quarks and the $W$ and $Z$ bosons are massive with spins $\tfrac12$, $\tfrac12$, $1$, $1$; the Higgs boson has spin $0$. The photon and the
gluons are massless with helicities $\pm1$, each pair forming a parity doublet (@exr-sr-pl-parity); the graviton would have $\pm2$. No
particle with continuous spin or tachyonic momentum has been observed.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The classification counts the physical states of a field. The second example compares a massive and a massless vector
field.

::: {#exm-sr-classification-counting}
#### Counting polarisations

A vector field $A^\mu$ has four components. A massive spin-one particle has $2s + 1 = 3$ states: the condition $\partial_\mu A^\mu = 0$ removes the
component along $p$. A massless one has $2$ helicity states: besides the Lorenz condition, the null rotations of the little group
remove one more, as gauge transformations (@exm-sr-little-gauge, @exm-cfb-lorenz-gauge). The jump from three to two states when $m \to 0$ is
the reason a massive vector field is not simply a massless one with a mass term.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The helicity of a massless particle is the limit of the spin component along the momentum of a massive one. The third
example makes this precise for a fast particle.

::: {#exm-sr-classification-limit}
#### From spin to helicity

For a massive particle of spin $s$ moving along $z$, the operator $\hat W^0/|\vec p| = \hat{\vec J}\cdot\hat p$ is the helicity, with eigenvalues $-s, \dots, s$. As $m \to 0$ at fixed
$|\vec p|$, the states with helicity $\pm s$ go over to the two massless helicity representations and the others decouple from the
null-rotation-invariant states; a massless particle "remembers" only the extreme helicities.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
