:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise computes the number of states for a few particles from the classification. The counts are the numbers of independent states that a field must describe.

::: {#exr-sr-classification-count}
#### Numbers of states

How many states of a given momentum have: a massive particle of spin $\tfrac32$; a massless particle of helicity $\tfrac32$ together with its parity
partner; a Dirac electron together with its positron; a massless Weyl neutrino together with its antineutrino?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$4$; $2$; $2 + 2 = 4$, the four components of the Dirac spinor of @def-dq-dirac-spinors; $1 + 1 = 2$, helicity $-\tfrac12$ for the neutrino and $+\tfrac12$ for the
antineutrino.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Helicity is quantised in half-integers because the rotation by $4\pi$ is the identity in $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$. The second exercise asks why the
same argument does not quantise it more finely.

::: {#exr-sr-helicity-quantised}
#### Why half-integers

Show that $D(g(\phi, 0)) = e^{-i\lambda\phi}$ is well defined on $G_k$ if and only if $\lambda \in \tfrac12\mathbb{Z}$, and that $\lambda \in \mathbb{Z}$ if the representation is to descend to $ISO^+(1, 3)$
itself. In three spacetime dimensions the corresponding little group is $\mathbb{R}$; what changes?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$g(\phi, 0)$ depends on $\phi$ modulo $4\pi$, so $e^{-4\pi i\lambda} = 1$, $\lambda \in \tfrac12\mathbb{Z}$. The element $g(2\pi, 0) = -1$ is the non-trivial element of the kernel of the covering;
the representation descends to $ISO^+(1, 3)$ iff it is trivial there, $e^{-2\pi i\lambda} = 1$, $\lambda \in \mathbb{Z}$. In three dimensions the rotation group $SO(2)$ has
the universal cover $\mathbb{R}$, so any real $\lambda$ is allowed: fractional spin, the anyons of @bekaert2006unitary [App. B].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The massive case of the classification can be tested on the Dirac field. The third exercise identifies the representation
carried by the positive-energy solutions.

::: {#exr-sr-dirac-induced}
#### The Dirac equation as an induced representation

Show that the positive-energy plane-wave solutions $u(p)e^{-ip\cdot x}$ of the Dirac equation, with $u(p) = S(B_{p/m})u(k)$ for the two rest spinors $u(k)$, carry the
massive spin-$\tfrac12$ representation of the classification.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
At rest the Dirac equation $(\gamma^0m - m)u = 0$ leaves a two-dimensional space of spinors, on which rotations act by the spin-$\tfrac12$ representation (the
two blocks of @exm-sr-weyl-group coincide for rotations). The solutions at momentum $p$ are $S(B_{p/m})u(k)$, the images under the standard boosts, and a
Lorentz transformation $S(\Lambda)$ maps $u(p)$ to $S(\Lambda)S(B_{p/m})u(k) = S(B_{\Lambda p/m})S(W)u(k)$ with $W$ the Wigner rotation of @exm-sr-induced-spin, acting on
the rest spinor by $D^{(1/2)}(W)$: this is @eq-sr-induced with $D = D^{(1/2)}$ (@def-dq-dirac-spinors).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises below use several steps of this part together. The first is the spinor description of a light ray, which
combines the double cover with null vectors [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.35].

::: {#exr-sr-null-spinor}
#### A light ray as a spinor

For a null vector $x$ with $x^0 + x^3 > 0$, let $u = N(x^0 + x^3, x^1 + ix^2)^T$. Show that $X(x) = uu^\dagger$ for $N = (x^0 + x^3)^{-1/2}$, and that for every $A \in SL(2, \mathbb{C})$,
$Au$ is (up to a phase) the spinor of $\Lambda(A)x$. Check for $x = (5, 3, 0, 4)$ and the boost $A = e^{-\theta\sigma_3/2}$ with $\tanh\theta = 0.6$, which is the passive boost along $z$ of
Blennow and Ohlsson.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$uu^\dagger = N^2\begin{pmatrix}(x^0 + x^3)^2 & (x^0 + x^3)(x^1 - ix^2) \\ (x^0 + x^3)(x^1 + ix^2) & (x^1)^2 + (x^2)^2\end{pmatrix}$, and with $N^2 = 1/(x^0 + x^3)$ and $(x^1)^2 + (x^2)^2 =
(x^0)^2 - (x^3)^2$ this is $X(x)$. Then $X(\Lambda(A)x) = AX(x)A^\dagger = Auu^\dagger A^\dagger = (Au)(Au)^\dagger$, and a spinor is determined by $uu^\dagger$ up to a phase:

{{< sage exr-sr-null-spinor >}}
:::

The second exercise takes a Lorentz matrix given only by its entries and extracts everything the part has defined:
component, polar decomposition, generator and spinor lift. The matrix is given numerically, so that every quantity has to be recovered by the methods of this part.

::: {#exr-sr-decompose-all}
#### Everything about one matrix

Let $\Lambda = B(\vec v)R_{\hat n}(0.7)P$ with $\vec v = (0.5, 0.2, 0.1)$ and $\hat n = (0, 1, 1)/\sqrt2$, given only as a numerical matrix. Find its component, write it as
$D\Lambda_+$ with $D \in \{1, P, T, PT\}$ and $\Lambda_+ \in SO^+(1, 3)$, find the polar decomposition of $\Lambda_+$ and a lift $A \in SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ of $\Lambda_+$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\det\Lambda = -1$ and $\Lambda^0{}_0 > 0$, so $\Lambda \in L^\uparrow_-$ and $\Lambda_+ = \Lambda P$ (since $P^2 = 1$). The polar decomposition of $\Lambda_+$ recovers $\vec v$ and the rotation by $0.7$
about $\hat n$, and $A = e^{\xi\hat v\cdot\vec\sigma/2}e^{-0.35i\,\hat n\cdot\vec\sigma}$, with $\xi = \operatorname{artanh}|\vec v|$, covers $\Lambda_+$:

{{< sage exr-sr-decompose-all >}}
:::

The third exercise follows the spin of an electron through two boosts, which combines the Wigner rotation, its lift to
$SU(2)$ and the induced representation. The answer is a measurable probability.

::: {#exr-sr-spin-two-boosts}
#### An electron boosted twice

An electron at rest has spin along $+\hat x$. It is boosted by $0.6\hat x$ and then by $0.7\hat y$. Relative to the state obtained by the single pure boost to
the final velocity, its spin is turned by the Wigner rotation. Find the direction of the spin and the probability of finding
it along $+\hat x$ in the rest frame reached by the single boost.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Wigner rotation is by $\Omega = 0.2706$ about $\hat z$ (@exm-sr-wigner-numbers), lifted to $e^{-i\Omega\sigma_3/2}$. The spin turns to $(\cos\Omega, \sin\Omega, 0)$ and the
probability of $+\hat x$ is $\cos^2\tfrac\Omega2 \approx 0.982$:

{{< sage exr-sr-spin-two-boosts >}}
:::

## Relativistic kinematics {#sec-sr-kinematics}

The group theory of the previous part says how four-vectors transform; this part uses the four-vectors of a particle.
Velocity and acceleration become four-vectors, energy and momentum combine into one, and their conservation in
collisions and decays becomes a single vector equation whose invariant content is computed with Minkowski products. The
results are the working tools of particle physics: invariant masses, decay momenta, thresholds and the Mandelstam
variables. The examples and exercises follow @blennow2022relativity [Secs. 1.4 and 1.6], with masses from the
particle-physics tables; units are $c = 1$ and energies in MeV unless stated.

For more on this topic, see @godinho2014introduction [Ch. 6], @gray2019student [Appendix A], @knauf2018mathematical [Ch. 16], @moretti2023analytical [Ch. 10], @paganini2023fundamentals [Ch. 2, Ch. 3], @pal2015introductory [Ch. 2] and @pierrus2018solved [Ch. 12].

### Four-velocity and four-momentum

A worldline parametrised by its proper time has a tangent of unit length. This tangent is the relativistic velocity, and
its derivative the relativistic acceleration; @fig-sr-mass-shell shows the mass shell on which the corresponding momenta
lie.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-sr-four-velocity}
#### Four-velocity

The **four-velocity** of a massive worldline parametrised by proper time is $u^\mu = dx^\mu/d\tau = \gamma(1, \vec v)$, with $\gamma = dt/d\tau$; it satisfies
$u\cdot u = 1$. The **four-acceleration** is $a^\mu = du^\mu/d\tau$, and $u\cdot a = 0$ (@exr-sr-u-dot-a).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
![The mass shell. The energy $E = \sqrt{p^2 + m^2}$ against the momentum $p = |\vec p|$ for an electron, a muon and a proton (MeV); the
massless line $E = p$ (dashed) is the asymptote of every curve, and the Newtonian approximation $m + p^2/(2m)$ (dotted, for the
muon) fails when $p \sim m$. Generated by `figures/sr-mass-shell.sage`.](figures/sr-mass-shell.svg){#fig-sr-mass-shell width=65%}

For uniform motion the four-velocity is constant. The first example writes it and checks its normalisation in two frames. The numbers are those of the boost of @exm-sr-boost-numbers.

::: {#exm-sr-u-uniform}
#### Uniform motion

A particle moving with $\vec v = (0.6, 0, 0)$ has $u = (1.25, 0.75, 0, 0)$ and $u\cdot u = 1.5625 - 0.5625 = 1$. In its rest frame $u = (1, 0, 0, 0)$;
the four-velocity is the unit vector along the worldline, the time axis $e'_0$ of the rest frame (@exm-sr-boost-basis).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A particle in circular motion has a constant speed but not a constant four-velocity. The second example computes its
four-acceleration, which is spacelike and points to the centre [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.51].

::: {#exm-sr-u-circle}
#### Circular motion

For $\vec x = r(\cos\omega t, \sin\omega t, 0)$ with $v = r\omega < 1$, $u = \gamma(1, -v\sin\omega t, v\cos\omega t, 0)$ and, since $\gamma$ is constant, $a = \gamma\,du/dt =
-\gamma^2r\omega^2(0, \cos\omega t, \sin\omega t, 0)$. So $a\cdot a = -\gamma^4r^2\omega^4$: the proper acceleration, the acceleration felt by the particle, is $\gamma^2v^2/r$,
larger than the coordinate value $v^2/r$ by $\gamma^2$ (@def-sr-proper-acceleration).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Minkowski product of two four-velocities is a Lorentz factor. The third example records this, used in
@exr-sr-relative-gamma, as the general way to compute relative speeds [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.44].

::: {#exm-sr-u-product}
#### Relative speed from four-velocities

For two observers $u_1\cdot u_2 = \gamma_{\mathrm{rel}}$, the Lorentz factor of either in the rest frame of the other, so $v_{\mathrm{rel}} = \sqrt{1 - (u_1\cdot u_2)^{-2}}$. For $u_1 =
(1.25, 0.75, 0, 0)$ and $u_2 = (1.25, -0.75, 0, 0)$, $u_1\cdot u_2 = 1.5625 + 0.5625 = 2.125$ and $v_{\mathrm{rel}} = \sqrt{1 - 1/2.125^2} = 0.882$, which is $0.6 \oplus 0.6 =
1.2/1.36$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The orthogonality of four-velocity and four-acceleration follows from the normalisation. The first exercise proves it
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.45]. The proof is one line, and its consequence is used repeatedly.

::: {#exr-sr-u-dot-a}
#### Velocity and acceleration are orthogonal

Show that $u\cdot a = 0$, and conclude that a non-zero four-acceleration is spacelike.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Differentiating $u\cdot u = 1$ gives $2u\cdot a = 0$. A non-zero vector orthogonal to the timelike $u$ is spacelike (@prp-sr-reverse-inequalities).
In the instantaneous rest frame $u = (1, \vec 0)$, so $a = (0, \vec a_0)$: the four-acceleration is the acceleration measured in that frame.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The four-velocity and four-acceleration of a given worldline are computed by the chain rule. The second exercise does it
for the worldline of @exm-sr-worldline-limited [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.38 b].

::: {#exr-sr-four-acceleration}
#### Four-acceleration on an accelerated path

For $x = \tfrac32at^2$, $y = 2at^2$, compute $a^\mu = \gamma\,d(\gamma(1, \vec v))/dt$, and check $u\cdot a = 0$ and that $-a\cdot a$ diverges as $t \to 1/(5a)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $s = 5at$, $\gamma = (1 - s^2)^{-1/2}$ and $d\gamma/dt = 5a\gamma^3s$, one finds $a^\mu = 5a\gamma^4\bigl(s, \tfrac35, \tfrac45, 0\bigr)$ and $-a\cdot a = 25a^2\gamma^6$, which diverges as $s \to 1$:

{{< sage exr-sr-four-acceleration >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Lorentz factor of an object in another frame can be computed without composing velocities. The third exercise does
so [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.44].

::: {#exr-sr-gamma-other-frame}
#### A Lorentz factor in a moving frame

An object has velocity $\vec u$ in $S$, and $S'$ moves with velocity $-v'\hat x$ relative to $S$. Using @exm-sr-u-product, find the Lorentz factor of the object
in $S'$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The four-velocity of $S'$ in $S$ is $\gamma'(1, -v', 0, 0)$, so $\gamma_{S'} = u_{\mathrm{obj}}\cdot u_{S'} = \gamma(u)\gamma'(1 + u_xv')$. For $\vec u = (0.6, 0, 0)$ and $v' = 0.6$:
$1.25 \cdot 1.25 \cdot 1.36 = 2.125$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

The four-velocity times the mass is the quantity conserved in collisions. Its time component is the energy, including the
rest energy, and its spatial part the relativistic momentum.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-sr-four-momentum}
#### Four-momentum

The **four-momentum** of a particle of mass $m > 0$ is $p^\mu = mu^\mu = (E, \vec p)$ with **energy** $E = \gamma m$ and **momentum** $\vec p = \gamma m\vec v$. It satisfies
$$
p\cdot p = E^2 - |\vec p|^2 = m^2, \qquad \vec v = \vec p/E ,
$$ {#eq-sr-mass-shell}
the **mass shell**. A massless particle has a null four-momentum, $E = |\vec p|$, and moves at the speed of light. The **kinetic energy** is $E - m$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The Newtonian kinetic energy is the first correction to the rest energy. The first example expands the energy in the
velocity.

::: {#exm-sr-kinetic-expansion}
#### The Newtonian limit of the energy

$E = m(1 - v^2)^{-1/2} = m + \tfrac12mv^2 + \tfrac38mv^4 + \dots$, so the kinetic energy is $\tfrac12mv^2$ to leading order; for an electron at $v = 0.1$ the
next term is $0.75\%$ of the first. The rest energy $m = mc^2$ of one kilogram is $9 \times 10^{16}\,$J, the energy that nuclear binding releases a
small fraction of [@boskoff2024journey, Theorem 9.2.14].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The energy measured by an observer is a Minkowski product. The second example states the rule, which removes the need to
transform the four-momentum [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.55].

::: {#exm-sr-energy-observer}
#### The energy an observer measures

An observer with four-velocity $u_{\mathrm{obs}}$ measures the energy $E_{\mathrm{obs}} = p\cdot u_{\mathrm{obs}}$, since in her rest frame $u_{\mathrm{obs}} = e_0$. For $p = (E, p_x, 0, 0)$ and an
observer moving with $v$ along $x$: $E_{\mathrm{obs}} = \gamma(E - vp_x)$, the time component of the boosted four-momentum.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A photon has energy and momentum but no rest frame. The third example shows that a system of photons nevertheless can have
one, and a mass [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.4].

::: {#exm-sr-photon-rest-frame}
#### Photons and rest frames

A single photon has $p\cdot p = 0$ and no rest frame: there is no observer for whom its momentum vanishes, since $E = |\vec p|$ in every
frame. Two photons with momenta $(\omega_1, \omega_1\hat n_1)$, $(\omega_2, \omega_2\hat n_2)$ have total $P$ with $P\cdot P = 2\omega_1\omega_2(1 - \hat n_1\cdot\hat n_2) > 0$ unless $\hat n_1 = \hat n_2$: then $P$
is timelike and its rest frame, the centre-of-momentum frame, exists.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Massive neutrinos from a supernova arrive later than light. The first exercise computes the delay [@blennow2022relativity,
Problem 1.110]. The tiny delay is still the best kinematic bound on neutrino masses from a supernova.

::: {#exr-sr-neutrino-delay}
#### Neutrinos from a supernova

Neutrinos of energy $E$ and mass $m$ travel a distance $L$. Find the delay relative to light exactly and for $m \ll E$, and evaluate it for $L = 50\,$kpc,
$E = 10\,$MeV, $m = 0.1\,$eV.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$v = |\vec p|/E = \sqrt{1 - m^2/E^2}$, so $\Delta t = L(1/v - 1) \approx Lm^2/(2E^2)$. With $L = 1.54 \times 10^{21}\,$m, $L/c = 5.1 \times 10^{12}\,$s and $m^2/(2E^2) = 5 \times 10^{-17}$:
$\Delta t \approx 2.6 \times 10^{-4}\,$s, well below the ten-second duration of the burst:

{{< sage exr-sr-neutrino-delay >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The energy of a particle in an observer's frame needs only the invariant product of @exm-sr-energy-observer. The second
exercise applies it to find also the velocity component [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.55].

::: {#exr-sr-energy-moving-observer}
#### Energy and velocity seen by a moving observer

A particle has $p = (E, \vec p)$ in $S$. An observer moves with $v$ along $x$. Find the energy she measures and the $x'$-component of the particle's velocity
in her frame.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$E' = \gamma(E - vp_x)$ and $p'_x = \gamma(p_x - vE)$, so $v'_x = p'_x/E' = (p_x - vE)/(E - vp_x) = (v_x - v)/(1 - vv_x)$ with $v_x = p_x/E$: the composition law of
@prp-sr-velocity-addition, recovered from the transformation of four-momentum.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The energy-momentum relation gives momenta from energies without velocities. The third exercise uses it in a decay chain
of cosmic rays [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.14].

::: {#exr-sr-muon-energy}
#### Muons that reach the ground

Muons (mass $106\,$MeV, proper lifetime $2.2\,\mu$s) are produced at $10\,$km. What energy must they have so that their mean decay length $\gamma v\tau_0c$
equals $10\,$km?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\gamma v = |\vec p|/m$, so the condition is $|\vec p| = m\cdot10\,\mathrm{km}/(c\tau_0) = 106 \cdot 10^4/659.6\,$MeV $\approx 1.61\,$GeV, and $E = \sqrt{p^2 + m^2} \approx 1.61\,$GeV:
muons above about $1.6\,$GeV typically survive the descent.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

### Collisions and decays

In every collision and decay the total four-momentum is conserved. Its square is the same in every frame and equals the
squared energy in the frame where the total momentum vanishes; this one number decides which reactions are possible.
@fig-sr-decay shows how a two-body decay looks in the laboratory.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-sr-invariant-mass}
#### Invariant mass

The **invariant mass** of a system of particles with four-momenta $p_1, \dots, p_n$ is $M$ with $M^2 = P\cdot P$, $P = \sum_ip_i$. When $P$ is timelike, the
**centre-of-momentum frame** is the frame in which $\vec P = 0$, and there $P = (M, \vec 0)$: the invariant mass is the total energy in that frame.
Conservation of four-momentum, $\sum p_{\mathrm{in}} = \sum p_{\mathrm{out}}$, implies that the invariant mass is the same before and after a reaction.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
![A two-body decay in the laboratory. For a parent of mass $M$ decaying isotropically into two particles of masses $m_1$, $m_2$
(here $B^0 \to J/\psi\,K^{*0}$, with $5280$, $3097$ and $892\,$MeV), the mean opening angle between the daughters (left) against the parent's
$E/M$, from a Monte Carlo sample of $2000$ decays per point, and the invariant mass of the daughters (right), equal to $M$ for every
event. Generated by `figures/sr-decay.sage`.](figures/sr-decay.svg){#fig-sr-decay width=95%}

Two photons that come from one particle carry its mass in their invariant mass. The first example computes it from the
energies and the angle [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.102].

::: {#exm-sr-two-photons}
#### The mass of a diphoton

For $p_1 = \omega_1(1, 1, 0, 0)$ and $p_2 = \omega_2(1, \cos\theta, \sin\theta, 0)$, $M^2 = 2p_1\cdot p_2 = 2\omega_1\omega_2(1 - \cos\theta)$. The Higgs boson was discovered in this channel:
two photons of $62.5\,$GeV emitted back to back give $M = 125\,$GeV.
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

Invariant masses forbid some reactions outright. The second example shows that an electron and a positron cannot become a
single photon [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.73].

::: {#exm-sr-no-single-photon}
#### No annihilation into one photon

$(p_{e^-} + p_{e^+})^2 = 2m_e^2 + 2p_{e^-}\cdot p_{e^+} \geq 4m_e^2 > 0$ by the reverse Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, while a photon has $k\cdot k = 0$: $e^+e^- \to \gamma$ is
impossible. For the same reason a free electron cannot emit a single photon, since $(p - k)^2 = m^2$ would require $p\cdot k = 0$, impossible
for future-directed $p$ timelike and $k$ null and non-zero. Two photons, $e^+e^- \to \gamma\gamma$, are allowed.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

When two particles merge, the mass of the product depends on their relative velocity only. The third example derives the
formula [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.77].

::: {#exm-sr-merge}
#### Two particles merge

$m^2 = (p_1 + p_2)^2 = m_1^2 + m_2^2 + 2m_1m_2\,u_1\cdot u_2 = m_1^2 + m_2^2 + 2m_1m_2\gamma_{\mathrm{rel}}$ (@exm-sr-u-product). Since $\gamma_{\mathrm{rel}} \geq 1$, $m \geq m_1 + m_2$: kinetic energy
becomes rest energy. Two $1\,$kg lumps of putty colliding at $v_{\mathrm{rel}} = 0.6$ make a lump of $\sqrt{2 + 2 \cdot 1.25}\,$kg $= 2.12\,$kg.
:::

A resonance shows up as a peak in the invariant mass of its decay products. The first exercise reconstructs one from two
muons [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.82].

::: {#exr-sr-resonance}
#### A resonance in two muons

Two muons (mass $106\,$MeV) are detected with momenta $2.2\,$GeV each, at $45°$ on either side of the beam axis. What is the mass of the parent?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The opening angle is $90°$, so $M^2 = 2m^2 + 2(E^2 - |\vec p|^2\cos90°) = 4m^2 + 2|\vec p|^2$, and $M \approx 3.12\,$GeV, close to the $J/\psi$ mass $3.097\,$GeV:

{{< sage exr-sr-resonance >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Pair annihilation in flight produces photons at angles fixed by the energy. The second exercise computes them
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.84].

::: {#exr-sr-annihilation-angle}
#### Annihilation in flight

An electron of total energy $E$ hits a positron at rest and they annihilate into two photons at angles $\pm\phi$ to the electron's direction. Show
that the photons have equal energies $\tfrac12(E + m)$ and that $\cos\phi = |\vec p|/(E + m) = \sqrt{(E - m)/(E + m)}$, which tends to $v/2$ for slow electrons.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Momentum along the beam: $|\vec p| = 2\omega\cos\phi$; across it the photon momenta cancel; energy: $E + m = 2\omega$. So $\cos\phi = |\vec p|/(E + m) = \sqrt{(E - m)/(E + m)}$, using
$|\vec p|^2 = (E - m)(E + m)$. For $v \ll 1$, $|\vec p| \approx mv$ and $E + m \approx 2m$, so $\cos\phi \approx v/2$: the photons come out almost back to back.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In a bubble chamber a neutral particle leaves no track, but its mass follows from the charged ones. The third exercise
reconstructs it [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.133 b].

::: {#exr-sr-missing-mass}
#### A missing mass

In the decay $\Sigma^- \to \pi^- + X^0$, the $\Sigma^-$ (mass $1197.4\,$MeV) has momentum $p_\Sigma$ and the $\pi^-$ (mass $139.6\,$MeV) momentum $p_\pi$, at an angle $\theta$. Show that
$m_X^2 = m_\Sigma^2 + m_\pi^2 - 2(E_\Sigma E_\pi - p_\Sigma p_\pi\cos\theta)$, and evaluate it for $p_\Sigma = 500\,$MeV, $p_\pi = 264\,$MeV, $\theta = 39°$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$p_X = p_\Sigma - p_\pi$ and $m_X^2 = (p_\Sigma - p_\pi)^2$ gives the formula. The numbers give $m_X \approx 940\,$MeV, a neutron:

{{< sage exr-sr-missing-mass >}}
:::

In the rest frame of a decaying particle the daughters of a two-body decay have fixed energies and momenta. The
proposition below gives them in terms of the masses alone, with the triangle function $\lambda(a, b, c) = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 - 2ab - 2bc - 2ca$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sr-two-body}
#### Two-body decay

In the rest frame of a particle of mass $M$ decaying into particles of masses $m_1$, $m_2$ with $M > m_1 + m_2$,
$$
E_1 = \frac{M^2 + m_1^2 - m_2^2}{2M}, \qquad E_2 = \frac{M^2 + m_2^2 - m_1^2}{2M}, \qquad |\vec p_1| = |\vec p_2| = \frac{\lambda^{1/2}(M^2, m_1^2, m_2^2)}{2M} ,
$$
with the directions opposite and otherwise arbitrary.

*Proof.* $P = (M, \vec 0) = p_1 + p_2$, so $\vec p_1 = -\vec p_2$. From $p_2 = P - p_1$, $m_2^2 = M^2 - 2P\cdot p_1 + m_1^2 = M^2 - 2ME_1 + m_1^2$, which gives $E_1$, and $E_2 = M - E_1$.
Then $|\vec p_1|^2 = E_1^2 - m_1^2 = \frac{(M^2 + m_1^2 - m_2^2)^2 - 4M^2m_1^2}{4M^2} = \frac{\lambda(M^2, m_1^2, m_2^2)}{4M^2}$. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The pion decay is the textbook case and produces the cosmic-ray muons. The first example evaluates the formulas
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.80].

::: {#exm-sr-pion-decay}
#### $\pi^+ \to \mu^+\nu_\mu$

With $m_\pi = 139.57\,$MeV, $m_\mu = 105.66\,$MeV and a massless neutrino, $|\vec p| = (m_\pi^2 - m_\mu^2)/(2m_\pi) = 29.79\,$MeV and the muon's kinetic energy is $E_\mu - m_\mu =
(m_\pi - m_\mu)^2/(2m_\pi) = 4.12\,$MeV. The muon is slow, $v = p/E \approx 0.27$, and travels on average $\gamma v c\tau_\mu \approx 186\,$m before it decays.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The formula is symmetric under exchanging the daughters, and the momentum vanishes at threshold. The second example
checks the threshold behaviour of the triangle function.

::: {#exm-sr-two-body-threshold}
#### At threshold

$\lambda(M^2, m_1^2, m_2^2) = (M^2 - (m_1 + m_2)^2)(M^2 - (m_1 - m_2)^2)$, so the momentum vanishes when $M = m_1 + m_2$ and the daughters are at rest; for $M <
m_1 + m_2$ the decay is forbidden. The neutron, with $M - m_p - m_e = 0.78\,$MeV, decays into three bodies precisely because the two-body
channel $n \to p\,e$ would violate angular momentum, not energy.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The momentum of one daughter can also be measured in the rest frame of the other. The third example computes it with
invariants [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.74].

::: {#exm-sr-daughter-frame}
#### One daughter seen from the other

In the rest frame of daughter 2, $E_1 = p_1\cdot p_2/m_2 = (M^2 - m_1^2 - m_2^2)/(2m_2)$, so $|\vec p_1| = \lambda^{1/2}(M^2, m_1^2, m_2^2)/(2m_2)$: the same triangle function, with $m_2$
in place of $M$. For the pion decay, in the rest frame of the muon the neutrino has energy $(m_\pi^2 - m_\mu^2)/(2m_\mu) = 39.4\,$MeV.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
In the laboratory the decay products of a moving particle are boosted. The first exercise finds the energy of a muon emitted
at right angles [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.78].

::: {#exr-sr-muon-right-angle}
#### A muon at right angles

A pion of energy $E_\pi$ moving along $x$ decays into a muon and a massless neutrino, and the muon moves perpendicular to $x$ in the laboratory. Find its
energy.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The neutrino carries all the $x$-momentum: $k = (\omega, p_\pi, -q, 0)$ with $\omega = \sqrt{p_\pi^2 + q^2}$, and the muon $(E_\mu, 0, q, 0)$. From $p_\mu = p_\pi - k$, $m_\mu^2 = m_\pi^2 - 2p_\pi\cdot k =
m_\pi^2 - 2(E_\pi\omega - p_\pi^2)$, so $\omega = (m_\pi^2 - m_\mu^2 + 2p_\pi^2)/(2E_\pi)$ and $E_\mu = E_\pi - \omega = (m_\pi^2 + m_\mu^2)/(2E_\pi)$, a neat result that decreases with the pion
energy.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A fast parent throws its daughters forward into a narrow cone. The second exercise simulates this with random isotropic
decays, as in @fig-sr-decay [@boudreau2018applied, Exercise 14.6].

::: {#exr-sr-opening-angle}
#### The opening angle of fast decays

Write a Sage function that decays a particle of four-momentum $P$ isotropically into masses $m_1$, $m_2$ in its rest frame and boosts the
daughters back. For $B^0 \to J/\psi\,K^{*0}$ check that $(p_1 + p_2)^2 = M^2$ for every event and compute the mean opening angle for $E/M = 1.5$ and $5$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The invariant mass is reproduced to machine precision; the mean opening angle falls from about $1.1\,$rad at $E/M = 1.5$ to about $0.26\,$rad at $E/M = 5$,
roughly in proportion to $1/\gamma$ for large $\gamma$:

{{< sage exr-sr-opening-angle >}}

**Veriphy.** Pending.

In a three-body decay the energies are not fixed, but their maximum is. The third exercise finds the largest energy of the
electron neutrino in muon decay [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.99].

::: {#exr-sr-muon-decay-max}
#### The most energetic neutrino

In $\mu^+ \to e^+\nu_e\bar\nu_\mu$ at rest, show that $E_{\nu_e}$ is largest when the invariant mass of the pair $e^+\bar\nu_\mu$ is smallest, and that its supremum is
$(m_\mu^2 - m_e^2)/(2m_\mu)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Treat $e^+\bar\nu_\mu$ as one system of invariant mass $m_{23}$; the two-body formula of @prp-sr-two-body gives $E_{\nu_e} = (m_\mu^2 - m_{23}^2)/(2m_\mu)$, decreasing in
$m_{23}$. Since $m_{23}^2 = m_e^2 + 2p_e\cdot p_{\bar\nu} \geq m_e^2$, with $p_e\cdot p_{\bar\nu} \to 0$ only as the antineutrino energy goes to zero (or, for a massless positron, when the two move
together), the supremum is $(m_\mu^2 - m_e^2)/(2m_\mu) = 52.83\,$MeV, essentially $m_\mu/2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

To create new particles, a collision must supply their rest energy in the centre-of-momentum frame. When the target is at
rest much of the beam energy is wasted on the motion of the products, and the threshold follows from the invariant mass.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sr-threshold}
#### Threshold of a reaction

For a reaction $a + b \to c_1 + \dots + c_n$ with $b$ at rest, the smallest kinetic energy of $a$ for which the reaction is possible is
$$
T_a^{\mathrm{th}} = \frac{(\sum_im_{c_i})^2 - (m_a + m_b)^2}{2m_b} .
$$

*Proof.* The invariant mass $s = (p_a + p_b)^2 = m_a^2 + m_b^2 + 2m_bE_a$ is conserved, and in the centre-of-momentum frame of the products their total energy is
at least $\sum m_{c_i}$, with equality when all of them are at rest there. So the reaction is possible iff $s \geq (\sum m_{c_i})^2$, that is $E_a \geq ((\sum m_{c_i})^2 - m_a^2 -
m_b^2)/(2m_b)$, and $T_a = E_a - m_a$ gives the formula. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The antiproton was discovered at the Bevatron, built for the threshold computed in the first example
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.103]. The number decided the energy of the machine.

::: {#exm-sr-antiproton}
#### Making antiprotons

For $p + p \to p + p + p + \bar p$ on a proton at rest, $T^{\mathrm{th}} = ((4m)^2 - (2m)^2)/(2m) = 6m = 5.63\,$GeV. A beam of $8\,$GeV is enough. In a collider with
two beams of equal energy the threshold is only $m$ of kinetic energy per beam: fixed targets waste energy.
:::

Pion beams on protons produce more pions. The second example evaluates a threshold with unequal masses
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.104]. It shows how little of the beam energy is wasted when the target is heavy.

::: {#exm-sr-pion-production}
#### $\pi^-p \to \pi^+\pi^-n$

With $m_\pi = 139.57$, $m_p = 938.27$, $m_n = 939.57\,$MeV, $T^{\mathrm{th}} = ((2m_\pi + m_n)^2 - (m_\pi + m_p)^2)/(2m_p) \approx 172\,$MeV, slightly more than the rest energy $2m_\pi + m_n - m_\pi -
m_p = 141\,$MeV that is created.

#### Making a $Z$ on a relic neutrino

For $\bar\nu + \nu \to Z^0$ on a relic neutrino of mass $0.15\,$eV at rest, $s = 2m_\nu E = m_Z^2$ (neglecting $m_\nu^2$) gives $E = m_Z^2/(2m_\nu) = (91.2\,\mathrm{GeV})^2/(0.3\,\mathrm{eV}) \approx 2.8
\times 10^{22}\,$eV, beyond the most energetic cosmic rays observed.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise compares a fixed target with the centre-of-momentum frame for pair production in electron collisions
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.107]. The ratio measures the price of a fixed target.

::: {#exr-sr-moller-threshold}
#### Pair production in electron collisions

For $e^-e^- \to e^-e^-e^-e^+$, find the total energy of one electron at threshold in the rest frame of the other, and its ratio to the total energy
needed in the centre-of-momentum frame.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$s = 2m^2 + 2mE = (4m)^2$ gives $E = 7m$. In the centre-of-momentum frame the total energy is $\sqrt s = 4m$, so the ratio is $7/4$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Colliders reach thresholds that fixed targets cannot. The second exercise compares the two for kaon production
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.108]. The difference is a factor of more than two.

::: {#exr-sr-kaon-threshold}
#### Kaons from protons

For $p + p \to p + p + K^0$ ($m_K = 497.6\,$MeV), find the threshold kinetic energy of the beam proton on a fixed target, and the total kinetic energy of two
protons with equal energies in a head-on collision.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Fixed target: $T = ((2m_p + m_K)^2 - 4m_p^2)/(2m_p) = 2m_K + m_K^2/(2m_p) \approx 1127\,$MeV. Collider: the laboratory is the centre-of-momentum frame, so the total kinetic
energy is just $m_K = 497.6\,$MeV:

{{< sage exr-sr-kaon-threshold >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Atoms are bound states whose binding energy shows up as a mass defect. The third exercise computes the photon energy
needed to ionise hydrogen exactly [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.94].

::: {#exr-sr-photoionisation}
#### Ionising hydrogen relativistically

A photon ionises a hydrogen atom at rest, $\gamma + H \to p + e$, with binding energy $B = 13.6\,$eV and $m_H = m_p + m_e - B$. Show that the threshold photon energy is
$B + B^2/(2m_H)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$s = m_H^2 + 2m_H\omega = (m_p + m_e)^2 = (m_H + B)^2$, so $\omega = (2m_HB + B^2)/(2m_H) = B + B^2/(2m_H)$. The correction $B^2/(2m_H) \approx 10^{-7}\,$eV is the recoil energy of the
products, negligible here but the reason thresholds exceed mass differences in general.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Mandelstam variables and Compton scattering

A two-body scattering $1 + 2 \to 3 + 4$ is described by four four-momenta linked by conservation. Its invariant content is
two numbers, and the Mandelstam variables are the standard choice; @fig-sr-compton shows the most famous scattering of
special relativity in their terms.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-sr-mandelstam}
#### Mandelstam variables

For $p_1 + p_2 = p_3 + p_4$ the **Mandelstam variables** are $s = (p_1 + p_2)^2$, $t = (p_1 - p_3)^2$ and $u = (p_1 - p_4)^2$. They are Lorentz invariant, $s$ is the squared
centre-of-momentum energy, $t$ the squared momentum transfer, and $s + t + u = m_1^2 + m_2^2 + m_3^2 + m_4^2$ (@exr-sr-stu-sum).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
![Compton scattering. Left: the wavelength shift $\lambda' - \lambda$ against the scattering angle, $\lambda_C(1 - \cos\theta)$ with the Compton
wavelength $\lambda_C = 2.426\,$pm, independent of the incident wavelength. Right: the scattered photon energy $\omega'$ against $\theta$ for incident
energies $0.1$, $0.511$ and $2\,$MeV. Generated by `figures/sr-compton.sage`.](figures/sr-compton.svg){#fig-sr-compton width=95%}

In elastic scattering the momentum transfer is determined by the angle. The first example computes $t$ in the
centre-of-momentum frame [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.88 a].

::: {#exm-sr-t-elastic}
#### Momentum transfer in elastic scattering

In the centre-of-momentum frame of elastic scattering the momenta keep their magnitude $p$ and turn by $\theta$; the energies are unchanged, so
$t = (p_1 - p_3)^2 = -|\vec p_1 - \vec p_3|^2 = -2p^2(1 - \cos\theta)$. It is negative, zero for forward scattering and $-4p^2$ for backward scattering.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The variable $s$ fixes the energy available in a collision. The second example evaluates it for a fixed-target and a
collider experiment.

::: {#exm-sr-s-values}
#### $s$ for two machines

Protons of $7\,$TeV colliding head on have $\sqrt s = 14\,$TeV. The same $\sqrt s$ on a fixed target needs $s = 2m_p^2 + 2m_pE$, $E \approx s/(2m_p) \approx 10^{17}\,$eV, the
energy of rare cosmic rays.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The relation among $s$, $t$ and $u$ leaves two independent invariants. The third example uses it for massless particles. The two independent invariants are then $s$ and the angle.

::: {#exm-sr-stu-massless}
#### Massless scattering

For four massless particles $s + t + u = 0$. In the centre-of-momentum frame with energy $\sqrt s/2$ per particle, $t = -\tfrac s2(1 - \cos\theta)$ and $u = -\tfrac s2(1 + \cos\theta)$:
the angle and the energy are all there is.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The sum rule is an identity among squared four-momenta. The first exercise proves it. It needs only conservation of four-momentum and the mass shells.

::: {#exr-sr-stu-sum}
#### $s + t + u$

Prove $s + t + u = \sum_im_i^2$, and check it with Sage for random momenta satisfying conservation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$s + t + u = 3m_1^2 + m_2^2 + m_3^2 + m_4^2 + 2p_1\cdot(p_2 - p_3 - p_4) = 3m_1^2 + m_2^2 + m_3^2 + m_4^2 - 2p_1\cdot p_1 = \sum_im_i^2$, using $p_2 - p_3 - p_4 = -p_1$:

{{< sage exr-sr-stu-sum >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The recoil of the target is a function of $t$ alone. The second exercise derives it [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.88 b].

::: {#exr-sr-recoil}
#### Recoil energy

In elastic $ep \to ep$ with the proton initially at rest, show that the kinetic energy of the recoiling proton is $T_p = -t/(2m_p)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$t = (p_p - p'_p)^2 = 2m_p^2 - 2p_p\cdot p'_p = 2m_p^2 - 2m_pE'_p$ in the laboratory, so $E'_p - m_p = -t/(2m_p)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The physical region of a scattering is the set of $(s, t)$ that real momenta can produce. The third exercise finds it for
elastic scattering of equal masses.

::: {#exr-sr-physical-region}
#### The physical region

For elastic scattering of two particles of mass $m$, show that the physical region is $s \geq 4m^2$, $4m^2 - s \leq t \leq 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In the centre-of-momentum frame $s = 4E^2 \geq 4m^2$ and $t = -2p^2(1 - \cos\theta)$ with $p^2 = s/4 - m^2$, so $t$ ranges over $[-4p^2, 0] = [4m^2 - s, 0]$. Then $u = 4m^2 - s - t$
covers the same interval: forward and backward scattering are exchanged by $t \leftrightarrow u$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

Compton's experiment of 1923 showed that X-rays scatter off electrons as particles with energy $\omega$ and momentum $\omega$. The shift
of their wavelength follows from the invariants alone.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sr-compton}
#### Compton scattering

A photon of energy $\omega$ scattered by an angle $\theta$ off an electron at rest has the energy
$$
\omega' = \frac{\omega}{1 + \frac{\omega}{m}(1 - \cos\theta)} , \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \lambda' - \lambda = \frac{2\pi}{m}(1 - \cos\theta) = \lambda_C(1 - \cos\theta) ,
$$
with $\lambda = 2\pi/\omega$ and the **Compton wavelength** $\lambda_C = h/(m_ec) = 2.426\,$pm.

*Proof.* With $k + p = k' + p'$, $p'^2 = m^2$ gives $(k + p - k')^2 = m^2$, that is $2p\cdot k - 2p\cdot k' - 2k\cdot k' = 0$ since $k^2 = k'^2 = 0$. With $p = (m, \vec 0)$, $p\cdot k = m\omega$,
$p\cdot k' = m\omega'$ and $k\cdot k' = \omega\omega'(1 - \cos\theta)$: $m(\omega - \omega') = \omega\omega'(1 - \cos\theta)$, which is the first formula, and dividing by $m\omega\omega'$ gives $1/\omega' - 1/\omega =
(1 - \cos\theta)/m$, the second. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The shift is independent of the wavelength, so it matters only for short wavelengths. The first example evaluates it for
X-rays.

::: {#exm-sr-compton-xray}
#### X-rays

For the molybdenum line $\lambda = 71\,$pm scattered at $90°$, $\lambda' = 73.4\,$pm, a $3.4\%$ shift; for visible light ($500\,$nm) the same $2.4\,$pm is a shift of
$5 \times 10^{-6}$, invisible. Compton's measurement of this shift was the decisive evidence that light carries momentum $h/\lambda$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For gamma rays the energy transfer is large. The second example evaluates the backscattered energy, which produces the
"Compton edge" in gamma-ray spectra.

::: {#exm-sr-compton-edge}
#### The Compton edge

A $1\,$MeV photon backscattered ($\theta = \pi$) keeps $\omega' = 1/(1 + 2/0.511)\,$MeV $= 0.204\,$MeV, and the electron takes the rest, $0.796\,$MeV: the largest energy a
detector electron can receive from a single scattering, seen as a sharp edge in the spectrum.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The kinetic energy of the recoiling electron follows from energy conservation. The third example writes it as a function of
the angle [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.97].

::: {#exm-sr-compton-electron}
#### The recoil electron

$T_e = \omega - \omega' = \frac{\omega^2(1 - \cos\theta)/m}{1 + \omega(1 - \cos\theta)/m}$, which grows from $0$ at $\theta = 0$ to $\frac{2\omega^2/m}{1 + 2\omega/m}$ at $\theta = \pi$, the edge of the second example.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The centre-of-momentum frame of Compton scattering is the natural frame for the theory. The first exercise finds the photon
energy there [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.96 b].

::: {#exr-sr-compton-cm}
#### Compton scattering in the centre-of-momentum frame

Show that in the centre-of-momentum frame the photon energy, before and after the scattering, is $\omega^* = m\omega/\sqrt{m^2 + 2m\omega}$, with $\omega$ the laboratory energy.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$s = m^2 + 2m\omega$, and in the centre-of-momentum frame the photon and the electron have opposite momenta of equal size $\omega^*$, with total energy $\sqrt s$.
This is the kinematics of @prp-sr-two-body with $M^2 = s$ and masses $0$ and $m$: $\omega^* = (s - m^2)/(2\sqrt s) = 2m\omega/(2\sqrt{m^2 + 2m\omega})$, which is the claim; the
same holds after the scattering, which only turns the momenta.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

When the electron is fast and the photon slow, the photon gains energy instead of losing it. The second exercise computes
this inverse Compton effect, which produces the X-rays of many astrophysical sources [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.98].

::: {#exr-sr-inverse-compton}
#### Inverse Compton scattering

A photon of energy $\omega$ moving along $+x$ meets head on an electron of Lorentz factor $\gamma$ moving along $-x$. Find the scattered photon energy at angle $\theta$ to $+x$, and evaluate the backscattered energy for $\gamma = 1000$ and $\omega = 1\,$eV.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
From $p\cdot k = p\cdot k' + k\cdot k'$ with $p = \gamma m(1, -v, 0, 0)$, $k = \omega(1, 1, 0, 0)$, $k' = \omega'(1, \cos\theta, \sin\theta, 0)$: $\omega' = \frac{\omega(1 + v)}{1 + v\cos\theta + \frac{\omega}{\gamma m}(1 -
\cos\theta)}$. At $\theta = \pi$ (photon sent back along $-x$, with the electron) $\omega' = \omega(1 + v)/(1 - v + 2\omega/(\gamma m)) \approx 4\gamma^2\omega/(1 + 4\gamma\omega/m)$, about
$4 \times 10^6\,$eV $\times 0.99$, a $4\,$MeV gamma ray from a $1\,$eV photon:

{{< sage exr-sr-inverse-compton >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Compton formula connects the angles of photon and electron. The third exercise derives the electron's recoil angle. It complements the photon angle of the proposition.

::: {#exr-sr-compton-angle}
#### The angle of the recoil electron

Show that the electron recoils at an angle $\phi$ to the incident direction with $\cot\phi = (1 + \omega/m)\tan(\theta/2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Momentum conservation gives $p'\cos\phi = \omega - \omega'\cos\theta$ and $p'\sin\phi = \omega'\sin\theta$, so $\cot\phi = (\omega/\omega' - \cos\theta)/\sin\theta$. With $\omega/\omega' = 1 + (\omega/m)(1 - \cos\theta)$:
$\cot\phi = \frac{(1 - \cos\theta)(1 + \omega/m)}{\sin\theta} = (1 + \omega/m)\tan\tfrac\theta2$. The electron always moves forward, $0 < \phi < \pi/2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Exercises

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises below combine thresholds, decays and invariants. The first is an accelerator experiment at Uppsala
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.105]. The masses are rounded as in the original problem.

::: {#exr-sr-celsius}
#### The CELSIUS reaction

Protons with kinetic energy $T_p$ hit deuterons at rest in $p + d \to p + p + n + \eta$, with $m_p \approx m_n = 940\,$MeV, $m_d \approx 2m_n$ and $m_\eta = 550\,$MeV. Is the reaction
possible for $T_p = 700\,$MeV? Find the threshold.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By @prp-sr-threshold, $T^{\mathrm{th}} = ((3m + m_\eta)^2 - (3m)^2)/(2 \cdot 2m) = (6mm_\eta + m_\eta^2)/(4m) = \tfrac32m_\eta + m_\eta^2/(4m) \approx 905\,$MeV. At $700\,$MeV the reaction is not possible:

{{< sage exr-sr-celsius >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The second exercise combines formation of a resonance with the threshold formula. It is the $\Delta$ resonance seen in pion-nucleon
scattering [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.89].

::: {#exr-sr-delta-resonance}
#### Forming the $\Delta(1232)$

What kinetic energy must a pion have to form the $\Delta(1232)$ on a proton at rest, $\pi + p \to \Delta$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$s = m_\Delta^2 = m_\pi^2 + m_p^2 + 2m_pE_\pi$, so $T_\pi = E_\pi - m_\pi = (m_\Delta^2 - (m_\pi + m_p)^2)/(2m_p) = (1232^2 - 1077.8^2)/1876.5\,$MeV $\approx 190\,$MeV, the energy of the famous peak
in the pion-proton cross section.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The third exercise is a nuclear reaction in which the photon carries away the binding energy, and recoil shifts its
energy slightly [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.93]. The recoil correction is small but measurable.

::: {#exr-sr-deuteron-photon}
#### Neutron capture by a proton

A thermal neutron (at rest) is absorbed by a proton at rest, $p + n \to d + \gamma$, with binding energy $B = 2.224\,$MeV, $m_d = m_p + m_n - B$. Find the photon energy
exactly and to first order in $B/m_d$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The initial state is at rest with energy $M = m_p + m_n$, so it is a two-body decay of mass $M$ into $m_d$ and a photon: $\omega = (M^2 - m_d^2)/(2M) = B(2M - B)/(2M) = B -
B^2/(2M) \approx 2.224 - 0.0026\,$MeV. The deuteron recoils with the remaining $B^2/(2M)$, about $2.6\,$keV.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

## Relativistic optics {#sec-sr-optics}

Light is the probe with which most relativistic effects are observed, and light itself transforms between frames. Its
frequency changes (the Doppler effect), its direction changes (aberration), and what an observer sees of a moving body is
assembled from light that left it at different times. All three follow from one fact: the phase of a wave is invariant,
so frequency and wave vector form a four-vector. Classical electrodynamics derives the Doppler effect and aberration in
@exm-cfb-doppler and @exr-cfb-aberration; here they are obtained in full generality and applied. The sources are
@blennow2022relativity [Sec. 1.5], @boskoff2024journey [Sec. 9.5] and @maggiore2023electrodynamics [Sec. 9.6].

### The wave four-vector and the Doppler effect

A plane wave has a phase that every observer agrees on, since it counts wave crests. Writing it as a Minkowski product
defines the wave four-vector, and its transformation law gives the frequency in any frame; @fig-sr-doppler plots the
result.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-sr-wave-vector}
#### Wave four-vector

A plane wave $e^{-i\phi}$ with phase $\phi = \omega t - \vec k\cdot\vec x = k\cdot x$ has the **wave four-vector** $k^\mu = (\omega, \vec k)$. Because the phase is a scalar,
$k^\mu$ transforms as a four-vector (@exm-sr-field-plane-wave). For light in vacuum $k$ is null, $\omega = |\vec k|$; a photon of the wave has four-momentum
$p^\mu = \hbar k^\mu$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
![The Doppler factor $\omega/\omega_0 = 1/(\gamma(1 - v\cos\theta))$ for a source moving with speed $v$, against the angle $\theta$ between its velocity
and the direction of the light received, for $v = 0.1$, $0.5$ and $0.9$. At $\theta = \pi/2$ (dotted) the shift is the transverse redshift $1/\gamma$;
the factor equals $1$ at the angle of @exr-sr-doppler-unshifted. Generated by `figures/sr-doppler.sage`.](figures/sr-doppler.svg){#fig-sr-doppler width=65%}

The phase of a wave travelling along $x$ is the simplest case. The first example writes it as a Minkowski product
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.62].

::: {#exm-sr-wave-along-x}
#### A wave along $x$

$E = E_0\sin(2\pi(x/\lambda - \nu t))$ has phase $-(\omega t - kx)$ with $\omega = 2\pi\nu$ and $k = 2\pi/\lambda = \omega/c$: the argument is $-k\cdot x$ with $k^\mu = (\omega, \omega, 0, 0)$, a
null vector. Under the boost along $x$ in rapidity form, $\omega' = \omega(\cosh\eta - \sinh\eta) = e^{-\eta}\omega$, the Doppler factor met in @exm-sr-rapidity-lightcone.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A photon is a quantum of the wave, and its momentum is the wave vector times $\hbar$. The second example relates the
transformation of the photon's energy to that of the wave's frequency.

::: {#exm-sr-photon-wave}
#### Photons and waves transform alike

Since $p = \hbar k$, the energy of a photon changes between frames by the same factor as the frequency of its wave. A $500\,$nm photon
has energy $hc/\lambda = 2.48\,$eV; seen from a frame receding at $v = 0.5$ along its direction, it has $2.48\sqrt{(1 - 0.5)/(1 + 0.5)} = 1.43\,$eV,
and wavelength $866\,$nm, in the infrared.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In a medium the wave vector of light is not null. The third example shows that its four-vector character still holds, and
gives Fizeau's result of @exm-sr-fizeau again [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.70].

::: {#exm-sr-wave-medium}
#### A wave in a medium

In a medium at rest, light of frequency $\omega$ has $|\vec k| = n\omega$, so $k = \omega(1, n\hat k)$ is spacelike for $n > 1$. In a frame where the medium moves with $-v$
along $\hat k$, $\omega' = \gamma\omega(1 + nv)$ and $k' = \gamma\omega(n + v)$, so the phase velocity is $\omega'/k' = (1 + nv)/(n + v) = (1/n + v)/(1 + v/n)$, the composition of
$1/n$ and $v$ (@exm-sr-fizeau).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise derives the longitudinal Doppler formula from the wave four-vector and writes it in terms of rapidity
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.62]. The answer is a single exponential.

::: {#exr-sr-doppler-rapidity}
#### The Doppler shift from the wave vector

For $k = (\omega, \omega, 0, 0)$ and an observer moving with velocity $v$ along $x$, compute $\omega'$ and express it with the rapidity. What is the observed
wavelength of a $1215\,$Å line if $v = -0.5$ (observer approaching the source)?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\omega' = \gamma(\omega - v\omega) = \omega\sqrt{(1 - v)/(1 + v)} = e^{-\eta}\omega$. For $v = -0.5$, $\omega' = \sqrt3\,\omega$ and $\lambda' = 1215/\sqrt3 = 701\,$Å: approaching observers see
blueshifted light.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The invariance of the phase can be checked on a concrete wave. The second exercise does so symbolically. The computation is symbolic in the frequency, the direction and the velocity.

::: {#exr-sr-phase-invariant}
#### The phase is invariant

With Sage, apply a boost with velocity $v$ along $x$ to both $x^\mu$ and $k^\mu$ for a wave with $\vec k$ in the $xy$-plane, and check that $k\cdot x$ is unchanged and
that $k$ stays null.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The product of the boosted vectors equals the original product identically, and $k'\cdot k' = 0$:

{{< sage exr-sr-phase-invariant >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A source moving through a medium with sound-like waves gives the classical Doppler effect in the limit. The third exercise
compares the two [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.70].

::: {#exr-sr-doppler-medium}
#### A source in a medium

A source of proper frequency $\omega_0$ moves with velocity $v$ through a medium in which waves travel at speed $u$. Show that the frequency of the waves
emitted forward, in the frame of the medium, is $\omega = \omega_0/(\gamma(1 - v/u))$, and discuss $v = u$ and the limit $v \ll 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In the medium frame the wave vector is $N = \omega(1, 1/u, 0, 0)$, and the source with four-velocity $\gamma(1, v, 0, 0)$ measures $\omega_0 = N\cdot u_s = \gamma\omega(1 - v/u)$. For $v
\to u$ the frequency diverges: the source keeps pace with its own waves, the sonic boom. For $v \ll 1$, $\gamma \approx 1$ and $\omega = \omega_0/(1 - v/u)$, the classical formula
for a moving source.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

The Doppler effect for an arbitrary direction follows from projecting the wave four-vector on the four-velocity of the
source. The proposition below gives the general formula, which contains the longitudinal effect of @boskoff2024journey
[Theorem 9.5.2] and the transverse effect, which has no classical analogue.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sr-doppler}
#### Relativistic Doppler effect

A source moving with velocity $\vec v$ emits light of frequency $\omega_0$ in its rest frame. An observer at rest receives it with frequency
$$
\omega = \frac{\omega_0}{\gamma(1 - v\cos\theta)} ,
$$ {#eq-sr-doppler}
where $\theta$ is the angle, in the observer's frame, between $\vec v$ and the direction in which the light propagates. For a source moving straight towards the
observer, $\omega = \omega_0\sqrt{(1 + v)/(1 - v)}$; straight away, $\omega = \omega_0\sqrt{(1 - v)/(1 + v)}$; and for $\theta = \pi/2$, $\omega = \omega_0/\gamma$.

*Proof.* In the observer's frame the light has $k = \omega(1, \hat n)$ and the source the four-velocity $u_s = \gamma(1, \vec v)$. The frequency measured by the source is
$k\cdot u_s$ (@exm-sr-energy-observer, applied to the wave), and it equals $\omega_0$: $\omega_0 = \gamma\omega(1 - \vec v\cdot\hat n) = \gamma\omega(1 - v\cos\theta)$. The special cases are $\cos\theta = 1,
-1, 0$, with $\gamma(1 \mp v) = \sqrt{(1 \mp v)/(1 \pm v)}$. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Large redshifts were first interpreted as Doppler shifts. The first example finds the speed of a quasar on that
interpretation [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.61].

::: {#exm-sr-quasar}
#### A receding quasar

The Lyman-$\alpha$ line, $1215\,$Å at rest, is observed at $3600\,$Å in the quasar 3C 9. As a pure Doppler shift, $\sqrt{(1 + v)/(1 - v)} = 3600/1215 = 2.963$ gives
$v = (2.963^2 - 1)/(2.963^2 + 1) = 0.795$: the quasar would recede at $80\%$ of the speed of light. Today the shift is understood as cosmological
(@sec-schwarzschild-flrw), but the kinematics of the formula is the same.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Time intervals are stretched by the same factor as wavelengths, since both are measured by the arrival of signals. The
second example uses this for gamma-ray bursts [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.63].

::: {#exm-sr-grb}
#### Stretched bursts

A gamma-ray burst that lasts twice as long as nearby ones, all bursts having the same duration at the source, has its signals
stretched by the factor $2$; the arrival times of successive crests are stretched by the same factor, so $\lambda/\lambda_0 = 2$. The duration of a
signal and the period of a wave are both intervals between emission events, received after travel times that grow with the
distance of the receding source.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The transverse Doppler effect is pure time dilation of the source. The third example describes its measurement. It was the first direct test of time dilation.

::: {#exm-sr-transverse-doppler}
#### The transverse Doppler effect

Light received at right angles to the source's velocity is redshifted by $1/\gamma$, a second-order effect with no Newtonian counterpart.
Ives and Stilwell (1938) measured it with fast hydrogen ions by comparing the forward and backward shifted lines: their average,
$\tfrac12\omega_0(\sqrt{(1 + v)/(1 - v)} + \sqrt{(1 - v)/(1 + v)}) = \gamma\omega_0$ in frequency, or $\gamma\lambda_0$ for the average of the wavelengths, differs from $\omega_0$ at second order in $v$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Two objects approaching each other at half the speed of light see each other's light strongly blueshifted. The first
exercise computes it for a ruby laser [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.64 b].

::: {#exr-sr-ruby}
#### A ruby laser between two ships

Two ships approach each other, each with speed $c/2$ in some frame. One fires a ruby laser ($694.3\,$nm) at the other. What wavelength does the other
receive?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Their relative speed is $0.8c$ (@exm-sr-half-plus-half), and the light travels along the relative velocity towards the receiver, so $\lambda = 694.3\sqrt{(1 - 0.8)/(1 + 0.8)} =
694.3/3 = 231.4\,$nm, in the ultraviolet.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Between the blueshift ahead and the redshift behind there is a direction of no shift. The second exercise finds it
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.65].

::: {#exr-sr-doppler-unshifted}
#### The direction of no shift

For which angle $\theta$ in @eq-sr-doppler is $\omega = \omega_0$? Evaluate it for $v = 0.5$ and $v = 0.99$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\gamma(1 - v\cos\theta) = 1$ gives $\cos\theta = (1 - 1/\gamma)/v$. For $v = 0.5$, $\cos\theta = 0.268$, $\theta = 74.5°$; for $v = 0.99$, $\cos\theta = 0.868$, $\theta = 29.8°$. The unshifted direction moves forward
as $v \to 1$, because the transverse redshift grows:

{{< sage exr-sr-doppler-unshifted >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A moving mirror changes both the frequency and the angle of reflected light. The third exercise computes both by
transforming to the mirror's frame and back [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.68].

::: {#exr-sr-moving-mirror}
#### A moving mirror

A mirror perpendicular to $x$ moves with velocity $v$ along $x$. Light of frequency $\omega$ propagates at angle $\theta_{\mathrm{in}}$ to the $+x$-axis towards it. Find the
frequency and the angle $\theta_{\mathrm{out}}$ (to $+x$) of the reflected light. What happens when $v < -\cos\theta_{\mathrm{in}}$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In the mirror frame $\omega' = \gamma\omega(1 - v\cos\theta_{\mathrm{in}})$ and $k'_x = \gamma\omega(\cos\theta_{\mathrm{in}} - v)$; reflection reverses $k'_x$; transforming back,
$\omega_{\mathrm{out}} = \gamma^2\omega(1 - 2v\cos\theta_{\mathrm{in}} + v^2)$ and $\cos\theta_{\mathrm{out}} = \frac{2v - (1 + v^2)\cos\theta_{\mathrm{in}}}{1 - 2v\cos\theta_{\mathrm{in}} + v^2}$. For $v = 0$ this is ordinary reflection. If
$v < -\cos\theta_{\mathrm{in}}$, the mirror recedes along $x$ faster than the light approaches it, $k'_x < 0$ in the mirror frame, and the light never reaches it:

{{< sage exr-sr-moving-mirror >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Aberration and the appearance of moving bodies

The wave four-vector changes direction as well as length under a boost. Stars seen from a moving ship crowd towards the
direction of motion, and a body moving fast does not look contracted but distorted and turned. @fig-sr-beaming shows the
crowding.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sr-aberration}
#### Aberration

Let light propagate at angle $\theta$ to the $x$-axis in a frame $K$, and let $K'$ move with velocity $v$ along $x$. In $K'$ it propagates at the angle $\theta'$ with
$$
\cos\theta' = \frac{\cos\theta - v}{1 - v\cos\theta}, \qquad \sin\theta' = \frac{\sin\theta}{\gamma(1 - v\cos\theta)}, \qquad \tan\frac{\theta'}{2} = \sqrt{\frac{1 + v}{1 - v}}\tan\frac\theta2 .
$$ {#eq-sr-aberration}

*Proof.* $k = \omega(1, \cos\theta, \sin\theta, 0)$ boosts to $\omega' = \gamma\omega(1 - v\cos\theta)$, $k'_x = \gamma\omega(\cos\theta - v)$, $k'_y = \omega\sin\theta$, and $\cos\theta' = k'_x/\omega'$, $\sin\theta' = k'_y/\omega'$. For the
half angle, $\tan\tfrac{\theta'}{2} = \frac{\sin\theta'}{1 + \cos\theta'} = \frac{\sin\theta}{\gamma(1 - v\cos\theta + \cos\theta - v)} = \frac{\sin\theta}{\gamma(1 - v)(1 + \cos\theta)} = \sqrt{\tfrac{1 + v}{1 - v}}\tan\tfrac\theta2$. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
![The headlight effect. Light emitted isotropically in the rest frame of a source moving along $x$ is concentrated, in the laboratory, into
a forward cone. The curves show the fraction of the light emitted within the angle $\theta$ of the direction of motion, for $v = 0$, $0.5$, $0.9$ and $0.99$;
half of it lies within $\cos\theta = v$, about $1/\gamma$ for fast sources. Generated by `figures/sr-beaming.sage`.](figures/sr-beaming.svg){#fig-sr-beaming width=65%}

The aberration of starlight was discovered by Bradley in 1727, long before relativity. The first example computes its size
for the orbital motion of the Earth.

::: {#exm-sr-stellar-aberration}
#### Stellar aberration

For light arriving perpendicular to the Earth's orbital velocity $v = 10^{-4}$ ($30\,$km/s), @eq-sr-aberration gives $\cos\theta' = -v$: the star appears tilted towards the
direction of motion by $\arcsin v \approx 10^{-4}\,$rad $= 20.6''$, and over a year its apparent position traces an ellipse of this size. The relativistic correction
is of order $v^2$, far below Bradley's precision.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For a fast source the effect concentrates its light forward. The second example computes the half-light angle shown in
@fig-sr-beaming.

::: {#exm-sr-headlight}
#### The headlight effect

Light emitted by the source at right angles in its own frame, $\theta' = \pi/2$, is seen in the laboratory at $\cos\theta = v$ (apply @eq-sr-aberration with $-v$).
Half of an isotropic emission therefore lies in the laboratory cone $\cos\theta > v$, of half-angle $\theta \approx 1/\gamma$ for $\gamma \gg 1$: synchrotron light from
electrons of $\gamma = 10^4$ is concentrated within $0.1\,$mrad of their direction.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The sky seen from a fast ship is distorted in the same way. The third example describes it [@blennow2022relativity, Problem
1.27].

::: {#exm-sr-starry-sky}
#### The sky from a fast ship

A star seen in the direction $\alpha$ from the ship's velocity (the light arriving with $\theta = \pi - \alpha$ to the motion) appears at $\alpha'$ with $\tan(\alpha'/2) =
\sqrt{(1 - v)/(1 + v)}\tan(\alpha/2)$. All stars move towards the forward direction; at $v = 0.9$ a star at $\alpha = 90°$ appears at $\alpha' = 25.8°$, and the Doppler
effect makes the forward stars bluer and brighter.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise asks for the fraction of the sky that appears in the forward hemisphere, as plotted in @fig-sr-beaming. The answer is surprisingly simple.

::: {#exr-sr-forward-fraction}
#### The forward hemisphere

For an observer moving with $v$ through an isotropic distribution of stars, show that the fraction of stars seen in the forward hemisphere is
$\tfrac12(1 + v)$, and evaluate it for $v = 0.9$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A star is seen forward when the light arrives with $\cos\theta' < 0$ in the observer's frame (it propagates backwards), that is $\cos\theta < v$ in the rest
frame of the stars by @eq-sr-aberration. For an isotropic distribution $\cos\theta$ is uniform on $[-1, 1]$, so the fraction is $(v + 1)/2$: $95\%$ at $v = 0.9$:

{{< sage exr-sr-forward-fraction >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Aberration can be derived from the composition of velocities as well. The second exercise checks that the two routes agree.

::: {#exr-sr-aberration-velocity}
#### Aberration from the composition law

Apply @eq-sr-velocity-addition to a light signal $\vec u = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta, 0)$ and show that it gives @eq-sr-aberration.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$u'_x = (\cos\theta - v)/(1 - v\cos\theta)$ and $u'_y = \sin\theta/(\gamma(1 - v\cos\theta))$, and $|\vec u'| = 1$ (@exm-sr-addition-light), so these are $\cos\theta'$ and $\sin\theta'$. The two derivations agree
because the velocity of light is $\vec k/\omega$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A medium moving through the beam can refract light without bending it, for a suitable index. The third exercise finds the
index [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.69].

::: {#exr-sr-moving-medium}
#### Refraction without bending

A slab of refractive index $n$ moves perpendicular to its surface. In the rest frame of the slab the laboratory moves with velocity $w > 0$ along the
normal $\hat x$, the direction in which the light enters, and the light arrives at angle $\theta'$ to $\hat x$. Show that in the laboratory the light keeps its
direction on entering the slab if and only if $n^2 = (1 - 2w\cos\theta' + w^2)/w^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In the slab frame the incident velocity is $(\cos\theta', \sin\theta')$ and the refracted one $\frac1n(\cos\theta'_r, \sin\theta'_r)$ with $n\sin\theta'_r = \sin\theta'$. By
@eq-sr-velocity-addition the laboratory directions have slopes $\frac{\sin\theta'}{\gamma(\cos\theta' - w)}$ and $\frac{\sin\theta'_r/n}{\gamma(\cos\theta'_r/n - w)}$, which are equal iff $\cos\theta' - w =
n\cos\theta'_r - n^2w$, that is $\sqrt{n^2 - \sin^2\theta'} = \cos\theta' + w(n^2 - 1)$. Squaring gives $(n^2 - 1)(1 - 2w\cos\theta' - w^2(n^2 - 1)) = 0$, and the non-trivial root is the
claim; it exceeds $1$ when $1 > 2w\cos\theta'$. A numerical check of the directions:

{{< sage exr-sr-moving-medium >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

What an observer sees, or photographs, is not the set of positions at one instant of her time but the set of positions
from which light arrives at one instant. For a moving body these were emitted at different times, and the image is
distorted in a way that depends on the direction of view.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sr-appearance}
#### Apparent length of a moving rod

A rod of rest length $L_0$ moves with velocity $v$ along its own direction. A distant observer, receiving light that propagates at angle $\theta$ to the velocity,
sees the rod with the apparent length, measured along the direction of motion,
$$
L_{\mathrm{app}} = \frac{L_0}{\gamma(1 - v\cos\theta)} .
$$
It is contracted, $L_0/\gamma$, only for $\theta = \pi/2$; it is stretched for an approaching rod and shortened further for a receding one.

*Proof.* The rod's ends are at $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t) = x_1(t) + L_0/\gamma$ (@prp-sr-dilation-contraction). For a distant observer the light rays are parallel, along $\hat n$ with
$\hat n\cdot\hat x = \cos\theta$, and the rays that arrive together were emitted from points $\vec x_1$, $\vec x_2$ at times $t_1$, $t_2$ with $t_2 - t_1 = \hat n\cdot(\vec x_2 - \vec x_1)$ (the
point further along $\hat n$ emits later). With $\vec x_2 - \vec x_1 = L_{\mathrm{app}}\hat x$, $L_{\mathrm{app}} = L_0/\gamma + v(t_2 - t_1) = L_0/\gamma + vL_{\mathrm{app}}\cos\theta$, which gives the formula. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Two lamps approaching an observer along the line of sight appear further apart than their rest distance. The first
example is @blennow2022relativity [Problem 1.23].

::: {#exm-sr-lamps-approach}
#### Approaching lamps

Two lamps at rest distance $\ell_0$ move towards an observer along the line of sight: the light propagates along the velocity, $\theta = 0$, and the
seen separation is $\ell_0/(\gamma(1 - v)) = \ell_0\sqrt{(1 + v)/(1 - v)}$. At $v = 0.6$ the lamps look twice as far apart as they are in their own frame.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A cube seen at right angles to its motion is not seen contracted and flattened but turned. The second example explains
this Terrell-Penrose rotation.

::: {#exm-sr-terrell}
#### A moving cube looks rotated

At $\theta = \pi/2$ the front face of a cube of side $a$ appears contracted to $a/\gamma$. Its rear face, hidden at rest, becomes visible: light from it that leaves at the
right moment passes the receding front edge, and it appears with width $av$. Faces of widths $a\sqrt{1 - v^2}$ and $av$ are what a cube rotated by the angle
$\arcsin v$ shows: a fast-moving object looks rotated, not contracted, an effect noticed only in 1959 by Terrell and by Penrose.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Blobs ejected by quasars sometimes appear to move faster than light across the sky. The third example shows how the
apparent length formula produces this illusion.

::: {#exm-sr-superluminal}
#### Apparent superluminal motion

A blob moving with speed $v$ at angle $\theta$ to the line of sight, towards the observer, moves across the sky by $v\sin\theta\,\Delta t$ while the light it emits
arrives over the shortened time $\Delta t(1 - v\cos\theta)$. Its apparent transverse speed is $v\sin\theta/(1 - v\cos\theta)$, maximal at $\cos\theta = v$ with the value $\gamma v$: for $\gamma = 5$,
five times the speed of light (@exr-sr-superluminal).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
