:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
A pole moving past an observer is seen at several angles at once. The first exercise reconstructs the position of a mark
on it from the angles under which its points are seen [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.17].

::: {#exr-sr-pole-marks}
#### Marks on a moving pole

A pole moves with speed $v$ in the negative $x$-direction, parallel to the $x$-axis at distance $h$. At one instant an observer at the origin sees its front at
angle $\pi/3$ to the $x$-axis, a mark at $\pi/4$ and its end at $\pi/6$. Find the ratio $r$ of the distance from the front to the mark to the length of the pole, as a
function of $v$, and its value for $v = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A point seen at angle $\alpha$ emitted its light from $x = h\cot\alpha$ at the time $-h/\sin\alpha$ before reception. In the rod frame, positions are proportional to $x + vt_{\mathrm{emit}}$
up to a constant, that is to $h(\cot\alpha - v/\sin\alpha)$. Hence $r = \frac{(\cot\frac\pi3 - \cot\frac\pi4) - v(\csc\frac\pi3 - \csc\frac\pi4)}{(\cot\frac\pi3 - \cot\frac\pi6) - v(\csc\frac\pi3 - \csc\frac\pi6)}$, which
equals $0.366$ for $v = 0$ and grows with $v$:

{{< sage exr-sr-pole-marks >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The superluminal speed of the third example can be maximised over the angle. The second exercise does it. The maximum is reached at a definite angle.

::: {#exr-sr-superluminal}
#### The largest apparent speed

Maximise $v_{\mathrm{app}}(\theta) = v\sin\theta/(1 - v\cos\theta)$ over $\theta$, and find $\gamma$ for a quasar jet with an observed apparent speed of $10c$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$dv_{\mathrm{app}}/d\theta = v(\cos\theta - v)/(1 - v\cos\theta)^2$ vanishes at $\cos\theta = v$, where $v_{\mathrm{app}} = v\sqrt{1 - v^2}/(1 - v^2) = \gamma v$. An apparent $10c$ needs $\gamma v \geq 10$, so $\gamma \geq
\sqrt{101} \approx 10.05$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The apparent length depends on the direction of view through the factor of the Doppler formula. The third exercise makes
the connection.

::: {#exr-sr-appearance-doppler}
#### Apparent length and Doppler factor

Show that $L_{\mathrm{app}} = L_0\,\omega/\omega_0$, where $\omega/\omega_0$ is the Doppler factor @eq-sr-doppler for light from the rod in the same direction, and explain why.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both are $1/(\gamma(1 - v\cos\theta))$ times the rest value. The rod is a "wave" of length $L_0$ in its rest frame: two ends play the role of two crests, emitted at
different places, and the reception compresses or stretches the pattern by the same factor as for successive crests of a wave from a moving source.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Exercises

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises below combine the Doppler effect with kinematics. The first follows a radar echo from a moving target,
which doubles the shift.

::: {#exr-sr-radar-echo}
#### A radar echo

A police radar of frequency $24\,$GHz is reflected by a car approaching at $v$. Show that the echo has frequency $\omega\frac{1 + v}{1 - v}$ and find the frequency shift for
$v = 30\,$m/s.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The car receives $\omega\sqrt{(1 + v)/(1 - v)}$ and re-emits it as a moving source, which multiplies it again by the same factor (equivalently, the mirror formula of
@exr-sr-moving-mirror with $\theta_{\mathrm{in}} = \pi$ and the mirror moving towards the source). The shift is $\approx 2v\omega = 2 \cdot 10^{-7} \cdot 24\,$GHz $= 4.8\,$kHz.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The second exercise relates the Doppler factor of a uniformly receding source to the rapidity, and shows that redshifts
compose multiplicatively. The answer explains why redshifts multiply rather than add.

::: {#exr-sr-redshift-compose}
#### Redshifts compose

A galaxy recedes from a second galaxy with $1 + z_1$, which recedes from us with $1 + z_2$, all along one line. Show that the redshift of the first galaxy seen from
us is $1 + z = (1 + z_1)(1 + z_2)$, and relate this to the addition of rapidities.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The longitudinal factor is $\sqrt{(1 + v)/(1 - v)} = e^\eta$ (@exm-sr-rapidity-lightcone). Collinear velocities add their rapidities, $\eta = \eta_1 + \eta_2$, so $e^\eta = e^{\eta_1}e^{\eta_2}$, that
is $1 + z = (1 + z_1)(1 + z_2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The third exercise is the transverse Doppler effect on a rotating disk, which the twin paradox of @exr-sr-disk-clocks
already explained; here the angle is computed directly. No longitudinal motion is involved.

::: {#exr-sr-transverse-disk}
#### Light from the rim of a turntable

A source on the rim of a disk rotating with speed $v$ emits light of proper frequency $\omega_0$ towards the centre. What frequency does an observer at the centre
receive?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In the inertial frame of the centre the light propagates radially inwards, perpendicular to the source velocity, so $\theta = \pi/2$ in @eq-sr-doppler and $\omega = \omega_0/\gamma$:
a pure transverse redshift, in agreement with the clock rates of @exr-sr-disk-clocks.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

## Relativistic dynamics {#sec-sr-dynamics}

Kinematics describes motion; dynamics explains it by forces. In special relativity the force becomes a four-vector, the
rate of change of four-momentum with proper time, and Newton's second law becomes a four-vector equation that follows from
the action of a free particle when interactions are added. The simplest accelerated motion, constant acceleration felt by
the moving body, turns out to be a hyperbola in spacetime, and the observers who move along a family of such hyperbolae
carry the coordinates of the Rindler frame, in which clocks at different heights run at different rates as in a
gravitational field. @sec-general-relativity takes this observation as its starting point. The sources are
@maggiore2023electrodynamics [Sec. 7.4], @boskoff2024journey [Sec. 9.6] and @blennow2022relativity [Secs. 1.4, 1.6 and
1.9].

### Four-force and the action of a particle

Newton's law equates the force with the rate of change of momentum. Its relativistic form uses the four-momentum and the
proper time, and the extra time component describes the rate of change of energy; @fig-sr-constant-force compares the
motion under a constant force with Newton's prediction.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-sr-four-force}
#### Four-force

The **four-force** on a particle is $F^\mu = dp^\mu/d\tau$. Writing $p = mu$ with a possibly varying rest mass, $F\cdot u = dm/d\tau$. A four-force with $F\cdot u = 0$,
which leaves the rest mass unchanged, is **pure**; then $F^\mu = \gamma(\vec f\cdot\vec v, \vec f)$ with the three-force $\vec f = d\vec p/dt$. A four-force parallel to $u$ is
**heat-like**: it changes only the rest mass.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
![A constant force. A particle starting from rest under a constant three-force $f$ along $x$ (in units with $f/m = 1$): its velocity (left) approaches $c$
instead of growing without bound as in Newton's law (dashed), and its position (right) approaches the light ray $x = t - 1$ asymptotically. This is
the hyperbolic motion of @prp-sr-hyperbolic-motion. Generated by `figures/sr-constant-force.sage`.](figures/sr-constant-force.svg){#fig-sr-constant-force width=95%}

A pure force does work at the rate $\vec f\cdot\vec v$. The first example derives the four-force from the three-force and checks that it
is orthogonal to the four-velocity.

::: {#exm-sr-pure-force}
#### A pure force from a three-force

For constant rest mass, $dp^\mu/d\tau = \gamma\,dp^\mu/dt = \gamma(dE/dt, \vec f)$, and $E^2 = |\vec p|^2 + m^2$ gives $E\,dE/dt = \vec p\cdot\vec f$, that is $dE/dt = \vec v\cdot\vec f$. So
$F = \gamma(\vec f\cdot\vec v, \vec f)$ and $F\cdot u = \gamma^2(\vec f\cdot\vec v - \vec f\cdot\vec v) = 0$. The Lorentz force of @prp-sr-lorentz-force is of this kind.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Heating a body increases its mass. The second example describes the heat-like four-force of isotropic absorption. Here only the rest mass changes.

::: {#exm-sr-heat-force}
#### Heating a body

A body at rest absorbing radiation equally from all directions receives energy and no momentum: in its rest frame $F = (dm/d\tau, \vec 0)$, so
$F = (dm/d\tau)u$ in every frame. A kilogram of water heated by $100\,$K gains $4.2 \times 10^5\,$J and its mass grows by $4.7 \times 10^{-12}\,$kg.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A four-force with no time component in one frame is not pure in general. The third example finds when it is
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.53].

::: {#exm-sr-spatial-force}
#### A force with no time component

For $F = (0, \vec f)$ acting on a particle with velocity $\vec v$, $dm/d\tau = F\cdot u = -\gamma\vec f\cdot\vec v$: the rest mass changes unless $\vec f \perp \vec v$. Such a force is pure only
when it does no work in the frame where it has no time component, for example a magnetic force (@prp-sr-lorentz-force).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise splits a four-force along a given direction into its effect on the mass and on the velocity
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.52]. Both effects follow from the decomposition of $F$ along and across $V$.

::: {#exr-sr-force-along-u}
#### A force along a fixed four-vector

An object of rest mass $M$ and four-velocity $V$ feels $F = fU$ with a fixed unit timelike $U$ and a scalar $f$. Show that $dM/d\tau = f\,U\cdot V$ and that its
proper acceleration is $\alpha = \frac{f}{M}\sqrt{(U\cdot V)^2 - 1}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$dM/d\tau = F\cdot V = fU\cdot V = f\gamma$ with $\gamma = U\cdot V$. Then $F = \dot MV + MA$ gives $A = \frac fM(U - \gamma V)$, and $-A\cdot A = \frac{f^2}{M^2}(2\gamma^2 - 1 - \gamma^2) = \frac{f^2}{M^2}(\gamma^2 - 1)$.
The force is pure only in the trivial case $f = 0$; it heats the object at the rate $f\gamma$ while accelerating it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A constant four-force along a null direction makes the mass grow. The second exercise integrates the motion
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.56].

::: {#exr-sr-null-force}
#### A constant null four-force

An object initially at rest with mass $m_0$ feels $F = f(1, 1, 0, 0)$. Find $m(\tau)$ and the coordinate time $t(\tau)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$p(\tau) = (m_0 + f\tau, f\tau, 0, 0)$, so $m^2 = p\cdot p = m_0^2 + 2m_0f\tau$, $m = \sqrt{m_0^2 + 2m_0f\tau}$. Then $dt/d\tau = p^0/m$, and substituting $w = m^2$ in the
integral gives $t = \frac{m^3 - m_0^3}{6m_0^2f} + \frac{m - m_0}{2f}$, which grows like $\tau^{3/2}$: the object is heated and pushed at once:

{{< sage exr-sr-null-force >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A linear accelerator applies a constant force. The third exercise computes the time an electron spends in one
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.111].

::: {#exr-sr-linac-time}
#### An electron in a linear accelerator

An electron starts from rest in a constant field of $10^4\,$V/m over $100\,$m. Find its final kinetic energy and the time it takes, using the energy as
integration variable.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The work is $eEL = 1\,$MeV, so $\gamma_f = 1 + 1/0.511 = 2.957$. With $dE/dt = eEv$ and $v = \sqrt{E^2 - m^2}/E$: $t = \int\frac{E\,dE}{eE\sqrt{E^2 - m^2}} = \frac{\sqrt{E_f^2 - m^2}}{eE} =
\frac{m\sqrt{\gamma_f^2 - 1}}{eE}$, which is $0.511\,\mathrm{MeV} \cdot 2.783/(10^4\,\mathrm{eV/m})/c = 142\,\mathrm{m}/c = 474\,$ns. A Newtonian estimate would give $L/(v_{\mathrm{avg}})$ with a final
speed above $c$:

{{< sage exr-sr-linac-time >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

The equations of motion of a free particle follow from an action, and so do those with interactions. The action must be a
Lorentz scalar and depend on the worldline only, so it is a multiple of the proper time (@thm-sr-twin, @maggiore2023electrodynamics
[Sec. 7.4.2]).

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sr-particle-action}
#### The action of a free particle

The action $S = -m\int d\tau = -m\int\sqrt{\eta_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu}\,d\lambda$ is invariant under Lorentz transformations and under reparametrisations $\lambda \mapsto
\lambda'(\lambda)$. Its Euler-Lagrange equations are $\frac{d}{d\lambda}\Bigl(\frac{m\dot x_\mu}{\sqrt{\dot x\cdot\dot x}}\Bigr) = 0$, that is $du^\mu/d\tau = 0$ in the proper-time parametrisation. With
$\lambda = t$ the Lagrangian is $L = -m\sqrt{1 - v^2}$, the canonical momentum $\vec p = \gamma m\vec v$ and the Hamiltonian $H = \sqrt{|\vec p|^2 + m^2}$.

*Proof.* $\eta_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu$ is a scalar and under $\lambda \mapsto \lambda'$ the integrand transforms as $\sqrt{\dot x\cdot\dot x}\,d\lambda = \sqrt{x'\cdot x'}\,d\lambda'$, so $S$ is
invariant. The Lagrangian $\mathcal{L} = -m\sqrt{\dot x\cdot\dot x}$ does not depend on $x$, so the Euler-Lagrange equations say $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\dot x^\mu = -m\dot x_\mu/\sqrt{\dot x\cdot\dot x}$ is
constant; with $\lambda = \tau$, $\sqrt{\dot x\cdot\dot x} = 1$ and this is $-mu_\mu$. With $\lambda = t$, $\dot x = (1, \vec v)$ and $L = -m\sqrt{1 - v^2}$; then $\partial L/\partial\vec v = m\vec v/\sqrt{1 - v^2} = \gamma m\vec v$
and $H = \vec p\cdot\vec v - L = \gamma mv^2 + m/\gamma = \gamma m = \sqrt{p^2 + m^2}$. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The sign and the factor of the action are fixed by the Newtonian limit. The first example expands the Lagrangian.

::: {#exm-sr-action-limit}
#### The Newtonian limit of the action

$L = -m\sqrt{1 - v^2} = -m + \tfrac12mv^2 + \tfrac18mv^4 + \dots$: up to the constant $-m$, which does not affect the equations of motion, the leading term is the
Newtonian kinetic energy. The minus sign makes the action of the straight worldline the minimum, since its proper time is the
maximum (@thm-sr-twin, @exm-sr-twin-action).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Interactions are added by terms in the action. The second example adds a potential and derives the relativistic Newton's
law for it.

::: {#exm-sr-action-potential}
#### A particle in a potential

$L = -m\sqrt{1 - v^2} - V(\vec x)$ gives $\frac{d}{dt}(\gamma m\vec v) = -\nabla V$: Newton's law with the relativistic momentum. This Lagrangian is not Lorentz invariant, since $V$
singles out a frame; the invariant coupling to the electromagnetic field, $-q\int A_\mu dx^\mu$, gives the Lorentz force (@exr-cfb-lorentz-force,
@prp-sr-lorentz-force).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Because of reparametrisation invariance, the four components of $\dot x$ are not independent dynamical variables. The third example
shows the resulting constraint among the momenta.

::: {#exm-sr-action-constraint}
#### The mass-shell constraint

The canonical momenta $p_\mu = -\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\dot x^\mu = m\dot x_\mu/\sqrt{\dot x\cdot\dot x}$ satisfy $p\cdot p = m^2$ identically, whatever the parametrisation: the mass shell is a
constraint, not an equation of motion. The canonical Hamiltonian $p_\mu\dot x^\mu - \mathcal{L}$ (with this sign convention) vanishes identically, a mark of
reparametrisation invariance that reappears in general relativity.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise derives the equations of motion of the relativistic harmonic oscillator and shows that its period
grows with the amplitude. Only the conserved energy is needed.

::: {#exr-sr-rel-oscillator}
#### The relativistic oscillator

For $L = -m\sqrt{1 - \dot x^2} - \tfrac12kx^2$, derive the equation of motion and the conserved energy, and compute with Sage the period for $m = k = 1$ and amplitudes $0.1$,
$1$ and $5$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\frac{d}{dt}(\gamma m\dot x) = -kx$, with the conserved energy $\gamma m + \tfrac12kx^2$. The period, $2\pi$ for small amplitudes, grows with the amplitude, and for large amplitudes
approaches $4A$, the time to cross the well at nearly the speed of light:

{{< sage exr-sr-rel-oscillator >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The square-root Lagrangian can be replaced by a quadratic one with the parameter fixed to proper time. The second exercise
shows the equivalence [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.150].

::: {#exr-sr-quadratic-lagrangian}
#### A quadratic Lagrangian

Show that $\mathcal{L} = \tfrac12m\eta_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu$, with $\dot x = dx/d\tau$, gives $\ddot x^\mu = 0$, that it conserves $\dot x\cdot\dot x$, and that adding $+q\dot x^\mu A_\mu$ gives
$m\ddot x_\mu = qF_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\nu$. Why does the coupling enter with the sign opposite to that of $-q\int A_\mu dx^\mu$ in the action $-m\int d\tau - q\int A_\mu dx^\mu$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Euler-Lagrange equations of $\tfrac12m\dot x\cdot\dot x$ are $m\ddot x_\mu = 0$, and $\frac{d}{d\tau}(\dot x\cdot\dot x) = 2\dot x\cdot\ddot x = 0$, so the normalisation $\dot x\cdot\dot x = 1$ can be imposed once.
With $+q\dot x^\nu A_\nu(x)$: $\frac{d}{d\tau}(m\dot x_\mu + qA_\mu) = q\dot x^\nu\partial_\mu A_\nu$, so $m\ddot x_\mu = q\dot x^\nu(\partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu) = qF_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\nu$, the covariant Lorentz force of
@prp-sr-lorentz-force. The quadratic Lagrangian reproduces $-m\sqrt{\dot x\cdot\dot x}$ only up to an overall sign (the Euler-Lagrange equations of $-m\sqrt{\dot x\cdot\dot x}$ in the
proper-time gauge are those of $-\tfrac12m\dot x\cdot\dot x$), so the whole action is multiplied by $-1$, coupling included.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Hamiltonian of the third statement of the proposition generates the motion. The third exercise checks Hamilton's
equations. The speed limit appears in the velocity equation.

::: {#exr-sr-hamilton}
#### Hamilton's equations of a free particle

Write Hamilton's equations (@def-hamilton-equations) for $H = \sqrt{|\vec p|^2 + m^2} + V(\vec x)$ and show that $\dot{\vec x} = \vec p/E$ with $E = \sqrt{|\vec p|^2 + m^2}$, so the speed never exceeds
$1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\dot{\vec x} = \partial H/\partial\vec p = \vec p/\sqrt{|\vec p|^2 + m^2}$ and $\dot{\vec p} = -\nabla V$. Since $|\vec p| < \sqrt{|\vec p|^2 + m^2}$ for $m > 0$, $|\dot{\vec x}| < 1$ however large the momentum: a force can increase
the momentum without bound but not the speed.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Constant proper acceleration

The acceleration that a passenger feels, measured with an accelerometer, is the acceleration in the instantaneous rest
frame. It is a Lorentz scalar, while the coordinate acceleration depends on the frame. @fig-sr-hyperbolic shows the
worldlines of constant felt acceleration.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-sr-proper-acceleration}
#### Proper acceleration

The **proper acceleration** of a worldline is $\alpha = \sqrt{-a\cdot a}$, the magnitude of its four-acceleration. In the instantaneous rest frame $a = (0, \vec a_0)$ and $\alpha = |\vec a_0|$,
the acceleration measured by an accelerometer carried along.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
![Hyperbolic motion. Left: worldlines of constant proper acceleration $\alpha$ starting from rest at the origin, for $\alpha = 0.5$, $1$, $2$ (units $c = 1$); they
approach light rays. Right: the proper time needed to reach a distance $d$ with $1g$ throughout (solid) or accelerating for the first half and
decelerating for the second (dashed), against $d$ in light-years; the dotted line is $d/c$. Generated by
`figures/sr-hyperbolic.sage`.](figures/sr-hyperbolic.svg){#fig-sr-hyperbolic width=95%}

In linear motion the proper acceleration exceeds the coordinate acceleration by $\gamma^3$. The first example derives the
factor. The rapidity makes the computation short.

::: {#exm-sr-proper-acc-linear}
#### Linear motion

For motion along $x$, $u = (\cosh\eta, \sinh\eta)$ with the rapidity $\eta(\tau)$, so $a = \dot\eta(\sinh\eta, \cosh\eta)$ and $\alpha = |\dot\eta|$. Since $d\eta = \gamma^2dv$ and $d\tau = dt/\gamma$,
$\alpha = \gamma^3|dv/dt|$: near the speed of light a large felt acceleration produces a tiny change of coordinate velocity.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In circular motion the factor is $\gamma^2$. The second example takes it from @exm-sr-u-circle and evaluates it for a storage ring.

::: {#exm-sr-proper-acc-circle}
#### Circular motion

$\alpha = \gamma^2v^2/r$ (@exm-sr-u-circle). For the muons of @exr-sr-muon-ring, $\gamma = 9.43$ and $v^2/r = 1.8 \times 10^{15}\,$m/s$^2$, so $\alpha \approx 1.6 \times 10^{17}\,$m/s$^2$, about $10^{16}g$; their
clocks still run at the rate $1/\gamma$ fixed by the speed alone (@exr-sr-muon-ring), the "clock hypothesis" confirmed by the muon experiments.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Coordinate accelerations transform in a complicated way, because both $dv$ and $dt$ change. The third example gives the law for
an object momentarily at rest [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.54].

::: {#exm-sr-acc-transform}
#### Acceleration seen from a moving frame

An object momentarily at rest in $S$ with acceleration $\vec a_0$ is seen from $S'$, moving with $v$ along $x$, to have acceleration components $a'_x = a_{0x}/\gamma^3$ and
$a'_\perp = a_{0\perp}/\gamma^2$. So $|\vec a'|$ lies between $\alpha/\gamma^3$ (for $\vec a_0 \parallel \vec v$) and $\alpha/\gamma^2$ (for $\vec a_0 \perp \vec v$): every moving observer measures less than the proper
acceleration.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The worldline of constant proper acceleration is a hyperbola, which every inertial observer sees as one. The first exercise
uses this to find a coordinate acceleration without computation [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.49].

::: {#exr-sr-hyperbola-invariant}
#### The same hyperbola in every frame

A rocket moves on $x^2 - t^2 = 1/\alpha^2$. Show that its proper acceleration is $\alpha$, and that in a frame $S'$ moving with any $v$ along $x$ its coordinate acceleration at $t' = 0$
is $\alpha$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$x = \cosh(\alpha\tau)/\alpha$, $t = \sinh(\alpha\tau)/\alpha$ gives $a = \alpha(\cosh\alpha\tau, \sinh\alpha\tau)$, $-a\cdot a = \alpha^2$. The boost preserves $x^2 - t^2$, so in $S'$ the worldline is the same hyperbola
$x'^2 - t'^2 = 1/\alpha^2$; at $t' = 0$ the rocket is at rest at $x' = 1/\alpha$, and its coordinate acceleration there equals the proper acceleration, $\alpha$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The particles of a circular accelerator feel a large proper acceleration. The second exercise computes it and the proper
time per turn [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.51].

::: {#exr-sr-accelerator-orbit}
#### Proper time per turn

A particle circulates with speed $v$ on a circle of radius $r$. Find its four-acceleration, its proper acceleration and the proper time of one turn, and
evaluate them for protons of $7\,$TeV on a circle of circumference $26.7\,$km, the size of the LHC.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$a = -\gamma^2(v^2/r)(0, \cos\omega t, \sin\omega t, 0)$, $\alpha = \gamma^2v^2/r$, and the proper time of a turn is $2\pi r/(\gamma v)$. For $\gamma = 7461$ and $r = 4.25\,$km: $\alpha \approx
\gamma^2c^2/r = 1.2 \times 10^{21}\,$m/s$^2$ and $\tau = 2\pi r/(\gamma c) = 11.9\,$ns, while a turn takes $89\,\mu$s in the laboratory:

{{< sage exr-sr-accelerator-orbit >}}
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

Passengers of a rocket feel one $g$ and want to know when they reach a given speed. The third exercise answers with the
rapidity.

::: {#exr-sr-one-g}
#### How long to $0.99c$

At a constant proper acceleration $g = 9.81\,$m/s$^2$, how much proper time and coordinate time are needed to reach $0.99c$ from rest, and how far has the rocket
gone?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The rapidity grows as $g\tau/c$ (@exm-sr-proper-acc-linear), so $\tau = (c/g)\operatorname{artanh}0.99$, $t = (c/g)\sinh(g\tau/c)$ and $x = (c^2/g)(\cosh(g\tau/c) - 1)$. With
$c/g = 0.969\,$yr: $\tau = 2.56\,$yr, $t = 6.80\,$yr and $x = 5.90\,$ly:

{{< sage exr-sr-one-g >}}
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

Constant proper acceleration is the relativistic version of uniform acceleration. The proposition below solves it, and
shows that the rapidity grows linearly with the proper time [@boskoff2024journey, Theorem 9.6.4].

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sr-hyperbolic-motion}
#### Hyperbolic motion

A particle that starts from rest at the origin and moves along $x$ with constant proper acceleration $\alpha$ has, in terms of its proper time,
$$
t = \frac{\sinh\alpha\tau}{\alpha}, \qquad x = \frac{\cosh\alpha\tau - 1}{\alpha}, \qquad v = \tanh\alpha\tau, \qquad x(t) = \frac{\sqrt{1 + \alpha^2t^2} - 1}{\alpha} .
$$
Its rapidity is $\alpha\tau$, and its worldline is the hyperbola $(x + 1/\alpha)^2 - t^2 = 1/\alpha^2$, asymptotic to the light ray $x = t - 1/\alpha$.

*Proof.* In one space dimension $u = (\cosh\eta, \sinh\eta)$ and $\alpha = |d\eta/d\tau|$ (@exm-sr-proper-acc-linear); with $\eta(0) = 0$ and $\eta$ increasing, $\eta = \alpha\tau$. Integrating $dt/d\tau = \cosh\alpha\tau$
and $dx/d\tau = \sinh\alpha\tau$ from $0$ gives $t$ and $x$, and $v = dx/dt = \tanh\alpha\tau$. Then $(x + 1/\alpha)^2 - t^2 = (\cosh^2 - \sinh^2)/\alpha^2 = 1/\alpha^2$, which solved for $x$ gives
$x(t)$. As $t \to \infty$, $x - t + 1/\alpha = \sqrt{t^2 + 1/\alpha^2} - t \to 0$. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The hyperbolic functions make interstellar travel possible within a lifetime, at least in principle. The first example
computes a trip to the Andromeda galaxy [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.41].

::: {#exm-sr-andromeda}
#### A trip to Andromeda

Andromeda is $d = 2.5 \times 10^6\,$ly away. Accelerating at $g = 10\,$m/s$^2$ all the way, the proper time is $\tau = (c/g)\operatorname{arcosh}(1 + gd/c^2)$; with $c/g = 0.95\,$yr (using
$1\,$yr $\approx \pi \cdot 10^7\,$s) and $gd/c^2 = 2.6 \times 10^6$, $\tau \approx 14.8\,$yr: a commander of $40$ arrives aged about $55$, while $2.5$ million years pass on the Earth.
Accelerating for half the way and decelerating for the other half takes $28.2\,$yr.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The light from home reaching the rocket is redshifted by the rapidity. The second example gives the exponential law. The law is exponential in the proper time.

::: {#exm-sr-rocket-redshift}
#### Signals from home

Light sent from the origin after the start catches the rocket, which at that moment has rapidity $\alpha\tau$ and recedes along the light's direction: by
@prp-sr-doppler its frequency is reduced by $e^{-\alpha\tau}$. After a year at $1g$ ($\alpha\tau \approx 1.03$) the signals from home arrive at a third of their frequency, and
they arrive ever more slowly: light emitted later than $t = c/g$ never reaches the rocket (@exr-sr-signal-to-rocket).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A real rocket accelerates by ejecting mass. The third example gives the relativistic rocket equation, which replaces
Tsiolkovsky's [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.42].

::: {#exm-sr-rocket-equation}
#### The relativistic rocket

A rocket that ejects matter with speed $w$ relative to itself reaches the speed $v$ when its rest mass has fallen from $m_0$ to $m = m_0\bigl(\frac{1 - v}{1 + v}\bigr)^{1/(2w)}$, that is
$m = m_0e^{-\eta/w}$ with the rapidity $\eta$ (@exr-sr-rocket-derivation). For a photon rocket, $w = 1$, reaching $v = 0.99$ requires $m/m_0 = 0.071$; Tsiolkovsky's $m_0e^{-v/w}$ is the
limit of small $v$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
A police officer accelerates to catch a speeding ship. The first exercise follows the pursuit in three frames
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.47].

::: {#exr-sr-police}
#### A relativistic pursuit

A ship passes a police officer at constant speed $v$; at that moment the officer starts with constant proper acceleration $a$. How long does the pursuit last
for the ship's crew, and for the officer, and what is their relative speed at the end?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The meeting condition $vt = (\sqrt{1 + a^2t^2} - 1)/a$ gives $t = 2v\gamma^2/a$ in the officer's initial frame. The crew's proper time is $t/\gamma = 2v\gamma/a$; the officer's is $\tau =
\operatorname{arsinh}(at)/a = \operatorname{arsinh}(2v\gamma^2)/a$. At the meeting the officer's speed is $at/\sqrt{1 + a^2t^2} = 2v/(1 + v^2)$, which is $v \oplus v$: the officer overtakes the ship at the relative
speed $v$:

{{< sage exr-sr-police >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A signal sent too late never reaches a uniformly accelerated rocket. The second exercise finds the deadline
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.50].

::: {#exr-sr-signal-to-rocket}
#### A signal to an accelerating rocket

$B$ starts from rest at the origin with proper acceleration $\alpha$; $A$ stays at the origin and sends a light signal at time $t_0$. When does $B$ receive it, in $A$'s time and
in $B$'s proper time? Discuss $\alpha t_0 \to 0$ and $\alpha t_0 \to 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$t - t_0 = (\sqrt{1 + \alpha^2t^2} - 1)/\alpha$ gives $t = \frac{t_0(2 - \alpha t_0)}{2(1 - \alpha t_0)}$ for $\alpha t_0 < 1$, and $B$'s proper time is $\tau = \operatorname{arsinh}(\alpha t)/\alpha$. For $\alpha t_0 \to 0$, $t \approx t_0$;
for $\alpha t_0 \to 1$, $t \to \infty$; for $\alpha t_0 \geq 1$ the signal never arrives: the light ray $x = t - t_0$ with $t_0 \geq 1/\alpha$ stays behind the asymptote $x = t - 1/\alpha$
(@prp-sr-hyperbolic-motion). This is the horizon of the Rindler frame:

{{< sage exr-sr-signal-to-rocket >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The rocket equation of the third example follows from conservation of four-momentum. The third exercise derives it. Only conservation of four-momentum in the rest frame is used.

::: {#exr-sr-rocket-derivation}
#### Deriving the rocket equation

In the instantaneous rest frame the rocket of mass $m$ ejects rest mass $dm_{\mathrm{ej}}$ backwards at speed $w$ and gains the velocity $dv'$. Using conservation of energy and
momentum, show that $m\,dv' = -w\,dm$ (with $dm$ the change of the rocket's rest mass) and conclude that $m = m_0e^{-\eta/w}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Momentum: $m\,dv' = \gamma_wdm_{\mathrm{ej}}w$; energy: $-dm = \gamma_wdm_{\mathrm{ej}}$ (the rest energy lost by the rocket becomes the energy of the exhaust). Eliminating $dm_{\mathrm{ej}}$:
$m\,dv' = -w\,dm$. In the instantaneous rest frame $dv' = d\eta$, an invariant, so $d\eta = -w\,dm/m$ and $m = m_0e^{-\eta/w}$; with $e^{2\eta} = (1 + v)/(1 - v)$ this is the formula of
@exm-sr-rocket-equation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Accelerated observers and the Rindler frame

A single accelerated observer has her own time and her own notion of simultaneity at each instant. A family of observers,
each with constant proper acceleration, chosen so that they stay at fixed distances from one another in their own frames,
carries a coordinate system in which the metric is static but not the Minkowski form; @fig-sr-rindler draws it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-sr-rindler}
#### Rindler coordinates

On the wedge $x > |t|$ of Minkowski spacetime the **Rindler coordinates** $(T, X, Y, Z)$, with $X > 0$ and a constant $a > 0$, are defined by
$$
t = X\sinh(aT), \qquad x = X\cosh(aT), \qquad y = Y, \qquad z = Z .
$$
In them the metric is $ds^2 = a^2X^2dT^2 - dX^2 - dY^2 - dZ^2$. The **Rindler frame** is the family of observers at fixed $(X, Y, Z)$; the boundary $x = |t|$ of the wedge is the **Rindler
horizon**.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
![The Rindler frame. In the wedge $x > |t|$, the worldlines of the Rindler observers (hyperbolae of constant $X$, blue) and the lines of constant $T$
(straight lines through the origin, grey), which are the lines of simultaneity of every observer at once; the light rays $x = \pm t$ (orange) are the
horizon. Generated by `figures/sr-rindler.sage`.](figures/sr-rindler.svg){#fig-sr-rindler width=60%}

The metric in Rindler coordinates follows by differentiation. The first example computes it [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.48 a]. The computation is two lines of differentials.

::: {#exm-sr-rindler-metric}
#### The Rindler metric

$dt = \sinh(aT)dX + aX\cosh(aT)dT$ and $dx = \cosh(aT)dX + aX\sinh(aT)dT$, so $dt^2 - dx^2 = a^2X^2dT^2 - dX^2$: the metric is static, independent of $T$, but $g_{TT} = a^2X^2$ depends
on $X$. It is Minkowski spacetime in other coordinates, flat, as the vanishing of its curvature, computed later in @exr-gr-rindler, confirms.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Rindler observers are uniformly accelerated, each with its own acceleration. The second example identifies them with the
hyperbolic motions of @prp-sr-hyperbolic-motion.

::: {#exm-sr-rindler-observers}
#### Each observer has constant proper acceleration

At fixed $X$, $x^2 - t^2 = X^2$: a hyperbolic worldline with proper acceleration $1/X$ (@exr-sr-hyperbola-invariant) and proper time $\tau = aXT$. The observer at $X = 1/a$ has proper
time $T$; observers closer to the horizon accelerate harder. Their distances $X_2 - X_1$, measured along the lines $T = \text{constant}$, never change: unlike the
spaceships of @exr-sr-bell, the Rindler observers form a rigid frame.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The radar construction of @exm-sr-radar, carried out by a uniformly accelerated observer, gives another set of coordinates. The third
example records them [@boskoff2024journey, Section 9.6].

::: {#exm-sr-radar-rindler}
#### Radar coordinates of an accelerated observer

An observer with proper acceleration $\alpha$ and proper time $\tau$ who assigns radar distances $\bar x$ to events obtains $t = \frac{e^{\alpha\bar x}}{\alpha}\sinh\alpha\tau$, $x = \frac{e^{\alpha\bar x}}{\alpha}\cosh\alpha\tau$
[@boskoff2024journey, Theorem 9.6.3]. This is the Rindler frame with $a = \alpha$, $T = \tau$ and $X = e^{\alpha\bar x}/\alpha$, and the metric becomes $e^{2\alpha\bar x}(d\tau^2 - d\bar x^2)$, conformal to
the Minkowski form.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Light moving in the Rindler frame has a wave vector with Rindler components. The first exercise computes them
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.48 b].

::: {#exr-sr-rindler-photon}
#### A photon in Rindler coordinates

A photon with $k = (\omega, \omega\cos\theta, 0, \omega\sin\theta)$ is emitted at $t = t_0$, $x = x_0$, $y = z = 0$ with $x_0 > |t_0|$. Compute its components $(k^T, k^X, k^Y, k^Z)$ in the Rindler
coordinates and check that they form a null vector of the Rindler metric.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $T = \frac1a\operatorname{artanh}(t/x)$, $X = \sqrt{x^2 - t^2}$: $k^T = \omega\frac{x_0 - t_0\cos\theta}{aX_0^2}$, $k^X = \omega\frac{x_0\cos\theta - t_0}{X_0}$, $k^Y = 0$, $k^Z = \omega\sin\theta$, with $X_0^2 = x_0^2 - t_0^2$;
and $a^2X_0^2(k^T)^2 - (k^X)^2 - (k^Z)^2 = 0$:

{{< sage exr-sr-rindler-photon >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A Rindler observer can move sideways in the frame. The second exercise computes her proper time [@blennow2022relativity,
Problem 1.48 c].

::: {#exr-sr-rindler-sideways}
#### Moving sideways in the Rindler frame

Find the proper time along $X = X_0$, $Y = vT$, $Z = 0$, $0 \leq T \leq T_0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$d\tau^2 = a^2X_0^2dT^2 - v^2dT^2$, so $\tau = T_0\sqrt{a^2X_0^2 - v^2}$, real for $v < aX_0$: the local speed of light at $X_0$ in the coordinates $(T, Y)$ is $aX_0$, smaller near the
horizon.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The radar coordinates of the third example can be inverted explicitly. The third exercise asks for the inverse and the
metric [@boskoff2024journey, Exercise 9.6.5].

::: {#exr-sr-radar-inverse}
#### Inverting the radar coordinates

Show that the inverse of $t = \frac{e^{\alpha\bar x}}{\alpha}\sinh\alpha\tau$, $x = \frac{e^{\alpha\bar x}}{\alpha}\cosh\alpha\tau$ is $\tau = \frac1\alpha\operatorname{artanh}\frac tx$, $\bar x = \frac{1}{2\alpha}\ln(\alpha^2(x^2 - t^2))$, and that $dt^2 - dx^2 =
e^{2\alpha\bar x}(d\tau^2 - d\bar x^2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$t/x = \tanh\alpha\tau$ and $x^2 - t^2 = e^{2\alpha\bar x}/\alpha^2$ give the inverse. The metric follows as in @exm-sr-rindler-metric with $X = e^{\alpha\bar x}/\alpha$, $dX = e^{\alpha\bar x}d\bar x$, $a = \alpha$:

{{< sage exr-sr-radar-inverse >}}
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

The Rindler observers resemble observers at rest in a gravitational field. Clocks at different heights run at different
rates, light climbing up is redshifted, and there is a horizon beyond which nothing can be seen. The proposition below
states these facts, which @boskoff2024journey [Section 9.6.1] uses to introduce gravity.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sr-rindler-redshift}
#### Clocks and light in the Rindler frame

In the Rindler frame:

1. A clock at rest at $X$ runs at the rate $d\tau/dT = aX$.
2. Light sent from the observer at $X_1$ to the observer at $X_2$ is received with the frequency $\omega_2 = \omega_1X_1/X_2$, both measured with proper clocks; in the radar
   coordinates of @exm-sr-radar-rindler, $\omega_2 = \omega_1e^{-\alpha(\bar x_2 - \bar x_1)}$.
3. No event with $t \geq x$ can send a signal to any Rindler observer.

*Proof.* (1) For $dX = dY = dZ = 0$, $d\tau = aX\,dT$. (2) The metric does not depend on $T$, so a light signal emitted at $T$ arrives after a coordinate time that does not
depend on $T$; two successive crests, emitted $\Delta T$ apart, arrive $\Delta T$ apart. Their proper periods are $aX_1\Delta T$ and $aX_2\Delta T$, so $\omega_2/\omega_1 = X_1/X_2$; with
$X = e^{\alpha\bar x}/\alpha$, $X_1/X_2 = e^{-\alpha(\bar x_2 - \bar x_1)}$. (3) Every event $q$ in the causal future of an event $p$ satisfies $t_q - t_p \geq |\vec x_q - \vec x_p| \geq x_q - x_p$, so $t_q - x_q \geq t_p - x_p$. If
$t_p \geq x_p$, every such $q$ has $t_q \geq x_q$, while every point of a Rindler worldline has $t < x$. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Near a Rindler observer the frame looks like a laboratory in a uniform gravitational field. The first example evaluates
the redshift for a tower on the Earth.

::: {#exm-sr-rindler-pound-rebka}
#### A tower in an accelerating rocket

Inside a rocket accelerating at $g$, light sent up a height $h$ is redshifted by $1 - gh/c^2$ to first order (part 2 with $X_2 = X_1 + h$, $X_1 = c^2/g$): for $h = 22.5\,$m, $gh/c^2 =
2.5 \times 10^{-15}$, the shift that Pound and Rebka measured in the gravitational field of the Earth (@exm-grb-pound-rebka, in the next chapter). The
equivalence principle, which @def-equivalence-principle states, asserts that a uniformly accelerated frame and a uniform gravitational
field are locally indistinguishable, so the two shifts must agree.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The horizon is at a definite distance behind each observer. The second example evaluates it for an acceleration of one $g$.

::: {#exm-sr-rindler-horizon}
#### The horizon behind a rocket

An observer with proper acceleration $\alpha$ is at $X = c^2/\alpha$ from the horizon. For $\alpha = g$ this is $c^2/g \approx 0.97\,$ly: events behind the rocket further than a light-year in its
frame are hidden from it as long as it accelerates, which is the horizon met in @exr-sr-signal-to-rocket.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The redshift in radar coordinates is exactly exponential. The third example states Boskoff and Capozziello's result and its
interpretation. It agrees with part 2 for small heights.

::: {#exm-sr-boskoff-redshift}
#### An exponential redshift

In the radar coordinates of an observer with acceleration $\alpha$, light emitted at the observer with frequency $\nu$ is received at the radar height $h$ with frequency
$\nu e^{-\alpha h}$ [@boskoff2024journey, Theorem 9.6.6]. For $\alpha h \ll 1$ this is $\nu(1 - \alpha h)$, the same as in the first example; the exponential holds for all $h$ because radar
heights add along the frame, as rapidities do along a line.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Two spaceships that accelerate identically in the launch frame do not form a rigid frame. The first exercise shows that a
string between them breaks [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.18].

::: {#exr-sr-bell}
#### Bell's spaceships

Two ships $40\,$km apart, at rest, start simultaneously in their launch frame with the same acceleration of $c/50$ per second in that frame and stop after
$30\,$s. Does a string tied between them break? What is their separation in their new rest frame?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In the launch frame their separation stays $40\,$km. After the stop they move at $v = 0.6c$, and their separation, contracted in the launch frame, is $\gamma \cdot 40\,$km $= 50\,$km in
their own frame: the string, whose rest length would have to grow, breaks. To stay rigid the rear ship must accelerate harder, as the Rindler observers
do:

{{< sage exr-sr-bell >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The accelerated observer receives signals redshifted by her own motion. The second exercise follows a signal and its
reflection [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.71].

::: {#exr-sr-reflected-signal}
#### A reflected signal

In @exr-sr-signal-to-rocket, $A$ sends the signal with frequency $\omega$. Show that $B$ receives the frequency $\omega e^{-\alpha\tau}$, with $\tau$ her proper time at reception, and that the signal
reflected by $B$ back to $A$ arrives with $\omega e^{-2\alpha\tau}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
At reception $B$ has rapidity $\alpha\tau$ and recedes along the light, so the Doppler factor is $e^{-\alpha\tau}$ (@exm-sr-rocket-redshift). The mirror re-emits this frequency in its own frame, and $A$
sees a receding source with the same rapidity: another factor $e^{-\alpha\tau}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Parts 1 and 2 of the proposition are two descriptions of one redshift. The third exercise checks their agreement on a
light ray followed explicitly.

::: {#exr-sr-rindler-ray}
#### Following a light ray

With $a = 1$, a light ray leaves the Rindler observer at $X_1 = 1$ at $T = 0$ towards larger $X$ and reaches $X_2 = 2$. Find its coordinate travel time $\Delta T$, show that it does not
depend on the emission time, and compute the received frequency ratio directly from the wave vectors.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Along the ray $dX = aX\,dT$ (null and outgoing in the Rindler metric), so $\Delta T = \frac1a\ln(X_2/X_1) = \ln2$, whatever the emission time. In inertial coordinates the ray
emitted at $T = 0$ is $x - t = 1$ with $k = \omega_1(1, 1)$; it meets $x^2 - t^2 = 4$ at $(t, x) = (1.5, 2.5)$, where the observer has the four-velocity $u_2 = (\cosh\ln2, \sinh\ln2) =
(1.25, 0.75)$. So $\omega_2/\omega_1 = k\cdot u_2/k\cdot u_1 = 1.25 - 0.75 = \tfrac12 = X_1/X_2$:

{{< sage exr-sr-rindler-ray >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

### Exercises

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises below combine forces, hyperbolic motion and the Rindler frame. The first is the linear accelerator at
Stanford [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.131].

::: {#exr-sr-slac}
#### An electron at SLAC

An electron is accelerated from rest through $U = 50\,$GV over $L = 3\,$km in a uniform field. Find $x(t)$, the time to traverse the accelerator, and $E(t)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The proper acceleration is $\alpha = eU/(mL)$, in units $c = 1$ equal to $97847/(3000\,\mathrm{m}) = 32.6\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}$, and @prp-sr-hyperbolic-motion gives $x = (\sqrt{1 + \alpha^2t^2} -
1)/\alpha$ and $E = m\sqrt{1 + \alpha^2t^2}$. The traversal time is $\sqrt{(1 + \alpha L)^2 - 1}/\alpha \approx L + 1/\alpha$, that is $L/c = 10.0069\,\mu$s plus $0.1\,$ns: after the first few
centimetres the electron moves essentially at the speed of light:

{{< sage exr-sr-slac >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The second exercise computes the four-force of a dust cloud on a ship and classifies it [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.145]. The classification uses the definitions of @def-sr-four-force.

::: {#exr-sr-dust}
#### A ship enters a dust cloud

A ship of cross section $A$ moves with velocity $v$ into dust of rest density $\rho_0$ at rest in the galaxy, absorbing all the dust it meets. Find the four-force on the
ship in the galaxy frame and in the ship's frame, and decide whether it is pure, heat-like or neither.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Per unit galactic time the ship absorbs dust of rest mass $\rho_0Av$ with zero momentum, so $dp/dt = \rho_0Av(1, \vec 0)$ and $F = dp/d\tau = \gamma\rho_0Av(1, \vec 0)$. Then $F\cdot u = \gamma^2\rho_0Av \neq 0$, so it is not
pure; in the ship's frame $F' = \gamma^2\rho_0Av(1, -v, 0, 0)$, which has a spatial part, so it is not heat-like either: the ship is both heated and slowed.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The third exercise is the twin paradox with realistic accelerations, which combines hyperbolic motion with the proper
time of @def-sr-proper-time. The numbers are those of a journey within a human lifetime.

::: {#exr-sr-twin-accelerated}
#### The twin paradox at one $g$

A traveller accelerates at $g$ for $\tau_1$ of proper time, decelerates for $\tau_1$, accelerates back for $\tau_1$ and decelerates for $\tau_1$, returning home. With $\tau_1 = 5\,$yr,
find the total proper time, the time elapsed on the Earth and the largest distance reached.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each phase covers the coordinate time $(c/g)\sinh(g\tau_1/c)$ and the distance $(c^2/g)(\cosh(g\tau_1/c) - 1)$. With $c/g = 0.969\,$yr and $g\tau_1/c = 5.16$: the traveller ages $20\,$yr, the Earth
about $338\,$yr, and the furthest point is about $167\,$ly from home:

{{< sage exr-sr-twin-accelerated >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

## Electrodynamics in covariant form {#sec-sr-electrodynamics}

Maxwell's equations were the origin of special relativity: they are invariant under Lorentz transformations, not under
Galilean ones. Their covariant form, with the potential $A^\mu$ and the field tensor $F_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu$, is developed in
@sec-complex-vector-fields (@def-field-strength-abelian, @exm-vector-field-strength, @exm-cfb-field-boost) and derived from an action in
@sec-actions (@exm-el-maxwell, @exr-cfb-lorentz-force); this part does not repeat that material. It adds what the group theory of this
chapter gives: the transformation of the fields under an arbitrary boost, the two invariants and the classification of fields
they imply, and the covariant equation of motion of a charge. The conventions are those of @sec-complex-vector-fields: Heaviside-Lorentz
units with $c = 1$, $F_{0i} = E^i$, $F_{ij} = -\epsilon_{ijk}B^k$, so that $F^{i0} = E^i$ and $F^{ij} = -\epsilon_{ijk}B^k$. The sources are
@maggiore2023electrodynamics [Secs. 8.5-8.6] and @blennow2022relativity [Sec. 1.7]. The same physics in vector form, with Maxwell's equations, the potentials, the fields of moving charges and
radiation, is in @sec-electromagnetism (@sec-em-maxwell, @sec-em-radiation); the covariant form adds the manifest invariance
under boosts.

For more on this topic, see @emam2021covariant [Ch. 4].

### The field tensor under Lorentz transformations

The electric and magnetic fields are the six components of one antisymmetric tensor, so they mix under boosts. For a boost
along a coordinate axis the mixing was written in @exm-cfb-field-boost; the proposition below gives it for any direction,
and @fig-sr-moving-charge shows its most famous consequence, the field of a moving charge.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sr-field-transformation}
#### Transformation of the electric and magnetic fields

In a frame moving with velocity $\vec v$ relative to the original one, with $\gamma = (1 - v^2)^{-1/2}$ and $\parallel$, $\perp$ denoting the components along and across
$\vec v$,
$$
\vec E'_\parallel = \vec E_\parallel, \qquad \vec B'_\parallel = \vec B_\parallel, \qquad \vec E'_\perp = \gamma(\vec E + \vec v\times\vec B)_\perp, \qquad \vec B'_\perp = \gamma(\vec B - \vec v\times\vec E)_\perp .
$$ {#eq-sr-field-transformation}

*Proof.* The fields transform as $F'^{\mu\nu} = \Lambda^\mu{}_\alpha\Lambda^\nu{}_\beta F^{\alpha\beta}$ (@eq-sr-tensor-law) with the passive boost $\Lambda = B(-\vec v)$. Both sides of @eq-sr-field-transformation are
built from vectors and are covariant under rotations (a rotation commutes with the boost up to rotating $\vec v$, @exr-sr-boost-conjugate), so it
suffices to take $\vec v = v\hat x$. Then $\Lambda^0{}_0 = \Lambda^1{}_1 = \gamma$, $\Lambda^0{}_1 = \Lambda^1{}_0 = -\gamma v$, and $\Lambda$ leaves $y$, $z$ alone. With $F^{i0} = E^i$ and $F^{ij} =
-\epsilon_{ijk}B^k$: $E'_x = F'^{10} = (\Lambda^1{}_1\Lambda^0{}_0 - \Lambda^1{}_0\Lambda^0{}_1)F^{10} = \gamma^2(1 - v^2)E_x = E_x$; $E'_y = F'^{20} = \Lambda^0{}_0F^{20} + \Lambda^0{}_1F^{21} = \gamma E_y - \gamma vB_z$, since
$F^{21} = -\epsilon_{213}B_z = B_z$; likewise $E'_z = \gamma(E_z + vB_y)$, $B'_x = B_x$, $B'_y = \gamma(B_y + vE_z)$ and $B'_z = \gamma(B_z - vE_y)$ (@exr-sr-field-general). These are
@eq-sr-field-transformation for $\vec v = v\hat x$, since $(\vec v\times\vec B)_y = -vB_z$, $(\vec v\times\vec B)_z = vB_y$, $(\vec v\times\vec E)_y = -vE_z$ and $(\vec v\times\vec E)_z = vE_y$. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

![The field of a moving charge. The magnitude of the electric field of a point charge in uniform motion along $x$, in the plane $z = 0$ at one instant,
for $v = 0$, $0.6$ and $0.9$ (logarithmic colour scale): the field lines stay radial, but the field is compressed into the plane perpendicular to the motion,
where it is stronger by $\gamma$, and weakened by $1/\gamma^2$ along the motion. Generated by `figures/sr-moving-charge.sage`.](figures/sr-moving-charge.png){#fig-sr-moving-charge width=95%}

A pure electric field acquires a magnetic part in a moving frame. The first example computes it for a field across the
motion [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.114].

::: {#exm-sr-field-electric-boost}
#### A boosted electric field

For $\vec E = (0, 0, E)$, $\vec B = 0$ and $\vec v = v\hat x$: $\vec E' = (0, 0, \gamma E)$ and $\vec B' = -\gamma\vec v\times\vec E = \gamma vE\hat y$. The moving observer sees the electric field
enhanced and a magnetic field perpendicular to both $\vec v$ and $\vec E$; to first order in $v$, $\vec B' = -\vec v\times\vec E$ [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.115].
:::

The field of a uniformly moving charge follows from the Coulomb field by a boost. The second example derives it, and
@fig-sr-moving-charge draws it [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.117; @maggiore2023electrodynamics, Sec. 10.3].
In vector form the field was obtained from the retarded potentials in @exm-emw-lw-uniform; the boost adds that the result is exact for any constant velocity without solving a wave equation.

::: {#exm-sr-moving-charge}
#### The field of a moving charge

A charge $q$ at rest at the origin of $S'$, which moves with $v$ along $x$, has $\vec E' = q\vec r'/(4\pi r'^3)$, $\vec B' = 0$. In $S$, at the instant $t = 0$ when the charge is at the
origin, $x' = \gamma x$, and the inverse of @eq-sr-field-transformation gives $\vec E = \frac{q\gamma\vec r}{4\pi(\gamma^2x^2 + y^2 + z^2)^{3/2}}$, still radial, and $\vec B = \vec v\times\vec E$. Across the motion
($x = 0$) the field is $\gamma$ times the Coulomb value, along it $1/\gamma^2$ times.
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

A current in a neutral wire produces only a magnetic field. The third example shows that a moving observer sees an
electric field as well, because the wire is charged in her frame [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.119].

::: {#exm-sr-wire}
#### A current-carrying wire

A neutral wire along $x$ with current $I$ has, at distance $r$, $\vec B = \frac{I}{2\pi r}\hat\phi$ and $\vec E = 0$. For an observer moving with $v$ along the wire,
@eq-sr-field-transformation gives $\vec E' = \gamma\vec v\times\vec B$, radial of size $\gamma vI/(2\pi r)$, and $\vec B' = \gamma\vec B$. The same follows by transforming the current
four-vector $j = (0, I, 0, 0)$ (per unit cross section): in the moving frame the charge density is $-\gamma vI$, and its Coulomb field is $\vec E'$.
:::

A field that is purely magnetic in one frame may become purely electric only if the invariants allow it. The second
exercise finds the electric field in a frame where the magnetic field vanishes [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.129].

::: {#exr-sr-b-vanishes}
#### A frame without magnetic field

In $S$ the fields are $\vec E$ and $\vec B$, and in $S'$, moving with $u$ along $x$, the magnetic field vanishes. Express $\vec E'$ in terms of $u$ and $\vec E$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\vec B' = 0$ requires $B_x = 0$, $B_y = -uE_z$ and $B_z = uE_y$, that is $\vec B = \vec u\times\vec E$. Then $\vec E'_\perp = \gamma(\vec E + \vec u\times(\vec u\times\vec E))_\perp = \gamma(1 - u^2)\vec E_\perp = \vec E_\perp/\gamma$ and
$E'_x = E_x$: $\vec E' = (E_x, E_y/\gamma, E_z/\gamma)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A magnetic field seen from a moving frame has an electric part. The third exercise computes it and checks the invariants
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.130].

::: {#exr-sr-b-boost}
#### A boosted magnetic field

In $S$ there is a uniform magnetic field $\vec B$ and no electric field. Find $\vec E'$ and $\vec B'$ in a frame moving with $v$ along $x$, and verify that $E'^2 - B'^2$ and $\vec E'\cdot\vec B'$ equal
their values in $S$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\vec E' = \gamma(\vec v\times\vec B)_\perp = \gamma v(0, -B_z, B_y)$, $\vec B' = (B_x, \gamma B_y, \gamma B_z)$. Then $\vec E'\cdot\vec B' = \gamma^2v(-B_zB_y + B_yB_z) = 0$ and $E'^2 - B'^2 = \gamma^2v^2(B_y^2 + B_z^2) - B_x^2 -
\gamma^2(B_y^2 + B_z^2) = -B^2$:

{{< sage exr-sr-b-boost >}}
:::

The six field components have two invariant combinations. They are the real and imaginary parts of the square of the
complex vector $\vec E + i\vec B$, which transforms by complex rotations (@exm-sr-field-pair), and they decide whether a field can be made
purely electric or purely magnetic by a choice of frame.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sr-field-invariants}
#### The invariants of the electromagnetic field

$E^2 - B^2 = -\tfrac12F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$ and $\vec E\cdot\vec B = \tfrac18\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}F_{\mu\nu}F_{\rho\sigma}$ are Lorentz invariants. Moreover:

1. If $\vec E\cdot\vec B \neq 0$, or if $\vec E\cdot\vec B = 0$ and $E^2 \neq B^2$, there is a frame in which $\vec E$ and $\vec B$ are parallel (or one of them vanishes), reached by a boost along
   $\vec E\times\vec B$ with the velocity $\vec v$ such that $\frac{\vec v}{1 + v^2} = \frac{\vec E\times\vec B}{E^2 + B^2}$.
2. If $\vec E\cdot\vec B = 0$ and $B^2 > E^2$, the field is purely magnetic in that frame; if $E^2 > B^2$, purely electric.
3. If both invariants vanish (a **null field**, such as a plane wave), no frame makes $\vec E$ and $\vec B$ parallel or removes either.

*Proof.* The contractions are scalars by @exr-sr-contraction-invariant, and $\epsilon$ is invariant under $SO^+(1, 3)$ (@exm-sr-invariant-tensors); their values in terms of $\vec E$,
$\vec B$ are computed in @exr-sr-invariants-components. (1) Choose axes with $\vec E\times\vec B = S\hat x$, so $\vec E$, $\vec B$ lie in the $yz$-plane, and boost with $\vec v = v\hat x$. By
@eq-sr-field-transformation, $\vec E' = \gamma(\vec E + \vec v\times\vec B)$, $\vec B' = \gamma(\vec B - \vec v\times\vec E)$, and with the identities $\vec E\times(\vec v\times\vec E) = \vec vE^2$, $(\vec v\times\vec B)\times\vec B =
-\vec vB^2$ and $(\vec v\times\vec B)\times(\vec v\times\vec E) = -\vec v(\vec v\cdot(\vec E\times\vec B))$, valid for $\vec v \perp \vec E, \vec B$:
$$
\vec E'\times\vec B' = \gamma^2\bigl(\vec E\times\vec B - \vec v(E^2 + B^2) + \vec v(\vec v\cdot\vec E\times\vec B)\bigr) = \gamma^2\hat x\bigl(S(1 + v^2) - v(E^2 + B^2)\bigr) .
$$
It vanishes for $v/(1 + v^2) = S/(E^2 + B^2)$, which has a solution $|v| < 1$ because $2S \leq 2|\vec E||\vec B| \leq E^2 + B^2$, with equality in both only if $\vec E \perp \vec B$ and $E =
B$. (2) In the new frame $\vec E' \parallel \vec B'$ and $\vec E'\cdot\vec B' = 0$, so one vanishes, and $E'^2 - B'^2$ has the sign of $E^2 - B^2$. (3) If both invariants vanish, a
frame with $\vec E' \parallel \vec B'$ would have $E'B' = 0$ and $E'^2 = B'^2$, so $\vec E' = \vec B' = 0$, and then $F = 0$ in every frame. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The Coulomb field is the simplest field with $E^2 > B^2$, and every moving charge carries one. The first example checks
the invariants for the field of @exm-sr-moving-charge [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.132 b].

::: {#exm-sr-invariants-moving-charge}
#### The invariants of a moving charge

For the moving charge, $\vec B = \vec v\times\vec E$, so $\vec E\cdot\vec B = 0$ and $E^2 - B^2 = E^2 - |\vec v\times\vec E|^2 > 0$: at every point the field is electric in some frame, the rest frame of
the charge. At the point $(0, y, 0)$, $E = \gamma q/(4\pi y^2)$ and $B = vE$, so $E^2 - B^2 = q^2/(16\pi^2y^4)$, the Coulomb value: the invariant knows the rest-frame field.
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A plane wave is a null field in every frame. The second example computes its invariants from the potential
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.121].
@exm-emw-pw-null noted that both invariants vanish for a plane wave; the covariant form explains why this holds in every frame.

::: {#exm-sr-plane-wave-null}
#### A plane wave is null

For $A_\mu = \epsilon_\mu e^{-ik\cdot x}$ with $k\cdot k = 0$ and $k\cdot\epsilon = 0$, $F_{\mu\nu} = -i(k_\mu\epsilon_\nu - k_\nu\epsilon_\mu)e^{-ik\cdot x}$, and $F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} \propto 2(k^2\epsilon^2 - (k\cdot\epsilon)^2) = 0$,
$\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}F_{\mu\nu}F_{\rho\sigma} \propto \epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}k_\mu\epsilon_\nu k_\rho\epsilon_\sigma = 0$. In every frame $|\vec E| = |\vec B|$ and $\vec E \perp \vec B$: light cannot be transformed away, nor into a static field.
:::

Crossed fields with $E < B$ become purely magnetic in the frame of the drift velocity. The third example applies part 1, recovering
@exm-cfb-crossed-fields.
The drift was found in vector form in @exm-ems-crossed-drift; the boost to the drift frame removes the electric field exactly.

::: {#exm-sr-crossed-drift}
#### The drift frame of crossed fields

For $\vec E = E\hat y$, $\vec B = B\hat z$, $0 < E < B$: $\vec E\times\vec B = EB\hat x$, and $v/(1 + v^2) = EB/(E^2 + B^2)$ has the root $v = E/B$ (the other root is $B/E > 1$). In the frame
moving with $\vec v = (E/B)\hat x$, $\vec E' = 0$ and $B' = \sqrt{B^2 - E^2}$: charges circle in the pure magnetic field and drift with $\vec E\times\vec B/B^2$ in the original frame.
:::

indices $\{0, 1\}$ and $\{2, 3\}$ each give $\epsilon^{0123}F_{01}F_{23} = (-1)(E^1)(-B^1)$. Sources with $\epsilon_{0123} = -1$, or with upper-index $F$, find $-8\vec E\cdot\vec B$:

The invariants determine unknown field components measured by another observer. The second exercise uses them as in
@blennow2022relativity [Problems 1.124 and 1.125].

::: {#exr-sr-unknown-components}
#### Unknown components from the invariants

Observer $A$ measures $\vec E = (\alpha, -\alpha, 0)$, $\vec B = (0, 0, 2\alpha)$. Observer $B$ measures $\vec E' = (0, 0, 2\alpha)$ and $\vec B' = (B_x, \alpha, B_z)$. Find $B_x$ and $B_z$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\vec E\cdot\vec B = 0$ gives $2\alpha B_z = 0$, so $B_z = 0$; $E^2 - B^2 = 2\alpha^2 - 4\alpha^2 = -2\alpha^2 = 4\alpha^2 - B_x^2 - \alpha^2$ gives $B_x^2 = 5\alpha^2$, $B_x = \pm\sqrt5\alpha$:

{{< sage exr-sr-unknown-components >}}
:::

The angle between $\vec E$ and $\vec B$ changes from frame to frame, but in a constrained way. The third exercise finds the constraint for fields
of equal magnitude [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.135].

::: {#exr-sr-angle-invariant}
#### The angle between $\vec E$ and $\vec B$

If $|\vec E| = |\vec B|$ in one frame and the angle between them is $\alpha$, show that in any other frame $|\vec E'| = |\vec B'|$ and $\cos\alpha' = (E^2/E'^2)\cos\alpha$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$E^2 - B^2 = 0$ is invariant, so $E' = B'$. $\vec E\cdot\vec B = E^2\cos\alpha$ is invariant, so $E'^2\cos\alpha' = E^2\cos\alpha$.
:::

### The covariant Lorentz force

The force on a charge in an electromagnetic field is the Lorentz force. In covariant form it is a single equation,
linear in the four-velocity and in the field tensor, whose antisymmetry guarantees that the rest mass is conserved
(@maggiore2023electrodynamics [Sec. 8.6.1]); @fig-sr-cyclotron shows a solution.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sr-lorentz-force}
#### The covariant Lorentz force

The equation $m\,du^\mu/d\tau = qF^\mu{}_\nu u^\nu$ is Lorentz covariant, defines a pure four-force, and is equivalent to
$$
\frac{d}{dt}(\gamma m\vec v) = q(\vec E + \vec v\times\vec B), \qquad \frac{d}{dt}(\gamma m) = q\vec E\cdot\vec v .
$$

*Proof.* Both sides are four-vectors, so the equation holds in every frame if it holds in one. $u_\mu F^\mu{}_\nu u^\nu = F_{\mu\nu}u^\mu u^\nu = 0$ by antisymmetry, so the force is pure
(@def-sr-four-force). With $F^{i0} = E^i$, $F^i{}_0 = F^{i0} = E^i$ and $F^i{}_j = F^{ik}\eta_{kj} = -F^{ij} = \epsilon_{ijk}B^k$, $F^i{}_\nu u^\nu = \gamma(E^i + \epsilon_{ijk}v^jB^k) = \gamma(\vec E + \vec v\times\vec B)^i$;
and $F^0{}_j u^j = -F^{0j}\gamma v^j = \gamma\vec E\cdot\vec v$. Dividing $m\,du^\mu/d\tau = \gamma m\,du^\mu/dt$ by $\gamma$ gives the two equations. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

the motion with @prp-sr-hyperbolic-motion [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.118].

#### A constant electric field

For $\vec E = E\hat x$ and a charge starting from rest, $d(\gamma mv)/dt = qE$ gives $\gamma v = qEt/m$, the hyperbolic motion with $\alpha = qE/m$. As a function of the displacement,
$\gamma = 1 + qEx/m$ (from $d(\gamma m)/dt = qEv$), so $v(x) = \sqrt{1 - (1 + qEx/m)^{-2}}$ (@exr-cfb-constant-electric).

A uniform magnetic field bends a charge into a circle at constant speed. The second example finds the frequency and the
radius [@blennow2022relativity, Problems 1.123 and 1.133 a].
@exm-ems-cyclotron solved the non-relativistic case; the covariant equation replaces $m$ by $\gamma m$ in the frequency.

::: {#exm-sr-constant-b}
#### A constant magnetic field

For $\vec E = 0$ the energy is constant, so $\gamma$ is, and $\gamma m\,d\vec v/dt = q\vec v\times\vec B$: circular motion with angular frequency $\omega = qB/(\gamma m)$ and radius $R = v/\omega = p/(qB)$.
Measuring $R$ in a bubble chamber of known field gives the momentum $p = qBR$; in practical units $p\,[\mathrm{GeV}] = 0.3\,B\,[\mathrm{T}]\,R\,[\mathrm{m}]$ for a unit charge.
:::

The force between moving charges includes a magnetic part that the boost of the Coulomb force reproduces. The third example
computes it for two charges moving side by side [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.143].

::: {#exm-sr-parallel-charges}
#### Two charges moving side by side

Two electrons a distance $d$ apart move in parallel with velocity $v$ perpendicular to the line joining them. In their rest frame the four-force is $(0, 0, f_0, 0)$ with
$f_0 = e^2/(4\pi d^2)$. A boost along $x$ leaves it unchanged, so in the laboratory the four-force is the same and the three-force is $f = F^y/\gamma = f_0/\gamma$: the
repulsion is weaker. In laboratory terms, the field of one electron at the other is $\gamma E_0$ (@exm-sr-moving-charge) with $B = v\gamma E_0$, and the force $e\gamma E_0(1 - v^2) =
f_0/\gamma$ is the electric repulsion reduced by the magnetic attraction of two parallel currents.
:::

Cosmic-ray muons are deflected by the magnetic field of the Earth. The first exercise estimates the deflection
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.128].

::: {#exr-sr-muon-deflection}
#### A muon in the field of the Earth

A muon of energy $2\,$GeV descends vertically from $10\,$km through a horizontal magnetic field of $50\,\mu$T. Find the radius of its orbit and its horizontal
deflection at the ground.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$p = \sqrt{E^2 - m^2} = 1.997\,$GeV and $R = p/(qB) = 1.997/(0.3 \cdot 5 \times 10^{-5})\,$m $= 133\,$km. After a vertical drop $h = 10\,$km the deflection is $R - \sqrt{R^2 - h^2} \approx h^2/(2R)
\approx 376\,$m, eastward or westward according to the charge:

{{< sage exr-sr-muon-deflection >}}
:::

A charge in a uniform magnetic field moves on a circle with constant speed. The second exercise integrates the covariant
equation numerically and checks the frequency.

::: {#exr-sr-cyclotron-numeric}
#### The cyclotron frequency by computer

Integrate $m\,du^\mu/d\tau = qF^\mu{}_\nu u^\nu$ for $\vec B = B\hat z$, $\vec E = 0$ and initial $\gamma = 3$ with Sage, and compare the period in coordinate time with $2\pi\gamma m/(qB)$ and in proper time
with $2\pi m/(qB)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In proper time the four-velocity rotates at the rate $qB/m$, so the proper period is $2\pi m/(qB)$, and $dt/d\tau = \gamma$ makes the coordinate period $\gamma$ times longer:

{{< sage exr-sr-cyclotron-numeric >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The covariant equation conserves $u\cdot u$, as it must. The third exercise proves this and finds the other conserved quantity in a
static field.

::: {#exr-sr-lorentz-conserved}
#### What the Lorentz force conserves

Show that $m\,du^\mu/d\tau = qF^\mu{}_\nu u^\nu$ preserves $u\cdot u$, and that in a static electric field $\vec E = -\nabla\phi$ the quantity $\gamma m + q\phi$ is constant along the motion.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\frac{d}{d\tau}(u\cdot u) = 2u_\mu\frac{du^\mu}{d\tau} = \frac{2q}{m}F_{\mu\nu}u^\mu u^\nu = 0$. From the proposition, $\frac{d}{dt}(\gamma m) = q\vec E\cdot\vec v = -q\nabla\phi\cdot\vec v = -q\frac{d\phi}{dt}$ for a static $\phi$, so $\gamma m + q\phi$ is
constant: the relativistic energy conservation that @exm-sr-constant-e used.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Exercises

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises below use the transformation of fields and the Lorentz force together. The first derives the field of a
moving charge from its potentials and checks the result with the invariants [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.132].
The vector-form computation of the same potentials is @exm-emw-lw-uniform-potential.

::: {#exr-sr-moving-charge-potential}
#### The field of a moving charge from its potential

The charge of @exm-sr-moving-charge has, in its rest frame, $A'^\mu = (q/(4\pi r'), \vec 0)$. Transform $A^\mu$ as a four-vector field to $S$, compute $\vec E = -\nabla A^0 - \partial_t\vec A$ and
$\vec B = \nabla\times\vec A$ with Sage, and check $\vec E\cdot\vec B = 0$ and $E^2 - B^2 = q^2/(16\pi^2r'^4)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$A^\mu(x) = \Lambda A'(\Lambda^{-1}x) = \gamma\frac{q}{4\pi r'}(1, \vec v)$ with $r'^2 = \gamma^2(x - vt)^2 + y^2 + z^2$, the Liénard-Wiechert potential of uniform motion. The fields agree with
@exm-sr-moving-charge, and the invariants with their rest-frame values:

{{< sage exr-sr-moving-charge-potential >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The second exercise finds where a moving observer could see a vanishing electric field around a particle with charge and
magnetic moment [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.141]. The answer is a disk.

::: {#exr-sr-dipole-region}
#### Where the electric field can vanish

A particle at rest has charge $q$ and magnetic moment $\vec m$: $\vec E = q\hat r/(4\pi r^2)$, $\vec B = (3(\vec m\cdot\hat r)\hat r - \vec m)/(4\pi r^3)$. At which points does some inertial frame see $\vec E = 0$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By @prp-sr-field-invariants this requires $\vec E\cdot\vec B = 0$ and $E^2 < B^2$. $\vec E\cdot\vec B = \frac{q\,2(\vec m\cdot\hat r)}{16\pi^2r^5} = 0$ means $\vec m \perp \hat r$, the equatorial plane, where $B =
m/(4\pi r^3)$; then $E < B$ means $r < m/q$. The region is the disk of radius $m/q$ in the equatorial plane.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The third exercise derives the Lorentz force from a Lagrangian in which the electromagnetic coupling enters through the
momentum, and checks the result to first order in the charge [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 1.150 b]. No expansion in the charge is needed.

::: {#exr-sr-minimal-coupling-force}
#### The Lorentz force from minimal coupling

Starting from the free Lagrangian of @exr-sr-quadratic-lagrangian, replace the momentum $m\dot x_\mu$ by $m\dot x_\mu + qA_\mu$ in the Hamiltonian $H = p^2/(2m)$, so that $H = (p - qA)^2/(2m)$, and
derive Hamilton's equations. Show that they give $m\ddot x_\mu = qF_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\nu$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\dot x^\mu = \partial H/\partial p_\mu = (p^\mu - qA^\mu)/m$ and $\dot p_\mu = -\partial H/\partial x^\mu = q\dot x^\nu\partial_\mu A_\nu$. With $m\dot x_\mu = p_\mu - qA_\mu$, $m\ddot x_\mu = \dot p_\mu - q\dot x^\nu\partial_\nu A_\mu =
q\dot x^\nu(\partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu) = qF_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\nu$, exactly: minimal coupling in the Hamiltonian reproduces the Lorentz force, and the corresponding Lagrangian is
$\tfrac12m\dot x\cdot\dot x + q\dot x\cdot A$ of @exr-sr-quadratic-lagrangian.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Sage.** Pending.

## Exercises {#sec-special-relativity-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises below use several parts of the chapter together. The first follows a rocket on its way out with the signals
it receives from home, combining hyperbolic motion, the Doppler effect and proper time.

::: {#exr-sr-final-rocket-signals}
#### Watching home from an accelerating rocket

A rocket leaves the Earth with constant proper acceleration $g$. The Earth broadcasts at frequency $\nu_0$. Show that the received frequency at the rocket's proper
time $\tau$ is $\nu_0e^{-g\tau/c}$ for the signals that reach it, and find how many cycles of the broadcast the rocket ever receives if the Earth broadcasts forever.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Doppler factor of a receding observer with rapidity $g\tau/c$ is $e^{-g\tau/c}$ (@exm-sr-rocket-redshift). Only signals emitted before $t = c/g$ arrive (@exr-sr-signal-to-rocket), so
the rocket receives $\nu_0c/g$ cycles in all, the number emitted before the horizon closes; it receives them over its whole infinite proper time,
since $\int_0^\infty\nu_0e^{-g\tau/c}d\tau = \nu_0c/g$. For $g = 9.81\,$m/s$^2$ this is $\nu_0 \cdot 0.97\,$yr.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

The second exercise is a threshold that the cosmic microwave background imposes on gamma rays, combining invariant masses
with the relativistic energies of photons. It explains a cutoff seen by gamma-ray telescopes.

::: {#exr-sr-final-breit-wheeler}
#### Gamma rays and the microwave background

A gamma ray of energy $E$ collides head on with a photon of the microwave background of energy $\epsilon = 6.3 \times 10^{-4}\,$eV. Find the threshold for $\gamma\gamma \to e^+e^-$ and explain why
the universe is opaque to photons above it.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$s = 2E\epsilon(1 - \cos\pi) = 4E\epsilon \geq (2m_e)^2$ gives $E \geq m_e^2/\epsilon = (0.511 \times 10^6)^2/(6.3 \times 10^{-4})\,$eV $\approx 4 \times 10^{14}\,$eV. Above this energy every gamma ray finds background
photons to annihilate with over intergalactic distances, so the extragalactic gamma-ray sky is cut off near $10^{14}$-$10^{15}\,$eV:

{{< sage exr-sr-final-breit-wheeler >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The third exercise combines the classification of particles with kinematics: a massive particle of spin one decays into two
massless ones, and the helicities of the products are constrained by angular momentum. It explains why the boson discovered in the two-photon channel cannot have spin one.

::: {#exr-sr-final-landau-yang}
#### A spin-one particle cannot decay into two photons

A massive particle of spin $1$ decays at rest into two photons with momenta $\pm k\hat z$. The final state has $J_z = \lambda_1 - \lambda_2$ with helicities $\lambda_{1,2} = \pm1$. Show that $J_z = \pm1$ is
impossible, and (assuming Bose symmetry forbids $J_z = 0$ for spin one) conclude that the decay is forbidden: the Landau-Yang theorem.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The photon along $+\hat z$ has $J_z = \lambda_1$ and the one along $-\hat z$ has $J_z = -\lambda_2$, so $J_z = \lambda_1 - \lambda_2 \in \{-2, 0, 2\}$ (@thm-sr-wigner-classification: helicities are $\pm1$, never $0$). A spin-one
particle has $|J_z| \leq 1$, so only $J_z = 0$ remains, which the exchange symmetry of the two photons excludes for total angular momentum one. Hence a
massive vector particle cannot decay into two photons, while a spin-zero one, such as the Higgs boson of @exm-sr-two-photons, can.
:::
